93	
94	## **2.5.1   |   Post-Fire Reproductive Trajectories**
95	
96	To analyse post-fire reproductive trajectories, we evaluated generalised additive mixed models (GAMMs) of TSF, herbivory and mean annual rainfall as a priori predictors of each of three population-level reproductive attributes: flowering rate (% individuals flowering), mean number of flowers per plant and mean number of closed cones per plant (for the three serotinous species only). Population-level attributes were calculated from all individuals surveyed, including resprouting and young (nonreproductive) plants, where present. We employed a model selection approach whereby we constructed a set of plausible models from subsets of the a priori predictors and compared these using Akaike's Information Criterion corrected for small sample size (AICc) and AICc model weights (ωAICc) which represent the probability or weight of evidence for each model (Burnham, Anderson, and Huyvaert [2011](#page-17-13); Hurvich and Tsai [1989\)](#page-19-25). Models with ΔAICc <5 generally represented a cumulative ωAICc of ≥0.95 and therefore are presented here as part of the 95% confidence set, following Symonds and Moussalli ([2011\)](#page-20-11). Models with ΔAICc<2 are considered to have substantial support (Burnham and Anderson [2002\)](#page-17-14). We conducted this analysis in *R* (version 4.0.3) (R Core Team [2020\)](#page-19-26) using the *FSSgam* package (Fisher et al. [2018\)](#page-18-23) which enables an all subsets approach and uses the *gam()* function from the *mgcv* package (Wood [2017\)](#page-20-12).
97	
98	Flowering rate, presented as proportions, was modelled using a binomial error distribution (logit link function) with data weighted by the number of individuals recorded per site. Mean number of flowers and cones per plant were modelled using a tweedie error distribution (log link function) to account for many zero values (i.e., non-flowering/non-fruiting individuals). TSF was logtransformed for analysis as responses are expected to change most rapidly in the first few years after fire, and to optimise the distribution of values across the predictor range. TSF was included as a continuous smoother in the model set to allow for non-linear relationships with time. In all models, the smoothing parameter was limited to a simple spline (k=3) to avoid overfitting. Mean annual rainfall was included as a linear predictor in all models, and any effects were presented as predictions at the 10th and 90th percentile of mean annual rainfall across the TSF chronosequence, representing post-fire reproductive trajectories for 'low' (~720mm) and 'high' (~790mm) rainfall sites, respectively.
99	
100	Herbivory was included as a two-level factor variable (absence or presence of kangaroo herbivores) in model sets for shrub species only (i.e., excluding *B. attenuata* and *B. prionotes*) as we lacked a strong a priori expectation of the effects of herbivory from kangaroos (generally <2m tall) on tree species that are typically >4m
101	
102	tall at maturity. A two-way interaction between log-transformed TSF and herbivory was included in the model set for *G. tomentosum* only to explore if effects of herbivory varied by TSF. Replication of different herbivory levels across the range of log-transformed TSF was not considered to be adequate for the other shrub species and therefore was only included as an additive effect in other model sets. An identifier for the year of survey was included as a random smoother in all models for species where measurements were recorded in two successive years to account for repeat measures and any annual variation in environmental conditions (e.g., rainfall) other than an increase in TSF by 1year.
103	
104	Modelling of flowering rate and flower counts was conducted separately for male and female plants of the dioecious species *A. humilis*. Top-ranking model comparisons are presented for models on female data only. Only female plants produce cones and seeds and so modelling of cone counts was necessarily restricted to female plant data. Juvenile period was calculated from the flowering rate of female plants. The sex ratio was, on average, 45% females and 55% males across all populations (excluding non-reproductive individuals), or 49% females and 51% males after the post-fire maturation period (i.e., after 4years) (Figure [S2\)](#page-20-8).
105	
106	#### **2.5.2**|**Time Since Fire as a Predictor of Reproduction**
107	
108	To assess the strength of TSF as a predictor of reproduction, we compared GAMMs with single predictors of either TSF or plant size (height, canopy volume or effective DBH) for each of the three reproductive attributes measured. Models using plant size as the predictor represent the mechanistic relationship between TSF and reproduction, where the growth of plants following fire enables greater access to resources and an increase in reproductive output. For single-cohort populations (i.e., fire-killed species), we would expect that models using single predictors of TSF and plant size would explain similar amounts of variation (i.e., *R*2 ) and have a similar weight of evidence (i.e., AICc and ωAICc). However, for multi-cohort populations (usually resprouters, but also possible for some fire-killed species), we would expect that models using size would explain much more variation and have a much greater weight of evidence than models using TSF.
109	
110	GAMMs were constructed as outlined above, where models of TSF or size alone were compared using *FSSgam*. Size measurements (height, canopy volume, effective DBH) were log-transformed to optimise the distribution of values across the predictor range and improve model fit. For the dioecious species (*A. humilis*), modelling was conducted separately for male and female plants, with top-ranking model comparisons presented for female data only.
111	
112	#### **3   |   Results**
113	
114	## **3.1   |   Flowering Rates and Juvenile Periods**
115	
116	TSF consistently appeared in top-ranked models of flowering rates for all species (Table [2](#page-6-0)). Flowering rate generally increased rapidly in the first few years after fire and stabilised thereafter (Figure [2](#page-6-1)). *Acacia pulchella* was the only species with an apparent decline in flowering rate in longer unburnt sites; in sites older than 30years, predicted flowering rate fell below 50%, however,

## **RESEARCH ARTICLE [OPEN ACCESS](https://doi.org/10.1111/aec.70023)**

# **Using Patterns of Post-Fire Plant Reproduction to Inform Minimum Fire Intervals for Conservation Management in a Fire-Prone Woodland**

Russell G. Mille[r1,2](#page-0-0) | Neal J. Enrigh[t1](#page-0-0) | David J. Merritt[2,3](#page-0-1) | Ben P. Miller[2,3](#page-0-1) | Joseph B. Fontain[e1](#page-0-0)

1School of Environmental and Conservation Sciences, Murdoch University, Murdoch, Western Australia, Australia | 2Biodiversity and Conservation Science, Department of Biodiversity, Conservation and Attractions, Kings Park, Western Australia, Australia | 3School of Biological Sciences, University of Western Australia, Crawley, Western Australia, Australia

**Correspondence:** Russell G. Miller [\(russell.miller@dbca.wa.gov.au\)](mailto:russell.miller@dbca.wa.gov.au)

**Received:** 19 May 2024 | **Revised:** 17 December 2024 | **Accepted:** 19 December 2024

**Funding:** This work was supported by an Australian Research Council Linkage grant (LP160100996) to NJE, JBF, and BPM.

**Keywords:** fire interval | fire management | generalised additive modelling | immaturity risk | juvenile period | seedling regeneration | southwestern Australia

#### **ABSTRACT**

The time interval between fires is a critical component of the fire regime that affects plant species persistence in fire-prone ecosystems. Fire intervals that are too short or too long may not support regeneration from seed banks or resprouting. Fire intervals that support adequate regeneration may also vary with other factors such as climate, herbivory, and population structure. Using field data on flowering and canopy seed banks, we modelled post-fire reproduction for woody fire-killed (obligate seeding) and resprouting species under varying rainfall and herbivory along a 35-year fire age chronosequence in Banksia woodlands in southwestern Australia. We found that fire-killed species attained reproductive maturity rapidly after fire with predicted juvenile periods (time to 50% flowering) of 1.5–2.3years for shrubs and 4 years for trees. Resprouting species had similar juvenile periods to fire-killed species (1–3.5 years for resprouting shrubs, 4.4 years for resprouting trees). Reproduction varied with rainfall and herbivory with juvenile periods at least doubling under low rainfall or high herbivory for some species. Serotinous species produced cones (woody fruits containing seeds) shortly after flowering commenced, with some evidence of seed bank decline in the oldest sites. While reproduction was clearly correlated with time since fire, plant size was a much stronger predictor. Some species form multi-cohort populations which can introduce large variation into post-fire reproductive trajectories, and this should be considered when making decisions about fire intervals that may impact species persistence. This study provides critical information to assess fire interval-related threats for Banksia woodlands and suggests that woody species of these woodlands are generally tolerant of a wide range of fire intervals. Only the slowest-maturing, fire-killed species (*Banksia prionotes*, Proteaceae) may require fire intervals >10 years to reduce immaturity risk under the least favourable growing conditions, and this species often occurs in discrete patches in the landscape such that fire management can be tailored accordingly.

#### **1   |   Introduction**

Fire is a dominant ecological disturbance that has long shaped terrestrial ecosystems and driven plant species evolution globally (Bond, Woodward, and Midgley [2005](#page-17-0); He and Lamont [2018;](#page-19-0) Keeley et al. [2011;](#page-19-1) Lamont [2022](#page-19-2)). Over evolutionary time periods, fire regimes (fire interval, severity, season and type at a point, which form spatial patterns at landscape scales) *sensu* (Gill [1981\)](#page-18-0) have driven the development of a diversity of plant traits and life history strategies that allow populations to persist

=== p2
in fire-prone landscapes (Harrison et al. [2021;](#page-19-3) Schwilk and Ackerly [2001](#page-20-0)). However, with ongoing climate change, fire is projected to occur with greater frequency and intensity in many regions (Jones et al. [2022](#page-19-4)), thereby imposing altered fire regimes on biota which may threaten their persistence (Bowman et al. [2014;](#page-17-1) Enright et al. [2015](#page-18-1); Le Breton et al. [2022](#page-19-5)). Fire intervals, in particular, are considered to have a strong influence on species persistence, especially in ecosystems characterised by high severity or stand-replacing fire regimes (Bowman et al. [2014;](#page-17-1) Enright et al. [2015;](#page-18-1) Gallagher et al. [2021\)](#page-18-2). Land management agencies tasked with conserving fire-prone ecosystems often include minimum fire-free intervals in their planning to maximise species persistence (Bradstock and Kenny [2003;](#page-17-2) Burrows and McCaw [2013](#page-17-3)).

Plant species which inhabit fire-prone environments are generally characterised as one of two major fire response types: (1) fire-killed (or obligate seeders), which are killed by complete canopy scorch and rely on soil or canopy-stored seeds for post-fire recovery; and (2) resprouters, which primarily survive fire and regrow from buds protected from the heat of fire, but can often also recruit new individuals from seed (Clarke et al. [2015;](#page-18-3) Pausas and Keeley [2014](#page-19-6)). Plants of both types face two key threats in relation to fire interval: immaturity risk and senescence risk. Immaturity risk occurs when intervals between lethal fires are shorter than the time required to reach reproductive maturity, establish a seed bank and/or develop resprouting capacity (Keeley, Ne'eman, and Fotheringham [1999\)](#page-19-7), whereas senescence risk occurs when fire intervals exceed the lifespan of mature plants and their seed bank or stock of live buds (Enright et al. [2011](#page-18-4); Gosper, Prober, and Yates [2013\)](#page-18-5). Tolerable fire intervals, defined by minimum and maximum inter-fire periods that avoid species loss through immaturity and senescence risk respectively, are widely used in planning fire management with conservation objectives (Gosper et al. [2022\)](#page-18-6). Immaturity risk and shortened fire intervals arguably pose the greatest risk to species persistence, with fire-killed species particularly vulnerable to decline or local extinction if they are slow maturing and require an ample fire-free period to flower and produce seeds (Bowman et al. [2014;](#page-17-1) Enright et al. [2014\)](#page-18-7). Resprouters, while generally considered to be more resilient to short fire intervals, may be vulnerable to unusually short intervals due to the depletion of resources required for resprouting and reduced recruitment probability from seed (Enright et al. [2014](#page-18-7), [2011;](#page-18-4) Fairman, Nitschke, and Bennett [2016\)](#page-18-8).

Defining potential immaturity or senescence risks in a population or species is often achieved using demographic or reproductive information such as the timing of post-fire reproductive maturity, long-term trajectories of reproductive output and adult lifespans (Enright, Lamont, and Marsula [1996;](#page-18-9) Gosper, Prober, and Yates [2013](#page-18-5); Kraaij et al. [2013](#page-19-8)). The juvenile period approach for quantifying post-fire reproductive maturity and estimating minimum tolerable fire intervals originates from a concept by Gill and Nicholls ([1989\)](#page-18-10) and has been applied to a variety of woody plant species in Australia and South Africa (Gill and McMahon [1986](#page-18-11); Gosper et al. [2022;](#page-18-6) Harvey et al. [2017;](#page-19-9) Kraaij et al. [2013;](#page-19-8) McCaw [2008;](#page-19-10) Muir, Vesk, and Hepworth [2014](#page-19-11)). The juvenile period can be defined in a number of ways, including the time to first flowering or fruiting after fire in the most

precocious individual, or the time to flowering or fruiting in a certain portion of the population, often 50% (Gosper et al. [2022;](#page-18-6) Kraaij et al. [2013\)](#page-19-8). While the first signs of reproduction may indicate the minimum time to maturity, several years of flowering and subsequent successful seed set may be required to accumulate a seed bank large enough for population replacement after fire, particularly for fire-killed species (Burrows, Wardell-Johnson, and Ward [2008;](#page-17-4) Burrows and Wardell-Johnson [2003\)](#page-17-5). A suggested rule of thumb, therefore, is that a fire interval equal to two times (or three times for particularly sensitive species) the juvenile period is the minimum period required for population persistence under average growing conditions (e.g., average post-fire rainfall) (Burrows and Wardell-Johnson [2003;](#page-17-5) Gill and Nicholls [1989](#page-18-10)). A rule of thumb applied in South African shrublands is that at least half a population must have flowered at least three times (Kraaij et al. [2013\)](#page-19-8). The juvenile period approach is specifically designed for fire-killed species where there is no persistence via resprouting, all individuals are normally killed by fire (i.e., fire is not patchy), there is little or no inter-fire seedling recruitment and seed banks are exhausted by fire (i.e., no residual seed bank) (Bell [2001\)](#page-17-6). While this approach is supported by a few single- or multi-species studies on post-fire maturation rates (Burrows and Wardell-Johnson [2003](#page-17-5); Treurnicht et al. [2016\)](#page-20-1), it was only originally intended to provide guidance until more detailed assessments were available (Gill and Nicholls [1989](#page-18-10)), and there has been little critical evaluation of whether the 2×rule of thumb is appropriate across a wide range of species.

Maximum tolerable fire intervals are not commonly defined, but can be identified from adult longevity (e.g., evidence of senescence) or a decline in reproductive output in the long absence of fire, where there is little or no inter-fire seedling recruitment to maintain populations in the absence of fire (Bond [1980](#page-17-7); Gosper, Prober, and Yates [2013](#page-18-5)). Maximum tolerable intervals for resprouters probably even precede adult senescence as the stock of live buds required for resprouting declines with plant age such that plants approaching the end of their lifespan have decreasing probability of survival through fire (Enright et al. [2011\)](#page-18-4).

Variation in post-fire juvenile periods at least partly depends on the mode of plant regeneration (Burrows, Wardell-Johnson, and Ward [2008;](#page-17-4) Harvey et al. [2017](#page-19-9)). The juvenile period for plants regenerating from seed after fire (termed the primary juvenile period) tends to be longer than that for plants resprouting or recovering vegetatively after fire (termed the secondary juvenile period) (Bradstock and Kenny [2003](#page-17-2); Zammit and Westoby [1987\)](#page-20-2). Given that fire-killed species typically recover entirely from seed, only the primary juvenile period is relevant, whereas postfire populations of resprouting species may contain a mix of resprouting individuals and post-fire seedlings so that both primary and secondary juvenile periods can be defined. In practice, reported juvenile periods for resprouting species are generally a composite value of both primary and secondary juvenile periods, but since new recruits are often infrequent, such estimates are best regarded as estimates of the secondary juvenile period (Enright and Goldblum [1999](#page-18-12)). Estimates of the primary juvenile period for resprouter species are rare due to sample size constraints associated with low rates of recruitment, and the usually much longer times to first reproduction (Keeley, Fotheringham, and Baer-Keeley [2006;](#page-19-12) Zammit and Westoby [1987](#page-20-2)). While the juvenile period approach largely focusses on fire-killed species, as 
=== p3
these are considered to be most sensitive to fire interval impacts (Bowman et al. [2014](#page-17-1); Enright et al. [2014](#page-18-7); Harvey et al. [2017\)](#page-19-9), successful reproduction and seedling recruitment are also required for the long-term persistence of resprouting species (Enright et al. [2014\)](#page-18-7).

Despite global applicability of the juvenile period approach for assessing immaturity risk and estimating minimum tolerable fire intervals, including widespread use in some regions, including southern Australia and South Africa, there has been limited evaluation of the relationship between the onset of flowering and seed bank accumulation for different species, or of the consequences of variation in environmental conditions or population size structure for sensitivities to shortened fire intervals (Gosper et al. [2022;](#page-18-6) McCaw [2008;](#page-19-10) Treurnicht et al. [2016](#page-20-1); von Takach Dukai, Lindenmayer, and Banks [2018](#page-20-3); Wooller, Wooller, and Brown [2002\)](#page-20-4). Variation in climate, herbivory and other environmental factors which affect plant growth and population structure can alter reproductive trajectories such that a single species-level juvenile period value may over- or under-estimate the fire-free period required for different populations (Gosper et al. [2022;](#page-18-6) Kraaij et al. [2013;](#page-19-8) McCaw [2008](#page-19-10); Morgan, McCarthy, and Willocks [2021](#page-19-13)). Longer juvenile periods are often associated with low-productivity environments, including sites with low average rainfall, or low rainfall in the few years following fire (Burrows, Wardell-Johnson, and Ward [2008;](#page-17-4) McCaw [2008\)](#page-19-10). Low environmental productivity can act to delay maturation, reduce growth, flowering and seed set, and increase the seedbank required for replacement after subsequent fires (Enright et al. [2015\)](#page-18-1). High herbivore pressure may also delay or reduce flowering and seed production by reducing the size of plants and altering the resources available for reproduction, although these effects are less well documented (Brown, Paczkowska, and Gibson [2016\)](#page-17-8). While variation in reproductive attributes across sites or years will always be a confounding factor in defining tolerable fire intervals, understanding the causal relationships behind variation in reproductive trajectories is particularly important for the management of contemporary landscapes with warming and drying climates alongside ongoing fragmentation and other human disturbances.

In this study, we used field data to model post-fire reproductive trajectories across varying environmental conditions for six woody plant species in fire-prone Banksia woodlands of southwestern Australia. Increasing understanding of fire intervalrelated population dynamics offers the opportunity to manage fire regimes for species conservation. We employed a space-fortime sampling approach to quantify reproduction (flowering rate, flower counts, and cone counts per plant) in co-occurring fire-killed and resprouting species along a post-fire chronosequence of 1–35 years since the last fire and across sites with varying rainfall and herbivory. Vegetation in this region regularly experiences fire, and native species exhibit a variety of firerelated traits and adaptation syndromes which we anticipate would be reflected in varying post-fire reproductive trajectories. Objectives for risk reduction through prescribed burning (managed fire intervals) indicate fire intervals of 13–33 years (Ritchie et al. [2021](#page-19-14)). Recent data show post-fire ages ranging from 1 to 56 years since the last fire, with some areas potentially older (Tangney et al. [2022\)](#page-20-5). During the period 1970–2009, median fire intervals (prescribed burns and wildfires combined) across the northern (drier) part of our study area was 9 years with an average of 37% of area burnt attributed to wildfires (Wilson et al. [2014](#page-20-6)).

We aim to quantify post-fire juvenile periods (defined here as time to 50% flowering), estimate minimum tolerable fire intervals based on the '2 × juvenile period' rule of thumb guideline, explore whether this rule of thumb reflects sufficient flowering and canopy seed bank accumulation and quantify reproduction in the long absence of fire. We also aim to quantify reproductive patterns under varying rainfall and herbivory conditions and how this affects minimum tolerable fire interval estimates. Populations of fire-killed and resprouting species may also be multi-cohort (Hobbs and Atkins [1990\)](#page-19-15) which can complicate reproductive dynamics; therefore, we also aim to evaluate models of reproduction relative to plant size (as a surrogate for age or cohort) to investigate the causal relationship between size and reproduction and test the strength of time since fire as a predictor of reproduction commonly used to inform fire management.

#### **2   |   Methods**

## **2.1   |   Study Area**

This study was conducted in urban and peri-urban reserves in the Swan Coastal Plain bioregion of southwestern Australia. Low open Banksia woodlands are the dominant vegetation type in this region, with an estimated 50%–60% of their original extent having been cleared in recent decades for the rapid urbanisation of Western Australia's capital city of Perth (Ritchie et al. [2021\)](#page-19-14). Most remaining vegetation is restricted to a few large conservation areas on the city margins, and small urban and peri-urban reserves, but even in these areas, there is projected ongoing species loss associated with time-delayed effects of habitat loss and fragmentation (Fowler et al. [2023](#page-18-13)). In 2016, Banksia woodlands were recognised as a Threatened Ecological Community under Australia's national environmental law, and smaller portions have conservation listings at the state level (Commonwealth of Australia [2016;](#page-18-14) Ramalho et al. [2014](#page-19-16); Ritchie et al. [2021\)](#page-19-14).

Banksia woodlands are characterised by a low (4–8m height), open canopy of *Banksia* (Proteaceae) trees (predominantly the resprouters *B. attenuata* and *B. menziesii*, and fire-killed *B. prionotes*) and a species-rich understorey dominated by sclerophyllous shrubs in the plant families Dilleniaceae, Ericaceae, Fabaceae, Myrtaceae and Proteaceae (Dodd and Griffin [1989;](#page-18-15) Ritchie et al. [2021](#page-19-14)). The nutrient-poor, deep sandy soils of the Swan Coastal Plain are comprised largely of two major Pleistocene dune complexes (Bassendean and Spearwood), distinguished by their age of origin (Spearwood sands: 120k—500ka old, Bassendean sands: ~2ma old) and nutrient content (particularly nitrogen and phosphorus, declining with age) (Turner, Hayes, and Laliberté [2018](#page-20-7)). The region has a Mediterranean-type climate, with cool, wet winters and hot, dry summers, making vegetation highly fire-prone during the dry season (austral summer and autumn; December–May). Average annual precipitation ranges from approximately 800mm in the south to 550mm in the north, 80% of which falls between May and October (Tangney et al. [2022\)](#page-20-5) (Figure [S1\)](#page-20-8).
=== p4
Fire is a regular occurrence on the Swan Coastal Plain, including low-moderate severity prescribed burning for risk reduction and conservation purposes during autumn and spring periods, and high severity wildfires mostly from human-caused ignitions during the hot, dry summer period (Densmore and Clingan [2019;](#page-18-16) Enright and Fontaine [2014;](#page-18-17) Howard et al. [2020](#page-19-17); Plucinski [2014\)](#page-19-18). The proximity of urban and peri-urban Banksia woodlands to human homes and infrastructure has placed substantial attention and importance on fire management in this ecosystem. While there are no direct estimates of historical or long-term fire intervals in Banksia woodlands that might suggest lower or upper limits to their adaptations, they share attributes (e.g., key plant functional types, surface and elevated fuel types) with surrounding vegetation types, including shrublands to the north and eucalypt forests to the east and south, where typical fire intervals have been estimated at 10–40+ years (shrublands) and 5–20 years (low severity, forest) or 20–100 years (high severity, forest) (Burrows, Ward, and Robinson [1995](#page-17-9); Enright et al. [2012;](#page-18-18) Enright and Thomas [2008](#page-18-19); Murphy et al. [2013\)](#page-19-19). Indigenous use of fire was widespread in the region prior to European colonisation but specific information regarding burning in Banksia woodlands is not clear (Lullfitz et al. [2020;](#page-19-20) Rodrigues et al. [2022](#page-20-9)).

## **2.2   |   Study Species**

To explore fire interval effects on reproduction, we chose six woody plant species with a range of growth forms, fire response traits and seed bank storage modes across four common plant families (Table [1](#page-3-0)). All species are native, common and widespread in Banksia woodlands and considered indicators of the vegetation type; although varying in their abundance and distribution within the landscape (Gibson et al. [1994](#page-18-20)). Serotinous (canopy seed bank) species typically accumulate woody fruits containing seeds (hereafter cones) in the canopy over multiple years, therefore allowing assessment

of cumulative reproductive output. In the study area, the two selected *Banksia* species are known to be weakly serotinous, with most seeds released from woody fruits (hereafter cones) within 1–2 years of cone maturity (Cowling and Lamont [1985](#page-18-21)). The dioecious shrub species *Allocasuarina humilis* is moderately serotinous with female plants retaining seeds in cones for up to 5 years (personal obs.). By pairing serotinous species with species with other seed storage modes, here specifically soil seed banks, we aim to gain an insight into the response of the broader plant community.

## **2.3   |   Site Selection**

To assess varying fire intervals, we employed a space-for-time approach and selected sites with a broad range of recent fire histories (time since fire, TSF). We first interrogated fire history data for remnant vegetation in urban and peri-urban reserves across the study region to identify a set of candidate sites with a wide range of fire ages, suitable access (with permission from land managers) and appropriate vegetation type (i.e., not wetland, riparian, or limestone vegetation). Year of last fire for each site was determined from spatial data layers maintained by the Western Australian Department of Biodiversity, Conservation and Attractions (DBCA-060, <https://catalogue.data.wa.gov.au/dataset/dbca-fire-history>); historical satellite and aerial imagery (Landgate, [https://map](https://map-viewer-plus.app.landgate.wa.gov.au/index.html)[viewer-plus.app.landgate.wa.gov.au/index.html](https://map-viewer-plus.app.landgate.wa.gov.au/index.html)); and local government records. Given limitations in fire history records and satellite and aerial imagery, we were unable to confirm exact ages for some sites beyond 35 years (occurring before approximately 1986). Sites with no assignable post-fire age are referred to here as long unburnt (LUB), and for analysis are given a notional age of 35 years.

#### **2.4   |   Field Surveys**

At each site, data were collected on reproductive and size attributes for live individuals. Seedlings less than 1–2 years old in sites older than 4years since fire (inter-fire seedlings) were excluded as these individuals can have a low survival rate and therefore have little consequence for the reproductive status of populations. Data on the abundance of inter-fire seedlings from the same sites are presented in Miller, Enright, Fontaine et al. [\(2024](#page-19-23)). Seedlings were distinguished by the presence of cotyledons, lack of signs of current or past reproduction, and were generally <10–20 cm tall for shrub species or <30 cm tall for tree species. Estimates of seedling age were confirmed by observations of seedlings of known age in post-fire sites.

Data were mostly collected within plots positioned to include as many of the target species as possible and ranging in size from 25 to 150 m2 as necessary to suit different species and plant densities, and to ensure sampling of at least 30 individuals. Plant densities were calculated from the number of individuals in each plot and scaled to the number of plants per hectare. Smaller plots were used for shrub species (density range 0.1–4.6 plants m−2), and larger plots for tree species (0.03–1.58 plants m−2). At least two plots were established at each site, but where plant density was particularly low, measurements were taken based on a nearest-neighbour search until a minimum of 30 plants were recorded. For some plotbased surveys, additional nearest plants outside of plots were measured to fulfil sample size criterion. Field surveys were undertaken from 2016 to 2018 during peak flowering times for each species (Table [1\)](#page-3-0).

Measurements recorded for each individual included: (1) number of flowers (or inflorescences; all species), (2) number of mature cones with unopened follicles (canopy seed bank species only) and (3) size (all species). *Allocasuarina humilis* is a dioecious species and we identified and recorded attributes of male and female plants separately (only female plants produce cones). The number of cones recorded represents the cumulative canopy seed bank from all previous reproductive seasons excluding seed loss from seed predation, disease and spontaneous follicle opening, among other factors. Size was recorded as aboveground plant height (*Gompholobium tomentosum* and *Acacia pulchella*), canopy volume (*Hibbertia hypericoides* and *Allocasuarina humilis*) or stem diameter at breast height (DBH, 1.37m above the ground; *Banksia attenuata, B. prionotes*). These measurements were chosen to best represent how size relates to reproductive performance given each species' growth form.

#### **2.5   |   Data Analysis**

## **2.5.1   |   Post-Fire Reproductive Trajectories**

To analyse post-fire reproductive trajectories, we evaluated generalised additive mixed models (GAMMs) of TSF, herbivory and mean annual rainfall as a priori predictors of each of three population-level reproductive attributes: flowering rate (% individuals flowering), mean number of flowers per plant and mean number of closed cones per plant (for the three serotinous species only). Population-level attributes were calculated from all individuals surveyed, including resprouting and young (nonreproductive) plants, where present. We employed a model selection approach whereby we constructed a set of plausible models from subsets of the a priori predictors and compared these using Akaike's Information Criterion corrected for small sample size (AICc) and AICc model weights (ωAICc) which represent the probability or weight of evidence for each model (Burnham, Anderson, and Huyvaert [2011](#page-17-13); Hurvich and Tsai [1989\)](#page-19-25). Models with ΔAICc <5 generally represented a cumulative ωAICc of ≥0.95 and therefore are presented here as part of the 95% confidence set, following Symonds and Moussalli ([2011\)](#page-20-11). Models with ΔAICc<2 are considered to have substantial support (Burnham and Anderson [2002\)](#page-17-14). We conducted this analysis in *R* (version 4.0.3) (R Core Team [2020\)](#page-19-26) using the *FSSgam* package (Fisher et al. [2018\)](#page-18-23) which enables an all subsets approach and uses the *gam()* function from the *mgcv* package (Wood [2017\)](#page-20-12).

Flowering rate, presented as proportions, was modelled using a binomial error distribution (logit link function) with data weighted by the number of individuals recorded per site. Mean number of flowers and cones per plant were modelled using a tweedie error distribution (log link function) to account for many zero values (i.e., non-flowering/non-fruiting individuals). TSF was logtransformed for analysis as responses are expected to change most rapidly in the first few years after fire, and to optimise the distribution of values across the predictor range. TSF was included as a continuous smoother in the model set to allow for non-linear relationships with time. In all models, the smoothing parameter was limited to a simple spline (k=3) to avoid overfitting. Mean annual rainfall was included as a linear predictor in all models, and any effects were presented as predictions at the 10th and 90th percentile of mean annual rainfall across the TSF chronosequence, representing post-fire reproductive trajectories for 'low' (~720mm) and 'high' (~790mm) rainfall sites, respectively.

Herbivory was included as a two-level factor variable (absence or presence of kangaroo herbivores) in model sets for shrub species only (i.e., excluding *B. attenuata* and *B. prionotes*) as we lacked a strong a priori expectation of the effects of herbivory from kangaroos (generally <2m tall) on tree species that are typically >4m

tall at maturity. A two-way interaction between log-transformed TSF and herbivory was included in the model set for *G. tomentosum* only to explore if effects of herbivory varied by TSF. Replication of different herbivory levels across the range of log-transformed TSF was not considered to be adequate for the other shrub species and therefore was only included as an additive effect in other model sets. An identifier for the year of survey was included as a random smoother in all models for species where measurements were recorded in two successive years to account for repeat measures and any annual variation in environmental conditions (e.g., rainfall) other than an increase in TSF by 1year.

Modelling of flowering rate and flower counts was conducted separately for male and female plants of the dioecious species *A. humilis*. Top-ranking model comparisons are presented for models on female data only. Only female plants produce cones and seeds and so modelling of cone counts was necessarily restricted to female plant data. Juvenile period was calculated from the flowering rate of female plants. The sex ratio was, on average, 45% females and 55% males across all populations (excluding non-reproductive individuals), or 49% females and 51% males after the post-fire maturation period (i.e., after 4years) (Figure [S2\)](#page-20-8).

#### **2.5.2**|**Time Since Fire as a Predictor of Reproduction**

To assess the strength of TSF as a predictor of reproduction, we compared GAMMs with single predictors of either TSF or plant size (height, canopy volume or effective DBH) for each of the three reproductive attributes measured. Models using plant size as the predictor represent the mechanistic relationship between TSF and reproduction, where the growth of plants following fire enables greater access to resources and an increase in reproductive output. For single-cohort populations (i.e., fire-killed species), we would expect that models using single predictors of TSF and plant size would explain similar amounts of variation (i.e., *R*2 ) and have a similar weight of evidence (i.e., AICc and ωAICc). However, for multi-cohort populations (usually resprouters, but also possible for some fire-killed species), we would expect that models using size would explain much more variation and have a much greater weight of evidence than models using TSF.

GAMMs were constructed as outlined above, where models of TSF or size alone were compared using *FSSgam*. Size measurements (height, canopy volume, effective DBH) were log-transformed to optimise the distribution of values across the predictor range and improve model fit. For the dioecious species (*A. humilis*), modelling was conducted separately for male and female plants, with top-ranking model comparisons presented for female data only.

#### **3   |   Results**

## **3.1   |   Flowering Rates and Juvenile Periods**

High mean annual rainfall increased the juvenile period of *B. attenuata* by 5.7years (Table [4](#page-8-0)).

## **3.2   |   Flower and Cone Counts**

TSF consistently appeared in top-ranked models of mean flower count and mean cone count per plant for all species (Table [5\)](#page-8-2). Models suggested that mean flower count increased steadily with increasing TSF for most species except *A. pulchella* (Figure [4\)](#page-9-0). *Acacia pulchella* instead showed a rapid increase in flowering until around 5–8years post-fire, followed by a slight decline thereafter (Figure [4A](#page-9-0)). Similarly, female plants of *A. humilis* showed an increase in flowering until around 10–15years post-fire, followed by a slight decline thereafter (Figure [4B\)](#page-9-0). Male plants of *A. humilis* showed a steady increase in flowering with increasing TSF. The peak mean flower count occurred beyond the predicted minimum tolerable fire interval for all species (Figure [4\)](#page-9-0). At this predicted minimum tolerable fire interval, populations of all species had reached 22%–84% of their peak flower count (Table [3\)](#page-7-0).

Mean annual rainfall appeared in the top-ranked models of mean flower count for the two fire-killed shrub species (*G. tomentosum* and *A. pulchella*) (Table [5\)](#page-8-2). Models predicted that mean flower count was 61% lower in low rainfall sites (10th

percentile) compared to high rainfall sites (90th percentile) for these two species across all ages (Figure [5](#page-10-0)). Herbivory did not appear in any top-ranked models of mean flower count (Table [5\)](#page-8-2).

Populations of *A. humilis* and *B. prionotes* first produced cones 3–4 years post-fire, and mean cone count increased up until 10–15 years post-fire, after which mean cone count was highly variable, with weak evidence of decline in the longer absence of fire (Figure [6](#page-10-1)). Populations of *B. attenuata* had produced cones even in the youngest sites sampled (1–2 years post-fire), and mean cone count increased steadily with increasing TSF (Figure [6](#page-10-1)). At the time of their respective predicted minimum tolerable fire intervals, populations of all three serotinous species had reached 45%–91% of their peak cone count (Table [3\)](#page-7-0). Mean annual rainfall did not appear in any top-ranked models for cone counts of these three species (Table [5\)](#page-8-2).

Canopy seed bank density, expressed as the number of cones per hectare, showed a similar although more pronounced nonlinear pattern for *B. prionotes* (Figure [S3\)](#page-20-8). On average, seed bank density for *B. prionotes* increased rapidly post-fire up to a maximum of approximately 5500 cones per ha around 10years and declined thereafter to <1000 cones per ha after 30years. These seed bank dynamics appear to be driven primarily by changes in plant density (Figure [S4\)](#page-20-8), especially a decline in the density of reproductive intermediate-sized trees (2–10cm DBH) in older sites (Figure [S5A\)](#page-20-8), with a minor influence of a decline in reproductive output across various sizes with increasing TSF (Figure [S5B\)](#page-20-8).

lines: +*Austral Ecology*
+## **RESEARCH ARTICLE** OPEN ACCESS
+# **Using Patterns of Post-Fire Plant Reproduction to Inform Minimum Fire Intervals for Conservation Management in a Fire-Prone Woodland**
+Russell G. Miller<sup>1,2</sup> | Neal J. Enright<sup>1</sup> | David J. Merritt<sup>2,3</sup> | Ben P. Miller<sup>2,3</sup> | Joseph B. Fontaine<sup>1</sup>

+<sup>1</sup>School of Environmental and Conservation Sciences, Murdoch University, Murdoch, Western Australia, Australia | <sup>2</sup>Biodiversity and Conservation Science, Department of Biodiversity, Conservation and Attractions, Kings Park, Western Australia, Australia | <sup>3</sup>School of Biological Sciences, University of Western Australia, Crawley, Western Australia, Australia
+**Correspondence:** Russell G. Miller (russell.miller@dbca.wa.gov.au)
+**Received:** 19 May 2024 | **Revised:** 17 December 2024 | **Accepted:** 19 December 2024
+**Funding:** This work was supported by an Australian Research Council Linkage grant (LP160100996) to NJE, JBF, and BPM.
+**Keywords:** fire interval | fire management | generalised additive modelling | immaturity risk | juvenile period | seedling regeneration | southwestern Australia
+#### **ABSTRACT**

+The time interval between fires is a critical component of the fire regime that affects plant species persistence in fire-prone ecosystems. Fire intervals that are too short or too long may not support regeneration from seed banks or resprouting. Fire intervals that support adequate regeneration may also vary with other factors such as climate, herbivory, and population structure. Using field data on flowering and canopy seed banks, we modelled post-fire reproduction for woody fire-killed (obligate seeding) and resprouting species under varying rainfall and herbivory along a 35-year fire age chronosequence in Banksia woodlands in southwestern Australia. We found that fire-killed species attained reproductive maturity rapidly after fire with predicted juvenile periods (time to 50% flowering) of 1.5–2.3 years for shrubs and 4 years for trees. Resprouting species had similar juvenile periods to fire-killed species (1–3.5 years for resprouting shrubs, 4.4 years for resprouting trees). Reproduction varied with rainfall and herbivory with juvenile periods at least doubling under low rainfall or high herbivory for some species. Serotinous species produced cones (woody fruits containing seeds) shortly after flowering commenced, with some evidence of seed bank decline in the oldest sites. While reproduction was clearly correlated with time since fire, plant size was a much stronger predictor. Some species form multi-cohort populations which can introduce large variation into post-fire reproductive trajectories, and this should be considered when making decisions about fire intervals that may impact species persistence. This study provides critical information to assess fire interval-related threats for Banksia woodlands and suggests that woody species of these woodlands are generally tolerant of a wide range of fire intervals. Only the slowest-maturing, fire-killed species (*Banksia prionotes*, Proteaceae) may require fire intervals > 10 years to reduce immaturity risk under the least favourable growing conditions, and this species often occurs in discrete patches in the landscape such that fire management can be tailored accordingly.
+#### **1 | Introduction**

+Fire is a dominant ecological disturbance that has long shaped terrestrial ecosystems and driven plant species evolution globally (Bond, Woodward, and Midgley 2005; He and Lamont 2018; Keeley et al. 2011; Lamont 2022). Over evolutionary time periods, fire regimes (fire interval, severity, season and type at a point, which form spatial patterns at landscape scales) *sensu* (Gill 1981) have driven the development of a diversity of plant traits and life history strategies that allow populations to persist

+© 2025 The Author(s). *Austral Ecology* published by John Wiley & Sons Australia, Ltd on behalf of Ecological Society of Australia.
+*Austral Ecology*, 2025; 50:e70023
+https://doi.org/10.1111/aec.70023 | 1 of 21
+<!-- PAGE BREAK -->

+in fire-prone landscapes (Harrison et al. 2021; Schwilk and Ackerly 2001). However, with ongoing climate change, fire is projected to occur with greater frequency and intensity in many regions (Jones et al. 2022), thereby imposing altered fire regimes on biota which may threaten their persistence (Bowman et al. 2014; Enright et al. 2015; Le Breton et al. 2022). Fire intervals, in particular, are considered to have a strong influence on species persistence, especially in ecosystems characterised by high severity or stand-replacing fire regimes (Bowman et al. 2014; Enright et al. 2015; Gallagher et al. 2021). Land management agencies tasked with conserving fire-prone ecosystems often include minimum fire-free intervals in their planning to maximise species persistence (Bradstock and Kenny 2003; Burrows and McCaw 2013).

+Plant species which inhabit fire-prone environments are generally characterised as one of two major fire response types: (1) fire-killed (or obligate seeders), which are killed by complete canopy scorch and rely on soil or canopy-stored seeds for post-fire recovery; and (2) resprouters, which primarily survive fire and regrow from buds protected from the heat of fire, but can often also recruit new individuals from seed (Clarke et al. 2015; Pausas and Keeley 2014). Plants of both types face two key threats in relation to fire interval: immaturity risk and senescence risk. Immaturity risk occurs when intervals between lethal fires are shorter than the time required to reach reproductive maturity, establish a seed bank and/or develop resprouting capacity (Keeley, Ne'eman, and Fotheringham 1999), whereas senescence risk occurs when fire intervals exceed the lifespan of mature plants and their seed bank or stock of live buds (Enright et al. 2011; Gosper, Prober, and Yates 2013). Tolerable fire intervals, defined by minimum and maximum inter-fire periods that avoid species loss through immaturity and senescence risk respectively, are widely used in planning fire management with conservation objectives (Gosper et al. 2022). Immaturity risk and shortened fire intervals arguably pose the greatest risk to species persistence, with fire-killed species particularly vulnerable to decline or local extinction if they are slow maturing and require an ample fire-free period to flower and produce seeds (Bowman et al. 2014; Enright et al. 2014). Resprouters, while generally considered to be more resilient to short fire intervals, may be vulnerable to unusually short intervals due to the depletion of resources required for resprouting and reduced recruitment probability from seed (Enright et al. 2014, 2011; Fairman, Nitschke, and Bennett 2016).

+Defining potential immaturity or senescence risks in a population or species is often achieved using demographic or reproductive information such as the timing of post-fire reproductive maturity, long-term trajectories of reproductive output and adult lifespans (Enright, Lamont, and Marsula 1996; Gosper, Prober, and Yates 2013; Kraaij et al. 2013). The juvenile period approach for quantifying post-fire reproductive maturity and estimating minimum tolerable fire intervals originates from a concept by Gill and Nicholls (1989) and has been applied to a variety of woody plant species in Australia and South Africa (Gill and McMahon 1986; Gosper et al. 2022; Harvey et al. 2017; Kraaij et al. 2013; McCaw 2008; Muir, Vesk, and Hepworth 2014). The juvenile period can be defined in a number of ways, including the time to first flowering or fruiting after fire in the most

+precocious individual, or the time to flowering or fruiting in a certain portion of the population, often 50% (Gosper et al. 2022; Kraaij et al. 2013). While the first signs of reproduction may indicate the minimum time to maturity, several years of flowering and subsequent successful seed set may be required to accumulate a seed bank large enough for population replacement after fire, particularly for fire-killed species (Burrows, Wardell-Johnson, and Ward 2008; Burrows and Wardell-Johnson 2003). A suggested rule of thumb, therefore, is that a fire interval equal to two times (or three times for particularly sensitive species) the juvenile period is the minimum period required for population persistence under average growing conditions (e.g., average post-fire rainfall) (Burrows and Wardell-Johnson 2003; Gill and Nicholls 1989). A rule of thumb applied in South African shrublands is that at least half a population must have flowered at least three times (Kraaij et al. 2013). The juvenile period approach is specifically designed for fire-killed species where there is no persistence via resprouting, all individuals are normally killed by fire (i.e., fire is not patchy), there is little or no inter-fire seedling recruitment and seed banks are exhausted by fire (i.e., no residual seed bank) (Bell 2001). While this approach is supported by a few single- or multi-species studies on post-fire maturation rates (Burrows and Wardell-Johnson 2003; Treurnicht et al. 2016), it was only originally intended to provide guidance until more detailed assessments were available (Gill and Nicholls 1989), and there has been little critical evaluation of whether the 2× rule of thumb is appropriate across a wide range of species.

+Maximum tolerable fire intervals are not commonly defined, but can be identified from adult longevity (e.g., evidence of senescence) or a decline in reproductive output in the long absence of fire, where there is little or no inter-fire seedling recruitment to maintain populations in the absence of fire (Bond 1980; Gosper, Prober, and Yates 2013). Maximum tolerable intervals for resprouters probably even precede adult senescence as the stock of live buds required for resprouting declines with plant age such that plants approaching the end of their lifespan have decreasing probability of survival through fire (Enright et al. 2011).

+Variation in post-fire juvenile periods at least partly depends on the mode of plant regeneration (Burrows, Wardell-Johnson, and Ward 2008; Harvey et al. 2017). The juvenile period for plants regenerating from seed after fire (termed the primary juvenile period) tends to be longer than that for plants resprouting or recovering vegetatively after fire (termed the secondary juvenile period) (Bradstock and Kenny 2003; Zammit and Westoby 1987). Given that fire-killed species typically recover entirely from seed, only the primary juvenile period is relevant, whereas post-fire populations of resprouting species may contain a mix of resprouting individuals and post-fire seedlings so that both primary and secondary juvenile periods can be defined. In practice, reported juvenile periods for resprouting species are generally a composite value of both primary and secondary juvenile periods, but since new recruits are often infrequent, such estimates are best regarded as estimates of the secondary juvenile period (Enright and Goldblum 1999). Estimates of the primary juvenile period for resprouter species are rare due to sample size constraints associated with low rates of recruitment, and the usually much longer times to first reproduction (Keeley, Fotheringham, and Baer-Keeley 2006; Zammit and Westoby 1987). While the juvenile period approach largely focusses on fire-killed species, as
+2 of 21 | *Austral Ecology*, 2025
+<!-- PAGE BREAK -->

+these are considered to be most sensitive to fire interval impacts (Bowman et al. 2014; Enright et al. 2014; Harvey et al. 2017), successful reproduction and seedling recruitment are also required for the long-term persistence of resprouting species (Enright et al. 2014).

+Despite global applicability of the juvenile period approach for assessing immaturity risk and estimating minimum tolerable fire intervals, including widespread use in some regions, including southern Australia and South Africa, there has been limited evaluation of the relationship between the onset of flowering and seed bank accumulation for different species, or of the consequences of variation in environmental conditions or population size structure for sensitivities to shortened fire intervals (Gosper et al. 2022; McCaw 2008; Treurnicht et al. 2016; von Takach Dukai, Lindenmayer, and Banks 2018; Wooller, Wooller, and Brown 2002). Variation in climate, herbivory and other environmental factors which affect plant growth and population structure can alter reproductive trajectories such that a single species-level juvenile period value may over- or under-estimate the fire-free period required for different populations (Gosper et al. 2022; Kraaij et al. 2013; McCaw 2008; Morgan, McCarthy, and Willocks 2021). Longer juvenile periods are often associated with low-productivity environments, including sites with low average rainfall, or low rainfall in the few years following fire (Burrows, Wardell-Johnson, and Ward 2008; McCaw 2008). Low environmental productivity can act to delay maturation, reduce growth, flowering and seed set, and increase the seedbank required for replacement after subsequent fires (Enright et al. 2015). High herbivore pressure may also delay or reduce flowering and seed production by reducing the size of plants and altering the resources available for reproduction, although these effects are less well documented (Brown, Paczkowska, and Gibson 2016). While variation in reproductive attributes across sites or years will always be a confounding factor in defining tolerable fire intervals, understanding the causal relationships behind variation in reproductive trajectories is particularly important for the management of contemporary landscapes with warming and drying climates alongside ongoing fragmentation and other human disturbances.

+In this study, we used field data to model post-fire reproductive trajectories across varying environmental conditions for six woody plant species in fire-prone Banksia woodlands of southwestern Australia. Increasing understanding of fire interval-related population dynamics offers the opportunity to manage fire regimes for species conservation. We employed a space-for-time sampling approach to quantify reproduction (flowering rate, flower counts, and cone counts per plant) in co-occurring fire-killed and resprouting species along a post-fire chronosequence of 1–35 years since the last fire and across sites with varying rainfall and herbivory. Vegetation in this region regularly experiences fire, and native species exhibit a variety of fire-related traits and adaptation syndromes which we anticipate would be reflected in varying post-fire reproductive trajectories. Objectives for risk reduction through prescribed burning (managed fire intervals) indicate fire intervals of 13–33 years (Ritchie et al. 2021). Recent data show post-fire ages ranging from 1 to 56 years since the last fire, with some areas potentially older (Tangney et al. 2022). During the period 1970–2009, median fire intervals (prescribed burns and wildfires combined) across the northern (drier) part of our study area was 9 years with an average of 37% of area burnt attributed to wildfires (Wilson et al. 2014).

+We aim to quantify post-fire juvenile periods (defined here as time to 50% flowering), estimate minimum tolerable fire intervals based on the '2 × juvenile period' rule of thumb guideline, explore whether this rule of thumb reflects sufficient flowering and canopy seed bank accumulation and quantify reproduction in the long absence of fire. We also aim to quantify reproductive patterns under varying rainfall and herbivory conditions and how this affects minimum tolerable fire interval estimates. Populations of fire-killed and resprouting species may also be multi-cohort (Hobbs and Atkins 1990) which can complicate reproductive dynamics; therefore, we also aim to evaluate models of reproduction relative to plant size (as a surrogate for age or cohort) to investigate the causal relationship between size and reproduction and test the strength of time since fire as a predictor of reproduction commonly used to inform fire management.
+#### **2.1 | Study Area**

+This study was conducted in urban and peri-urban reserves in the Swan Coastal Plain bioregion of southwestern Australia. Low open Banksia woodlands are the dominant vegetation type in this region, with an estimated 50%–60% of their original extent having been cleared in recent decades for the rapid urbanisation of Western Australia's capital city of Perth (Ritchie et al. 2021). Most remaining vegetation is restricted to a few large conservation areas on the city margins, and small urban and peri-urban reserves, but even in these areas, there is projected ongoing species loss associated with time-delayed effects of habitat loss and fragmentation (Fowler et al. 2023). In 2016, Banksia woodlands were recognised as a Threatened Ecological Community under Australia's national environmental law, and smaller portions have conservation listings at the state level (Commonwealth of Australia 2016; Ramalho et al. 2014; Ritchie et al. 2021).

+Banksia woodlands are characterised by a low (4–8 m height), open canopy of *Banksia* (Proteaceae) trees (predominantly the resprouters *B. attenuata* and *B. menziesii*, and fire-killed *B. prionotes*) and a species-rich understorey dominated by sclerophyllous shrubs in the plant families Dilleniaceae, Ericaceae, Fabaceae, Myrtaceae and Proteaceae (Dodd and Griffin 1989; Ritchie et al. 2021). The nutrient-poor, deep sandy soils of the Swan Coastal Plain are comprised largely of two major Pleistocene dune complexes (Bassendean and Spearwood), distinguished by their age of origin (Spearwood sands: 120k—500ka old, Bassendean sands: ~2 ma old) and nutrient content (particularly nitrogen and phosphorus, declining with age) (Turner, Hayes, and Laliberté 2018). The region has a Mediterranean-type climate, with cool, wet winters and hot, dry summers, making vegetation highly fire-prone during the dry season (austral summer and autumn; December–May). Average annual precipitation ranges from approximately 800 mm in the south to 550 mm in the north, 80% of which falls between May and October (Tangney et al. 2022) (Figure S1).
+*Austral Ecology*, 2025 | 3 of 21
+<!-- PAGE BREAK -->

+Fire is a regular occurrence on the Swan Coastal Plain, including low-moderate severity prescribed burning for risk reduction and conservation purposes during autumn and spring periods, and high severity wildfires mostly from human-caused ignitions during the hot, dry summer period (Densmore and Clingan 2019; Enright and Fontaine 2014; Howard et al. 2020; Plucinski 2014). The proximity of urban and peri-urban Banksia woodlands to human homes and infrastructure has placed substantial attention and importance on fire management in this ecosystem. While there are no direct estimates of historical or long-term fire intervals in Banksia woodlands that might suggest lower or upper limits to their adaptations, they share attributes (e.g., key plant functional types, surface and elevated fuel types) with surrounding vegetation types, including shrublands to the north and eucalypt forests to the east and south, where typical fire intervals have been estimated at 10–40+ years (shrublands) and 5–20 years (low severity, forest) or 20–100 years (high severity, forest) (Burrows, Ward, and Robinson 1995; Enright et al. 2012; Enright and Thomas 2008; Murphy et al. 2013). Indigenous use of fire was widespread in the region prior to European colonisation but specific information regarding burning in Banksia woodlands is not clear (Lullfitz et al. 2020; Rodrigues et al. 2022).
+#### **2.2 | Study Species**

+To explore fire interval effects on reproduction, we chose six woody plant species with a range of growth forms, fire response traits and seed bank storage modes across four common plant families (Table 1). All species are native, common and widespread in Banksia woodlands and considered indicators of the vegetation type; although varying in their abundance and distribution within the landscape (Gibson et al. 1994). Serotinous (canopy seed bank) species typically accumulate woody fruits containing seeds (hereafter cones) in the canopy over multiple years, therefore allowing assessment of cumulative reproductive output. In the study area, the two selected *Banksia* species are known to be weakly serotinous, with most seeds released from woody fruits (hereafter cones) within 1–2 years of cone maturity (Cowling and Lamont 1985). The dioecious shrub species *Allocasuarina humilis* is moderately serotinous with female plants retaining seeds in cones for up to 5 years (personal obs.). By pairing serotinous species with species with other seed storage modes, here specifically soil seed banks, we aim to gain an insight into the response of the broader plant community.
+#### **2.3 | Site Selection**

+To assess varying fire intervals, we employed a space-for-time approach and selected sites with a broad range of recent fire histories (time since fire, TSF). We first interrogated fire history data for remnant vegetation in urban and peri-urban reserves across the study region to identify a set of candidate sites with a wide range of fire ages, suitable access (with permission from land managers) and appropriate vegetation type (i.e., not wetland, riparian, or limestone vegetation). Year of last fire for each site was determined from spatial data layers maintained by the Western Australian Department of Biodiversity, Conservation and Attractions (DBCA-060, https://catalogue.data.wa.gov.au/dataset/dbca-fire-history); historical satellite and aerial imagery (Landgate, https://map-viewer-plus.app.landgate.wa.gov.au/index.html); and local government records. Given limitations in fire history records and satellite and aerial imagery, we were unable to confirm exact ages for some sites beyond 35 years (occurring before approximately 1986). Sites with no assignable post-fire age are referred to here as long unburnt (LUB), and for analysis are given a notional age of 35 years.
+We visited candidate sites to confirm the above criteria as well as the presence of the study species and the absence of

+| Species | Growth form<sup>a</sup> | Fire response | Seed bank | N sites | Peak flowering times |
+| *Gompholobium tomentosum* (Fabaceae) | Shrub (single-stemmed; 0.3–1 m) | Fire-killed | Soil | 17 | Sept–Oct |

+| *Banksia prionotes* (Proteaceae) | Tree (up to 10 m) | Fire-killed | Canopy (weakly serotinous) | 11 | Feb |
+| *Hibbertia hypericoides* (Dilleniaceae) | Subshrub (multi-stemmed; 0.2–1 m) | Resprouter (basal) | Soil | 17 | Aug–Sept |

+human-caused soil or vegetation disturbances that could otherwise alter population attributes. This produced a total of 34 sites across a fire interval chronosequence from 1 to 35 years (or more), with each site containing one to five study species. The number of sites surveyed for each species ranged from 11 to 17, all spanning a similar post-fire chronosequence (Table 1). Some sites were surveyed over two successive years, creating two nonindependent TSF samples.

+Sites were mostly (91%) located on Spearwood sands across a 100 km north–south extent of the Swan Coastal Plain (Figure 1). Mean annual rainfall ranged from 698 mm in the north (Muchea, 1971–2000) to 843 mm in the south (Halls Head, 1971–2000; Australian Bureau of Meteorology 2020) (Figure S1). All species except *B. prionotes* were sampled across the full extent of this rainfall gradient. *Banksia prionotes* was only found across a very narrow (negligible) range (30 mm mean annual rainfall difference) in the sampled study area, but occur more broadly in the region, as do the other study species. The presence (*n* = 19) or absence (*n* = 15) of kangaroos (western grey kangaroo, *Macropus fuliginosus*) as major herbivores was assessed at each site based on sightings of individuals or their scats as well as local knowledge and records (City of Joondalup 2015; City of Nedlands 2014; Ecoscape (Australia Pty Ltd) 2008; Government of Western Australia 2000; Natural Area Consulting 2012). Where present in urban reserves, kangaroos (or signs of their presence) are easily observed, and populations often achieve high density. There was no discernible change in kangaroo abundance over the study period.
+#### **2.4 | Field Surveys**

+At each site, data were collected on reproductive and size attributes for live individuals. Seedlings less than 1–2 years old in sites older than 4 years since fire (inter-fire seedlings) were excluded as these individuals can have a low survival rate and therefore have little consequence for the reproductive status of populations. Data on the abundance of inter-fire seedlings from the same sites are presented in Miller, Enright, Fontaine et al. (2024). Seedlings were distinguished by the presence of cotyledons, lack of signs of current or past reproduction, and were generally <10–20 cm tall for shrub species or <30 cm tall for tree species. Estimates of seedling age were confirmed by observations of seedlings of known age in post-fire sites.

+Data were mostly collected within plots positioned to include as many of the target species as possible and ranging in size from 25 to 150 m<sup>2</sup> as necessary to suit different species and plant densities, and to ensure sampling of at least 30 individuals. Plant densities were calculated from the number of individuals in each plot and scaled to the number of plants per hectare. Smaller plots were used for shrub species (density range 0.1–4.6 plants m<sup>−2</sup>), and larger plots for tree species (0.03–1.58 plants m<sup>−2</sup>). At least two plots were established at each site, but where plant density was particularly low, measurements were taken based on a nearest-neighbour search until a minimum of 30 plants were recorded. For some plot-based surveys, additional nearest plants outside of plots were measured to fulfil sample size criterion. Field surveys were undertaken from 2016 to 2018 during peak flowering times for each species (Table 1).

+Measurements recorded for each individual included: (1) number of flowers (or inflorescences; all species), (2) number of mature cones with unopened follicles (canopy seed bank species only) and (3) size (all species). *Allocasuarina humilis* is a dioecious species and we identified and recorded attributes of male and female plants separately (only female plants produce cones). The number of cones recorded represents the cumulative canopy seed bank from all previous reproductive seasons excluding seed loss from seed predation, disease and spontaneous follicle opening, among other factors. Size was recorded as aboveground plant height (*Gompholobium tomentosum* and *Acacia pulchella*), canopy volume (*Hibbertia hypericoides* and *Allocasuarina humilis*) or stem diameter at breast height (DBH, 1.37 m above the ground; *Banksia attenuata, B. prionotes*). These measurements were chosen to best represent how size relates to reproductive performance given each species' growth form.

+#### **2.5 | Data Analysis**
+#### **2.5.1 | Post-Fire Reproductive Trajectories**

+To analyse post-fire reproductive trajectories, we evaluated generalised additive mixed models (GAMMs) of TSF, herbivory and mean annual rainfall as a priori predictors of each of three population-level reproductive attributes: flowering rate (% individuals flowering), mean number of flowers per plant and mean number of closed cones per plant (for the three serotinous species only). Population-level attributes were calculated from all individuals surveyed, including resprouting and young (nonreproductive) plants, where present. We employed a model selection approach whereby we constructed a set of plausible models from subsets of the a priori predictors and compared these using Akaike's Information Criterion corrected for small sample size (AICc) and AICc model weights (ωAICc) which represent the probability or weight of evidence for each model (Burnham, Anderson, and Huyvaert 2011; Hurvich and Tsai 1989). Models with ΔAICc <5 generally represented a cumulative ωAICc of ≥0.95 and therefore are presented here as part of the 95% confidence set, following Symonds and Moussalli (2011). Models with ΔAICc<2 are considered to have substantial support (Burnham and Anderson 2002). We conducted this analysis in *R* (version 4.0.3) (R Core Team 2020) using the *FSSgam* package (Fisher et al. 2018) which enables an all subsets approach and uses the *gam()* function from the *mgcv* package (Wood 2017).

+Flowering rate, presented as proportions, was modelled using a binomial error distribution (logit link function) with data weighted by the number of individuals recorded per site. Mean number of flowers and cones per plant were modelled using a tweedie error distribution (log link function) to account for many zero values (i.e., non-flowering/non-fruiting individuals). TSF was log-transformed for analysis as responses are expected to change most rapidly in the first few years after fire, and to optimise the distribution of values across the predictor range. TSF was included as a continuous smoother in the model set to allow for non-linear relationships with time. In all models, the smoothing parameter was limited to a simple spline (k=3) to avoid overfitting. Mean annual rainfall was included as a linear predictor in all models, and any effects were presented as predictions at the 10th and 90th percentile of mean annual rainfall across the TSF chronosequence, representing post-fire reproductive trajectories for 'low' (~720 mm) and 'high' (~790 mm) rainfall sites, respectively.

+Herbivory was included as a two-level factor variable (absence or presence of kangaroo herbivores) in model sets for shrub species only (i.e., excluding *B. attenuata* and *B. prionotes*) as we lacked a strong a priori expectation of the effects of herbivory from kangaroos (generally <2 m tall) on tree species that are typically >4 m tall at maturity. A two-way interaction between log-transformed TSF and herbivory was included in the model set for *G. tomentosum* only to explore if effects of herbivory varied by TSF. Replication of different herbivory levels across the range of log-transformed TSF was not considered to be adequate for the other shrub species and therefore was only included as an additive effect in other model sets. An identifier for the year of survey was included as a random smoother in all models for species where measurements were recorded in two successive years to account for repeat measures and any annual variation in environmental conditions (e.g., rainfall) other than an increase in TSF by 1 year.

+Modelling of flowering rate and flower counts was conducted separately for male and female plants of the dioecious species *A. humilis*. Top-ranking model comparisons are presented for models on female data only. Only female plants produce cones and seeds and so modelling of cone counts was necessarily restricted to female plant data. Juvenile period was calculated from the flowering rate of female plants. The sex ratio was, on average, 45% females and 55% males across all populations (excluding non-reproductive individuals), or 49% females and 51% males after the post-fire maturation period (i.e., after 4 years) (Figure S2).

+To assess the strength of TSF as a predictor of reproduction, we compared GAMMs with single predictors of either TSF or plant size (height, canopy volume or effective DBH) for each of the three reproductive attributes measured. Models using plant size as the predictor represent the mechanistic relationship between TSF and reproduction, where the growth of plants following fire enables greater access to resources and an increase in reproductive output. For single-cohort populations (i.e., fire-killed species), we would expect that models using single predictors of TSF and plant size would explain similar amounts of variation (i.e., *R*<sup>2</sup>) and have a similar weight of evidence (i.e., AICc and ωAICc). However, for multi-cohort populations (usually resprouters, but also possible for some fire-killed species), we would expect that models using size would explain much more variation and have a much greater weight of evidence than models using TSF.

+GAMMs were constructed as outlined above, where models of TSF or size alone were compared using *FSSgam*. Size measurements (height, canopy volume, effective DBH) were log-transformed to optimise the distribution of values across the predictor range and improve model fit. For the dioecious species (*A. humilis*), modelling was conducted separately for male and female plants, with top-ranking model comparisons presented for female data only.
