For *Allocasuarina humilis*, models presented are for female data only. 25 === p13 26 cones per plant for trees 40–50 cm diameter at breast height (Figure [8B\)](#page-13-0). Maximum predicted cone count for *B. prionotes* barely exceeded one cone per plant, although individuals held up to 10 cones (Figure [8B](#page-13-0)). 27 28 ### **4   |   Discussion** 29 30 ## **4.1   |   Juvenile Periods and Tolerable Fire Intervals** 31 32 The shape of post-fire reproductive trajectories provides direct evidence of fire frequencies that permit species persistence and is critical information for the conservation and management of fire-prone ecosystems globally, especially with ongoing climate and fire regime change. We modelled reproduction in six woody plant species with a variety of fire-related traits across a range of fire ages in Banksia woodlands and found juvenile periods of 1–4 years, with little difference attributable to fire response type. Minimum tolerable fire intervals under average growing conditions based on primary juvenile periods for fire-killed species and a mix of primary and secondary juvenile periods for resprouters ranged from approximately 3–8 years and 2–9 years, respectively. Although there was some evidence of decline in reproduction in the oldest sites (>30 years since the last fire), reproductive capacity was likely still adequate for post-fire seedling recruitment after these long fire intervals. Variation in juvenile periods and reproductive output across all fire ages were associated with variation in growth forms and with changes in site productivity (rainfall) and herbivory. Taken together, our observations of rapid post-fire reproductive recovery and no fatal decline in reproduction in the long absence of fire are consistent with the suggestion that Banksia woodlands are adapted to mixed-severity fire regimes including widely varying intervals, where species have the capacity to cope with short and long fire intervals (Miller, Enright, Fontaine et al. [2024\)](#page-19-23). 33 34 The species studied here, potentially representing a larger suite of Banksia woodland species with similar growth forms, fire response and seed bank storage modes, would all likely tolerate fire intervals of 10 years under average growing conditions, and the most rapidly maturing would likely tolerate intervals as short as 5 years under average growing conditions. While juvenile period data for resprouters is important for understanding effects on reproduction from seed, which is crucial for longterm population persistence, minimum tolerable fire intervals for resprouters based on the juvenile period method disregard the often-overriding contribution of resprouting to the post-fire recovery of species with this capability. Resprouters, therefore, may be able to tolerate even shorter intervals (i.e., less than 5 years) if resprouting capacity develops rapidly post-fire. However, several repeated short fire intervals (less than 5years) may preclude recruitment and erode adult resprouting capacity 35 36 **FIGURE 7**    |    Relationships between plant size and flowering rate for all six study species. Maximum canopy height (cm), canopy volume (m3, ellipsoid form) or effective DBH (cm) was used as the best representative of size given each species' typical growth form. Solid black lines represent generalised additive mixed model fits, and shaded ribbons represent 95% confidence intervals. 37 === p14 38 (Enright et al. [2011;](#page-18-4) Fairman, Nitschke, and Bennett [2016\)](#page-18-8), acting as a separate mechanism of sensitivity to short fire intervals (i.e., separate to immaturity risk). Rather than resprouters, a more appropriate focus for understanding community-level minimum tolerable fire intervals is the slowest maturing, firekilled species (*B. prionotes*). *Banksia prionotes* likely requires longer intervals of at least 8–10 years for sufficient post-fire recruitment where it occurs, especially where low rainfall delays or reduces flowering and seed production. Current managed fire interval objectives of 13–33 years for risk reduction (Ritchie et al. [2021\)](#page-19-14) should, therefore, support the persistence of the woody plant functional types studied here; however, continued regional warming and drying associated with climate change 39 40 may pose a threat of shortening wildfire intervals, consistent with the interval squeeze concept *sensu* (Enright et al. [2015](#page-18-1)). 41 42 Our juvenile period and minimum tolerable fire interval findings are consistent with evidence from the region on the same or similar species (Enright et al. [2014](#page-18-7); Wilson et al. [2014\)](#page-20-6). However, corresponding minimum fire interval recommendations (8–16 years) suggested by Wilson et al. [\(2014](#page-20-6)) are based on population-level maturity of resprouters (a combination of primary and secondary juvenile periods) which, as explained above, are not the primary focus of the juvenile period approach as they largely recover via resprouting. Instead, minimum fire intervals based on juvenile period data for fire-killed species 43 44 **FIGURE 8**    |    Relationships between (A) plant size and flower count, and (B) plant size and cone count (serotinous species only). Maximum canopy height (cm), canopy volume (m3, ellipsoid form) or effective DBH (cm) was used as the best representative of size given each species' typical growth form. Solid or dashed lines represent generalised additive mixed model fits, and shaded ribbons represent 95% confidence intervals. Relationships between plant size and flower count for *A. humilis*, a dioecious species, are presented separately for male and female plants. 45 === p15 46 presented in Wilson et al. [\(2014](#page-20-6)) are up to 8–10 years for the most sensitive, slow-maturing species, which is consistent with our findings. 47 48 Suggested minimum tolerable fire intervals for fire-killed serotinous species (including *B. prionotes*) in drier (less productive) shrublands north of our study region range from 10 to 15 years for high versus low post-fire winter rainfall years, respectively (Enright et al. [2014](#page-18-7)). As our minimum tolerable interval estimates (2–9 years) suggest, minimum tolerable fire intervals should be somewhat shorter in the more productive (higher rainfall) Banksia woodlands. Consistent with this hypothesis, our estimates of minimum tolerable fire intervals of around 3–5 years for fire-killed shrubs with soil seed banks are somewhat shorter than the equivalent 5–6 years reported in Enright et al. [\(2014\)](#page-18-7). Interestingly, however, estimates for resprouting shrubs show little difference between the two regions; resprouting shrubs with canopy seed banks showed minimum tolerable intervals of around 5–7 years and resprouting shrubs with soil seed banks showed little risk of even the shortest intervals sampled (Enright et al. [2014](#page-18-7)). Post-fire growth and maturation rates of fire-killed shrubs, which regenerate from seedlings, are strongly contingent on environmental productivity (Gosper et al. [2022\)](#page-18-6), whereas post-fire growth rates in resprouting shrubs may be less contingent on environmental conditions during the post-fire period as already-established plants draw on stored energy reserves for post-fire growth and reproduction (Clarke et al. [2013](#page-18-24)), acknowledging again that seedling recruitment is not the major form of post-fire recovery for resprouters. A strength of the analysis of Enright et al. [\(2014\)](#page-18-7) is that estimates of minimum tolerable fire intervals were based on robust, direct measures of resprouter survival and seedling recruitment, and therefore we suggest that further targeted study of seed availability and subsequent postfire seedling recruitment at various fire intervals in Banksia woodlands is warranted to confirm minimum tolerable fire intervals and further explore variation along environmental gradients. 49 50 Additional evidence is also needed to test the assumptions of the juvenile period approach for estimating minimum intervals, including whether the 2×rule of thumb (Gill and Nicholls [1989](#page-18-10)) adequately covers natural variation in (1) seed bank accumulation rates and (2) flowering, pollination and seed set for species with different traits. At our estimated minimum tolerable fire intervals, populations had reached 22%–84% of their predicted maximum flowering output, and serotinous species had produced cones over at least 3–4 years and had reached 45%–91% of their predicted maximum canopy seed bank accumulation. Variation in post-fire reproductive attributes among species potentially indicates that the efficacy of the 2×approximation of minimum tolerable fire intervals varies between species. Perhaps species with soil-stored seed banks might be more adequately covered by the 2×approximation than those with canopy seed banks, as species with soil-stored seed may possess a residual seed bank after fire (i.e., seed banks are not completely exhausted by fire) (Auld and Denham [2006](#page-17-15)) and do not have to produce a persistent woody fruit requiring resources like serotinous species (Cramer and Midgley [2009;](#page-18-25) Tonnabel et al. [2012\)](#page-20-13). Our results also demonstrate substantial variation in reproduction owing to varying environmental conditions, suggesting that, in some cases, the 2×approximation may be inadequate to account for delays in reproduction. For example, for *G. tomentosum*, the presence of herbivores and low mean annual rainfall delayed the juvenile period beyond the estimated minimum tolerable fire interval under average growing conditions. 51 52 ## **4.2   |   Post-Fire Reproduction** 53 54 Fire-killed species are generally considered to have longer primary juvenile periods than the secondary juvenile periods of cooccurring resprouters (Gosper, Prober, and Yates [2013;](#page-18-5) Harvey et al. [2017\)](#page-19-9), but we observed little difference. Similar juvenile periods for these species groups, however, do not necessarily mean that they have equivalent reproductive trajectories or would be expected to have similar fire interval responses given differences in other traits. For example, resprouters may have a much lower maximum reproductive output at peak maturity compared to co-occurring fire-killed species owing to differences in resource allocation to reproduction versus energy storage (Enright and Lamont [1989\)](#page-18-26). Also, by the onset of reproductive maturity, resprouters have likely developed a strong resprouting capacity, potentially surviving through several fires before reaching a highly reproductive stage (Enright and Lamont [1992\)](#page-18-27), although resprouting and reproductive capacity may be eroded by a series of short fire intervals (Enright et al. [2011](#page-18-4); Fairman, Nitschke, and Bennett [2016](#page-18-8)). In contrast, fire-killed species may require several years after reaching reproductive maturity to develop adequate reproductive capacity for recovery after subsequent fires and therefore could be at risk of decline at the same intervals at which resprouters can readily resprout. There is an obvious advantage for fire-killed species in fire-prone habitats to reach maximum reproductive capacity as quickly as possible, and probably soon after the onset of reproduction, as indicated by our juvenile period data. 55 56 For the fire-killed species with the longest juvenile period studied here (*B. prionotes*), some plants produced cones following the first year of flowering (4 years post-fire), and the corresponding estimated minimum tolerable fire interval (8years) allowed populations to reach, on average, 56% of their maximum flower production and 91% of their maximum canopy seed bank size. For a related, fire-killed *Banksia* species, Enright, Lamont, and Marsula [\(1996](#page-18-9)) similarly showed that plants began producing cones after the first year of flowering and produced an increasing number of cones in the following few years. Despite being the slowest-maturing, fire-killed species in this study, and probably in Banksia woodlands generally, *B. prionotes* appears to have a relatively short juvenile period compared to other fire-killed species in southwestern Australia (Gosper et al. [2022](#page-18-6); Harvey et al. [2017](#page-19-9); Wooller, Wooller, and Brown [2002\)](#page-20-4). Populations of *B. prionotes* also often occur in discrete stands such that a conservative minimum interval of 10 years, under average growing conditions, may not necessarily be relevant to apply to the entire landscape, or where fires are sufficiently patchy or of low severity to allow established individuals to survive fire (Burrows and Middleton [2016](#page-17-16)). Intervals less than 10years are relatively rare on the Swan Coastal Plain, especially in areas with managed fire regimes, although changing climate regimes and increasing human disturbance do not necessarily preclude such intervals (Fontaine [2022\)](#page-18-28). 57 === p16 58 Our findings are consistent with previous efforts from the region in quantifying post-fire seed production in the resprouting *B. attenuata* in showing that mature trees are capable of producing cones in the first year or two after fire because they can resprout epicormically (Densmore and Clingan [2019;](#page-18-16) Valentine et al. [2014](#page-20-14)). Post-fire cone production is mediated by fire severity, where there are minimal interruptions to reproduction after low severity fire, but trees may take several years to regain the same level of cone production after high severity fire (Densmore and Clingan [2019](#page-18-16)). By the time of the species-specific minimum tolerable fire interval estimated here (~9 years), Valentine et al. [\(2014](#page-20-14)) estimated that mature adults (>2m tall) had accumulated, on average, approximately 6 cones per plant, which is higher than estimates presented here (~1 cone per plant). Our dataset includes smaller juvenile plants and a subset of our data on *B. attenuata* trees >2m tall shows cone counts across a similar range of values to Valentine et al. [\(2014\)](#page-20-14). Johnston, Stock, and Mawson [\(2016](#page-19-27)) and Densmore and Clingan [\(2019](#page-18-16)) report around 1.3 and 7 times higher estimates of *B. attenuata* mean canopy seed bank density (cones per ha), respectively, than we find here (mean 746 cones per ha; Figure [S3\)](#page-20-8). However, Johnston, Stock, and Mawson [\(2016\)](#page-19-27) included higher rainfall sites on the Swan Coastal Plain and Densmore and Clingan [\(2019](#page-18-16)) reported on the entire crop of cones for ease of recording regardless of whether they had closed follicles or not, where, in both cases, it would be reasonable to expect higher canopy seed bank estimates. Interestingly, the much higher estimates of cones per ha reported by Densmore and Clingan [\(2019\)](#page-18-16) can be explained by the weakly serotinous nature of *B. attenuata* in the region (Cowling and Lamont [1985](#page-18-21)), where most seeds are released from cones within two years of seed maturity, but opened cones are likely retained on the plant for many years, and could therefore give the impression of a much larger canopy seed bank. Johnston, Stock, and Mawson [\(2016](#page-19-27)) reported a similar trend of gradually increasing seed bank size with increasing time since fire for *B. attenuata* and a similar range of values for cones per ha for *B. prionotes*. 59 60 We show that plants of fire-killed shrubs that regenerate via seed following fire gain reproductive capacity quickly. Likewise, Monk, Pate, and Loneragan [\(1981](#page-19-28)) observed that the fire-killed *A. pulchella* began producing flowers and seeds in the second year after fire, and achieved maximum seed production shortly thereafter (3–4 years post-fire). These observations differ from those for fire-killed Proteaceae shrubs from southeastern Australia where cone and seed production was not observed for a few years after first flowering, and was slower overall (Jenkins, Morrison, and Auld [2010](#page-19-29)). For fast-growing species such as *A. pulchella*, a doubling of the juvenile period as a general rule of thumb for estimating the minimum tolerable fire interval may be adequate to sustain populations under average growing conditions, even if this only allows for one or two additional years of seed production. Rapid post-fire reproductive maturity and abundant seed production are important mechanisms to cope with short fire intervals for species adapted to frequent canopy scorch, whether that be understorey shrubs scorched in all but the lowest severity fires, or trees burnt in crown fire regimes (Enright, Lamont, and Marsula [1996;](#page-18-9) Gauthier, Bergeron, and Simon [1996\)](#page-18-29). Likewise, soil-stored seed banks, variable seed dormancy and residual seedbanks are traits that allow species to cope with short fire intervals. Banksia woodlands may be adapted to mixed severity fire regimes where understorey and overstorey components experience a range of low, moderate and high severity fire at widely varying intervals, potentially as short as 5–10 years in the understorey (Hobbs and Atkins [1990](#page-19-15); Miller, Enright, Fontaine et al. [2024\)](#page-19-23). 61 62 Our findings for the resprouting shrub *A. humilis* are consistent with expectations for dioecious species in that patterns of postfire flowering appear to be driven by the costs of male versus female reproduction (Barrett and Hough [2012;](#page-17-17) Obeso [2002\)](#page-19-30). Flower and pollen production in male plants is less costly than flower, cone and seed production in female plants and so we would expect to observe precocious male flowering (Field, Pickup, and Barrett [2013](#page-18-30)). In comparison to female plants, male *A. humilis* plants had a shorter juvenile period (2.5 vs. 3.5years on average), produced more flowers per plant on average across all fire ages (927 vs. 269) and produced more flowers on average at any given plant size. 63 64 Wilson et al. [\(2014\)](#page-20-6) provided an estimate of 40 years for the maximum tolerable fire interval for Banksia woodlands based on the maximum longevity of serotinous, fire-killed *Banksia* species. However, *Banksia* longevity was derived for a different species (*B. hookeriana*) from a nearby region with different climate and fire regimes, and for a species that grows as a tall shrub rather than a tree, and therefore presumably has a shorter lifespan (Cowling and Lamont [1985\)](#page-18-21). We expect *Banksia* tree longevity in the range of 40–60 years for *B. prionotes* (fire-killed) and to exceed 100 years for *B. attenuata* (resprouter). Over the approximately 35-year chronosequence studied here, we found no evidence of decline in reproduction for *B. attenuata*, but some evidence for a minor decline in reproduction in *B. prionotes* which appears primarily driven by a decline in plant density of mature stages with a minor contribution from a decline in reproductive output per plant. Although *B. prionotes* can have low levels of inter-fire seedling recruitment (Miller, Enright, Fontaine et al. [2024\)](#page-19-23), this input of non-reproductive individuals does not appear to have a noticeable effect on population-level reproduction (Figure [S5\)](#page-20-8). There is little evidence of major population senescence in *B. prionotes*, and therefore, maximum tolerable intervals are likely to exceed 40years, which are very rare regardless (Wilson et al. [2014](#page-20-6)). 65 66 #### **4.3   |   Reproduction Under Varying Environmental and Demographic Conditions** 67 68 Environmental productivity (mean annual rainfall) and the presence or absence of herbivory were found to be important factors associated with post-fire reproductive trajectories (Burrows, Wardell-Johnson, and Ward [2008;](#page-17-4) Gosper et al. [2022;](#page-18-6) McCaw [2008\)](#page-19-10). In sites with low mean rainfall (low productivity) or herbivore presence, predicted juvenile periods were delayed by up to 3 years, and therefore minimum tolerable fire intervals by up to 6 years for fire-killed understorey shrubs (*A. pulchella* and *G. tomentosum*). Low mean rainfall also decreased flower production by up to 61% for the same species. For short-lived species, this may represent a doubling (or more) of the minimum fire-free period required for population replacement, and potentially a reduction in lifetime reproductive output. 69 === p17 70 While these data pertain to mean rainfall and the prevailing presence or absence of herbivores, our results suggest that delayed reproductive maturity and reduced reproductive output could occur under abrupt environmental changes such as the introduction of native or non-native herbivores, or the increasing severity of drought conditions associated with climate change (Gosper et al. [2022;](#page-18-6) Matusick et al. [2018\)](#page-19-31). Modelling suggests that primary juvenile periods for serotinous obligate seeders (here represented by *B. prionotes*) could more than double in the study area under 2050 climate change scenarios, including lower mean annual rainfall (Gosper et al. [2022\)](#page-18-6), potentially requiring longer fire intervals to conserve vulnerable populations. In general, we sampled across a relatively narrow mean annual rainfall gradient (~150mm difference) compared to the variation present in the broader region, and in particular, our sampling of *B. prionotes* populations occurred across a very narrow range (30mm difference). It is not surprising, therefore, that we did not detect an effect of rainfall for *B. prionotes*; however, if sampling was repeated across a wider rainfall gradient (spatial or temporal), we would expect to detect slower maturity rates under low rainfall. This is a broad concern for fire-killed species which rely on post-fire recruitment from seeds for persistence, and is consistent with the concept of 'interval squeeze' where populations are vulnerable to decline with the simultaneous shortening of fire intervals and reduced seed production and post-fire recruitment associated with climate change impacts (Enright et al. [2015\)](#page-18-1). Invasive grassy weeds are also a significant threat in Banksia woodlands (Ritchie et al. [2021\)](#page-19-14), and may pose an additional limitation on population recovery if weeds reduce post-fire seedling recruitment or delay maturation and reproductive maturity. 71 72 The effects of varying mean annual rainfall on flowering rate (juvenile period) provided a curious result for *B. attenuata*, where populations in high mean rainfall sites appeared to mature more slowly than populations in low mean rainfall sites. Rather than higher rainfall delaying maturation, we believe this relates to differences in the demographic structure of populations under varying rainfall regimes altering population-level calculations. In the study area, higher rainfall and longer growing seasons likely facilitate higher rates of inter-fire seedling recruitment (Miller, Enright, Fontaine et al. [2024\)](#page-19-23), although not to a level that would result in densification or canopy closure that would, in turn, preclude recruitment of shade-intolerant seedlings and probably reduce reproductive output. Flowering rates reported here are a composite of reproduction (or lack thereof) in seedlings, juveniles and adults, and therefore a higher proportion of non-reproductive seedlings and juveniles resulting from higher recruitment will lower flowering rate estimates. 73 74 Canopy seed banks (closed cone counts per plant) for both *Banksia* species were very low, with *B. attenuata* generally having less than two seed-bearing cones per plant on average, and *B. prionotes* generally less than one. Low cone counts can be explained by a combination of the weakly serotinous nature of these *Banksia* species in the study area, and demographic structures with a high proportion of juvenile plants with little to no reproduction (Figures [S5](#page-20-8) and [S6](#page-20-8)). Cowling and Lamont [\(1985](#page-18-21)) reported a gradient in the degree of serotiny of *Banksia* species in the region with populations in our study area being weakly or non-serotinous, meaning that the majority of the accumulated canopy seed bank originates from the most recent seed crop minus any losses from 75 76 disease and predation. Whelan and Ayre [\(2020\)](#page-20-15) likewise reported very low canopy seed bank accumulation for a serotinous *Banksia* shrub species from southeastern Australia. Both weakly serotinous *Banksia* species studied here develop multi-cohort populations, especially in the absence of fire (Hobbs and Atkins [1990;](#page-19-15) Miller, Enright, Fontaine et al. [2024](#page-19-23)). Like the effect of rainfall on *B. attenuata* flowering rate noted above, a high proportion of non-reproductive juvenile plants lowers population-level seed bank size estimates which likely underestimates the reproductive potential of mature individuals. While mature individuals have the potential to contribute much larger seed banks, weak serotiny will ultimately limit the maximum size of the canopy seed bank. This contrasts with the seed bank dynamics of highly serotinous *Banksia* species in ecosystems with more regular crown fire regimes where canopy seed banks can accumulate over many years (Enright, Lamont, and Marsula [1996\)](#page-18-9). 77 78 Top-ranked models explained up to 92% of variation in the data (mean=43%, inter-quartile range=30%–51%; Table [2,](#page-6-0) Table [5\)](#page-8-2), leaving, in some cases, substantial variation unexplained by the variables considered in this study. More detailed analyses of the effects of interannual weather variation and spatially varying site variables (e.g., soil type, aspect, elevation) could explain greater variation in the data and provide a deeper understanding of the drivers of reproduction. The analysis presented here using mean annual rainfall could also be extended to quantify the effects of varying rainfall at different demographic stages—for example, during seedling establishment (1–2years post-fire), floral initiation and fruit development—to assess the sensitivity of post-fire reproduction to extreme dry climate conditions. Such analyses could help predict scenarios or sites under which fire managers may need to consider longer managed fire intervals to accommodate delayed juvenile periods under increasingly common droughts and heatwave events (Matusick et al. [2018;](#page-19-31) Ruthrof et al. [2021\)](#page-20-16). 79 80 #### **4.4   |   Time Since Fire Versus Size as a Predictor of Reproduction** 81 82 While we found that TSF was a clear indicator of reproduction, we also show that plant size is a much stronger predictor of reproductive capacity as also reported elsewhere by Andrus et al. [\(2020\)](#page-17-18), Gauthier, Bergeron, and Simon [\(1993](#page-18-31)) and von Takach Dukai, Lindenmayer, and Banks [\(2018\)](#page-20-3). Many plant species that inhabit fire-prone environments (especially fire-killed species in stand-replacing fire regimes) are often assumed to follow a specific post-fire trajectory where a single, post-fire seedling cohort matures and grows larger at a similar rate (Gill and McMahon [1986](#page-18-11)). However, this assumption may weaken in noncrown fire regimes, or for multi-cohort populations resulting from inter-fire recruitment, post-fire resprouting, or both. Interfire recruitment is evident for most of the species studied here (Hobbs and Atkins [1990](#page-19-15); Miller, Enright, Fontaine et al. [2024\)](#page-19-23), and therefore, population-level metrics of reproduction may be more closely related to varying demographic structure or environmental conditions rather than TSF. 83 84 We acknowledge TSF and post-fire juvenile periods as simplistic yet useful indicators of post-fire reproductive maturity, but here we show that the effects of other environmental and demographic conditions can introduce substantial variation into species 85 === p18 86 responses, and therefore are important to consider when making decisions about fire intervals that may impact species persistence (Gosper et al. [2022](#page-18-6)). As originally recognised, the juvenile period approach for estimating minimum tolerable fire intervals can provide rapid and low-cost guidance for fire management planning, but advances in ecological understanding and technology for measuring vegetation attributes should allow for the development of more sophisticated models for predicting variation in reproduction by including multiple environmental and demographic variables. Other metrics of species reproductive maturity and minimum tolerable fire intervals that may provide useful alternative or supplemental information for fire managers include the assessment of (1) the reproductive output (and density) of the largest individuals as the plants that contribute most to the reproductive capacity of the population and (2) average understorey plant height and litter cover as surrogates of plant growth and fuel accumulation. Ongoing advances in the mapping of vegetation structure from remote sensing data (e.g., through airborne or terrestrial laser scanning) (Moudrý et al. [2023;](#page-19-32) Turner et al. [2023](#page-20-17)) may provide an opportunity to measure plant size and density across large areas and combine with environmental and demographic data, such as that presented in this study, to calculate metrics of reproduction at a similar landscape scale to traditional fire age mapping currently used extensively in fire management planning. 87 88 #### **Author Contributions** 89 90 **Russell G. Miller:** conceptualization, data curation, formal analysis, investigation, methodology, visualization, writing – original draft, writing – review and editing. **Joseph B. Fontaine:** conceptualization, formal analysis, funding acquisition, investigation, methodology, visualization, writing – review and editing. **Ben P. Miller:** conceptualization, formal analysis, funding acquisition, investigation, methodology, visualization, writing – review and editing. **Neal J. Enright:** conceptualization, formal analysis, funding acquisition, investigation, methodology, visualization, writing – review and editing. **David J. Merritt:** conceptualization, formal analysis, investigation, methodology, visualization, writing – review and editing. 91 92 #### **Acknowledgements** 93 94 We thank the undergraduate students who assisted with field data collection. We acknowledge the Whadjuk and Pindjarup Noongar peoples as the Traditional Owners of the land on which this work was conducted, and their continuing connection to land, sea, and community. We pay our respects to them, their culture and their elders past and present. Open access publishing facilitated by Murdoch University, as part of the Wiley - Murdoch University agreement via the Council of Australian University Librarians. 95 96 #### **Conflicts of Interest** 97

=== p11 Canopy seed bank density for *B. attenuata* followed a similar trend to cones per plant, showing an increase from an average of around 500–600 cones per ha in the first five years after fire to an average of around 800–1000 cones per ha in sites older than 20years (Figure [S3](#page-20-8)). In contrast to *B. prionotes*, seed bank dynamics for the resprouter *B. attenuata* appear to be driven primarily by an increase in individual reproductive output (cones per plant) with increasing TSF (especially in the most productive, largest (>8cm DBH) trees; Figure [S6B](#page-20-8)), rather than any changes in tree density of this reproductive cohort (Figures [S4](#page-20-8) and [S6A\)](#page-20-8). #### **3.3   |   Time Since Fire Versus Size as a Predictor of Reproduction** Models using size as a predictor of each of three reproductive attributes were almost always supported by a greater weight of evidence than those using TSF (Table [6](#page-11-0)). Models of the flowering rate of *A. humilis* showed similar support for size and TSF as the best predictor, although size was still ranked higher than TSF based on AICc (Table [6\)](#page-11-0). This indicates that TSF is not a strong predictor of reproduction in comparison to the underlying mechanistic relationship between size and reproduction. In all but one case (*A. humilis* flowering rate), models using size as a predictor explained greater variation in the data (*R*2 ) than models using TSF (Table [6\)](#page-11-0). For all species, predicted flowering rate increased rapidly with an increase in size in small plants, with no evidence of a decrease in flowering rate in the largest, and presumably oldest, plants observed (Figure [7\)](#page-12-0). The predicted height at which 50% of individuals were flowering was approximately 12 cm (95% CI [9.6, 16.2]) for *G. tomentosum* and 58 cm (95% CI [54.3, 61.5]) for *A. pulchella* (Figure [7](#page-12-0)). The predicted canopy volume at 50% flowering was approximately 0.008m3 (95% CI [0.002, 0.04]) for *H. hypericoides* and 0.14m3 (95% CI [0.03, 0.40]) for *A. humilis* (approximately equivalent to a plant with dimensions of 25×25×25 cm and 65×65×65 cm, respectively; Figure [7](#page-12-0)). For the tree species, predicted DBH at 50% flowering was 3.3 cm (95% CI [1.9, 5.8]) for *B. attenuata* and 2.9 cm (95% CI [2.5, 3.3]) for *B. prionotes* (Figure [7](#page-12-0)). For *A. pulchella*, predicted flower count initially increased with size for plants up to approximately 150 cm tall, but any further increase in size (and presumably age) did not necessarily translate into higher predicted flower counts (Figure [8A\)](#page-13-0). **FIGURE 5**    |    Relationships between time (years) since fire and mean flower count per plant as a function of high (90th percentile) vs. low (10th percentile) mean annual rainfall where present in top-ranked generalised additive models (Table [5](#page-8-2)). Solid and dashed lines represent top-ranked generalised additive mixed model fits (ΔAICc=0), and shaded ribbons represent 95% confidence intervals. Maximum predicted cone count for *B. prionotes* barely exceeded one cone per plant, although individuals held up to 10 cones (Figure [8B](#page-13-0)). ### **4   |   Discussion** ## **4.1   |   Juvenile Periods and Tolerable Fire Intervals** The shape of post-fire reproductive trajectories provides direct evidence of fire frequencies that permit species persistence and is critical information for the conservation and management of fire-prone ecosystems globally, especially with ongoing climate and fire regime change. We modelled reproduction in six woody plant species with a variety of fire-related traits across a range of fire ages in Banksia woodlands and found juvenile periods of 1–4 years, with little difference attributable to fire response type. Minimum tolerable fire intervals under average growing conditions based on primary juvenile periods for fire-killed species and a mix of primary and secondary juvenile periods for resprouters ranged from approximately 3–8 years and 2–9 years, respectively. Although there was some evidence of decline in reproduction in the oldest sites (>30 years since the last fire), reproductive capacity was likely still adequate for post-fire seedling recruitment after these long fire intervals. Variation in juvenile periods and reproductive output across all fire ages were associated with variation in growth forms and with changes in site productivity (rainfall) and herbivory. Taken together, our observations of rapid post-fire reproductive recovery and no fatal decline in reproduction in the long absence of fire are consistent with the suggestion that Banksia woodlands are adapted to mixed-severity fire regimes including widely varying intervals, where species have the capacity to cope with short and long fire intervals (Miller, Enright, Fontaine et al. [2024\)](#page-19-23). The species studied here, potentially representing a larger suite of Banksia woodland species with similar growth forms, fire response and seed bank storage modes, would all likely tolerate fire intervals of 10 years under average growing conditions, and the most rapidly maturing would likely tolerate intervals as short as 5 years under average growing conditions. While juvenile period data for resprouters is important for understanding effects on reproduction from seed, which is crucial for longterm population persistence, minimum tolerable fire intervals for resprouters based on the juvenile period method disregard the often-overriding contribution of resprouting to the post-fire recovery of species with this capability. Resprouters, therefore, may be able to tolerate even shorter intervals (i.e., less than 5 years) if resprouting capacity develops rapidly post-fire. However, several repeated short fire intervals (less than 5years) may preclude recruitment and erode adult resprouting capacity **FIGURE 7**    |    Relationships between plant size and flowering rate for all six study species. Maximum canopy height (cm), canopy volume (m3, ellipsoid form) or effective DBH (cm) was used as the best representative of size given each species' typical growth form. Solid black lines represent generalised additive mixed model fits, and shaded ribbons represent 95% confidence intervals. === p14 (Enright et al. [2011;](#page-18-4) Fairman, Nitschke, and Bennett [2016\)](#page-18-8), acting as a separate mechanism of sensitivity to short fire intervals (i.e., separate to immaturity risk). Rather than resprouters, a more appropriate focus for understanding community-level minimum tolerable fire intervals is the slowest maturing, firekilled species (*B. prionotes*). *Banksia prionotes* likely requires longer intervals of at least 8–10 years for sufficient post-fire recruitment where it occurs, especially where low rainfall delays or reduces flowering and seed production. Current managed fire interval objectives of 13–33 years for risk reduction (Ritchie et al. [2021\)](#page-19-14) should, therefore, support the persistence of the woody plant functional types studied here; however, continued regional warming and drying associated with climate change may pose a threat of shortening wildfire intervals, consistent with the interval squeeze concept *sensu* (Enright et al. [2015](#page-18-1)). Our juvenile period and minimum tolerable fire interval findings are consistent with evidence from the region on the same or similar species (Enright et al. [2014](#page-18-7); Wilson et al. [2014\)](#page-20-6). However, corresponding minimum fire interval recommendations (8–16 years) suggested by Wilson et al. [\(2014](#page-20-6)) are based on population-level maturity of resprouters (a combination of primary and secondary juvenile periods) which, as explained above, are not the primary focus of the juvenile period approach as they largely recover via resprouting. Instead, minimum fire intervals based on juvenile period data for fire-killed species **FIGURE 8**    |    Relationships between (A) plant size and flower count, and (B) plant size and cone count (serotinous species only). Relationships between plant size and flower count for *A. humilis*, a dioecious species, are presented separately for male and female plants. === p15 presented in Wilson et al. [\(2014](#page-20-6)) are up to 8–10 years for the most sensitive, slow-maturing species, which is consistent with our findings. Suggested minimum tolerable fire intervals for fire-killed serotinous species (including *B. prionotes*) in drier (less productive) shrublands north of our study region range from 10 to 15 years for high versus low post-fire winter rainfall years, respectively (Enright et al. [2014](#page-18-7)). As our minimum tolerable interval estimates (2–9 years) suggest, minimum tolerable fire intervals should be somewhat shorter in the more productive (higher rainfall) Banksia woodlands. Consistent with this hypothesis, our estimates of minimum tolerable fire intervals of around 3–5 years for fire-killed shrubs with soil seed banks are somewhat shorter than the equivalent 5–6 years reported in Enright et al. [\(2014\)](#page-18-7). Interestingly, however, estimates for resprouting shrubs show little difference between the two regions; resprouting shrubs with canopy seed banks showed minimum tolerable intervals of around 5–7 years and resprouting shrubs with soil seed banks showed little risk of even the shortest intervals sampled (Enright et al. [2014](#page-18-7)). Post-fire growth and maturation rates of fire-killed shrubs, which regenerate from seedlings, are strongly contingent on environmental productivity (Gosper et al. [2022\)](#page-18-6), whereas post-fire growth rates in resprouting shrubs may be less contingent on environmental conditions during the post-fire period as already-established plants draw on stored energy reserves for post-fire growth and reproduction (Clarke et al. [2013](#page-18-24)), acknowledging again that seedling recruitment is not the major form of post-fire recovery for resprouters. A strength of the analysis of Enright et al. [\(2014\)](#page-18-7) is that estimates of minimum tolerable fire intervals were based on robust, direct measures of resprouter survival and seedling recruitment, and therefore we suggest that further targeted study of seed availability and subsequent postfire seedling recruitment at various fire intervals in Banksia woodlands is warranted to confirm minimum tolerable fire intervals and further explore variation along environmental gradients. Additional evidence is also needed to test the assumptions of the juvenile period approach for estimating minimum intervals, including whether the 2×rule of thumb (Gill and Nicholls [1989](#page-18-10)) adequately covers natural variation in (1) seed bank accumulation rates and (2) flowering, pollination and seed set for species with different traits. At our estimated minimum tolerable fire intervals, populations had reached 22%–84% of their predicted maximum flowering output, and serotinous species had produced cones over at least 3–4 years and had reached 45%–91% of their predicted maximum canopy seed bank accumulation. Variation in post-fire reproductive attributes among species potentially indicates that the efficacy of the 2×approximation of minimum tolerable fire intervals varies between species. Perhaps species with soil-stored seed banks might be more adequately covered by the 2×approximation than those with canopy seed banks, as species with soil-stored seed may possess a residual seed bank after fire (i.e., seed banks are not completely exhausted by fire) (Auld and Denham [2006](#page-17-15)) and do not have to produce a persistent woody fruit requiring resources like serotinous species (Cramer and Midgley [2009;](#page-18-25) Tonnabel et al. [2012\)](#page-20-13). Our results also demonstrate substantial variation in reproduction owing to varying environmental conditions, suggesting that, in some cases, the 2×approximation may be inadequate to account for delays in reproduction. For example, for *G. tomentosum*, the presence of herbivores and low mean annual rainfall delayed the juvenile period beyond the estimated minimum tolerable fire interval under average growing conditions. ## **4.2   |   Post-Fire Reproduction** Fire-killed species are generally considered to have longer primary juvenile periods than the secondary juvenile periods of cooccurring resprouters (Gosper, Prober, and Yates [2013;](#page-18-5) Harvey et al. [2017\)](#page-19-9), but we observed little difference. Similar juvenile periods for these species groups, however, do not necessarily mean that they have equivalent reproductive trajectories or would be expected to have similar fire interval responses given differences in other traits. For example, resprouters may have a much lower maximum reproductive output at peak maturity compared to co-occurring fire-killed species owing to differences in resource allocation to reproduction versus energy storage (Enright and Lamont [1989\)](#page-18-26). Also, by the onset of reproductive maturity, resprouters have likely developed a strong resprouting capacity, potentially surviving through several fires before reaching a highly reproductive stage (Enright and Lamont [1992\)](#page-18-27), although resprouting and reproductive capacity may be eroded by a series of short fire intervals (Enright et al. [2011](#page-18-4); Fairman, Nitschke, and Bennett [2016](#page-18-8)). In contrast, fire-killed species may require several years after reaching reproductive maturity to develop adequate reproductive capacity for recovery after subsequent fires and therefore could be at risk of decline at the same intervals at which resprouters can readily resprout. There is an obvious advantage for fire-killed species in fire-prone habitats to reach maximum reproductive capacity as quickly as possible, and probably soon after the onset of reproduction, as indicated by our juvenile period data. For the fire-killed species with the longest juvenile period studied here (*B. prionotes*), some plants produced cones following the first year of flowering (4 years post-fire), and the corresponding estimated minimum tolerable fire interval (8years) allowed populations to reach, on average, 56% of their maximum flower production and 91% of their maximum canopy seed bank size. For a related, fire-killed *Banksia* species, Enright, Lamont, and Marsula [\(1996](#page-18-9)) similarly showed that plants began producing cones after the first year of flowering and produced an increasing number of cones in the following few years. Despite being the slowest-maturing, fire-killed species in this study, and probably in Banksia woodlands generally, *B. prionotes* appears to have a relatively short juvenile period compared to other fire-killed species in southwestern Australia (Gosper et al. [2022](#page-18-6); Harvey et al. [2017](#page-19-9); Wooller, Wooller, and Brown [2002\)](#page-20-4). Populations of *B. prionotes* also often occur in discrete stands such that a conservative minimum interval of 10 years, under average growing conditions, may not necessarily be relevant to apply to the entire landscape, or where fires are sufficiently patchy or of low severity to allow established individuals to survive fire (Burrows and Middleton [2016](#page-17-16)). Intervals less than 10years are relatively rare on the Swan Coastal Plain, especially in areas with managed fire regimes, although changing climate regimes and increasing human disturbance do not necessarily preclude such intervals (Fontaine [2022\)](#page-18-28). === p16 Our findings are consistent with previous efforts from the region in quantifying post-fire seed production in the resprouting *B. attenuata* in showing that mature trees are capable of producing cones in the first year or two after fire because they can resprout epicormically (Densmore and Clingan [2019;](#page-18-16) Valentine et al. [2014](#page-20-14)). Post-fire cone production is mediated by fire severity, where there are minimal interruptions to reproduction after low severity fire, but trees may take several years to regain the same level of cone production after high severity fire (Densmore and Clingan [2019](#page-18-16)). By the time of the species-specific minimum tolerable fire interval estimated here (~9 years), Valentine et al. [\(2014](#page-20-14)) estimated that mature adults (>2m tall) had accumulated, on average, approximately 6 cones per plant, which is higher than estimates presented here (~1 cone per plant). Our dataset includes smaller juvenile plants and a subset of our data on *B. attenuata* trees >2m tall shows cone counts across a similar range of values to Valentine et al. [\(2014\)](#page-20-14). Johnston, Stock, and Mawson [\(2016](#page-19-27)) and Densmore and Clingan [\(2019](#page-18-16)) report around 1.3 and 7 times higher estimates of *B. attenuata* mean canopy seed bank density (cones per ha), respectively, than we find here (mean 746 cones per ha; Figure [S3\)](#page-20-8). However, Johnston, Stock, and Mawson [\(2016\)](#page-19-27) included higher rainfall sites on the Swan Coastal Plain and Densmore and Clingan [\(2019](#page-18-16)) reported on the entire crop of cones for ease of recording regardless of whether they had closed follicles or not, where, in both cases, it would be reasonable to expect higher canopy seed bank estimates. Interestingly, the much higher estimates of cones per ha reported by Densmore and Clingan [\(2019\)](#page-18-16) can be explained by the weakly serotinous nature of *B. attenuata* in the region (Cowling and Lamont [1985](#page-18-21)), where most seeds are released from cones within two years of seed maturity, but opened cones are likely retained on the plant for many years, and could therefore give the impression of a much larger canopy seed bank. Johnston, Stock, and Mawson [\(2016](#page-19-27)) reported a similar trend of gradually increasing seed bank size with increasing time since fire for *B. attenuata* and a similar range of values for cones per ha for *B. prionotes*. We show that plants of fire-killed shrubs that regenerate via seed following fire gain reproductive capacity quickly. Likewise, Monk, Pate, and Loneragan [\(1981](#page-19-28)) observed that the fire-killed *A. pulchella* began producing flowers and seeds in the second year after fire, and achieved maximum seed production shortly thereafter (3–4 years post-fire). These observations differ from those for fire-killed Proteaceae shrubs from southeastern Australia where cone and seed production was not observed for a few years after first flowering, and was slower overall (Jenkins, Morrison, and Auld [2010](#page-19-29)). For fast-growing species such as *A. pulchella*, a doubling of the juvenile period as a general rule of thumb for estimating the minimum tolerable fire interval may be adequate to sustain populations under average growing conditions, even if this only allows for one or two additional years of seed production. Rapid post-fire reproductive maturity and abundant seed production are important mechanisms to cope with short fire intervals for species adapted to frequent canopy scorch, whether that be understorey shrubs scorched in all but the lowest severity fires, or trees burnt in crown fire regimes (Enright, Lamont, and Marsula [1996;](#page-18-9) Gauthier, Bergeron, and Simon [1996\)](#page-18-29). Likewise, soil-stored seed banks, variable seed dormancy and residual seedbanks are traits that allow species to cope with short fire intervals. Banksia woodlands may be adapted to mixed severity fire regimes where understorey and overstorey components experience a range of low, moderate and high severity fire at widely varying intervals, potentially as short as 5–10 years in the understorey (Hobbs and Atkins [1990](#page-19-15); Miller, Enright, Fontaine et al. [2024\)](#page-19-23). Our findings for the resprouting shrub *A. humilis* are consistent with expectations for dioecious species in that patterns of postfire flowering appear to be driven by the costs of male versus female reproduction (Barrett and Hough [2012;](#page-17-17) Obeso [2002\)](#page-19-30). Flower and pollen production in male plants is less costly than flower, cone and seed production in female plants and so we would expect to observe precocious male flowering (Field, Pickup, and Barrett [2013](#page-18-30)). In comparison to female plants, male *A. humilis* plants had a shorter juvenile period (2.5 vs. 3.5years on average), produced more flowers per plant on average across all fire ages (927 vs. 269) and produced more flowers on average at any given plant size. Wilson et al. [\(2014\)](#page-20-6) provided an estimate of 40 years for the maximum tolerable fire interval for Banksia woodlands based on the maximum longevity of serotinous, fire-killed *Banksia* species. However, *Banksia* longevity was derived for a different species (*B. hookeriana*) from a nearby region with different climate and fire regimes, and for a species that grows as a tall shrub rather than a tree, and therefore presumably has a shorter lifespan (Cowling and Lamont [1985\)](#page-18-21). We expect *Banksia* tree longevity in the range of 40–60 years for *B. prionotes* (fire-killed) and to exceed 100 years for *B. attenuata* (resprouter). Over the approximately 35-year chronosequence studied here, we found no evidence of decline in reproduction for *B. attenuata*, but some evidence for a minor decline in reproduction in *B. prionotes* which appears primarily driven by a decline in plant density of mature stages with a minor contribution from a decline in reproductive output per plant. Although *B. prionotes* can have low levels of inter-fire seedling recruitment (Miller, Enright, Fontaine et al. [2024\)](#page-19-23), this input of non-reproductive individuals does not appear to have a noticeable effect on population-level reproduction (Figure [S5\)](#page-20-8). There is little evidence of major population senescence in *B. prionotes*, and therefore, maximum tolerable intervals are likely to exceed 40years, which are very rare regardless (Wilson et al. [2014](#page-20-6)). #### **4.3   |   Reproduction Under Varying Environmental and Demographic Conditions** Environmental productivity (mean annual rainfall) and the presence or absence of herbivory were found to be important factors associated with post-fire reproductive trajectories (Burrows, Wardell-Johnson, and Ward [2008;](#page-17-4) Gosper et al. [2022;](#page-18-6) McCaw [2008\)](#page-19-10). In sites with low mean rainfall (low productivity) or herbivore presence, predicted juvenile periods were delayed by up to 3 years, and therefore minimum tolerable fire intervals by up to 6 years for fire-killed understorey shrubs (*A. pulchella* and *G. tomentosum*). Low mean rainfall also decreased flower production by up to 61% for the same species. For short-lived species, this may represent a doubling (or more) of the minimum fire-free period required for population replacement, and potentially a reduction in lifetime reproductive output. === p17 While these data pertain to mean rainfall and the prevailing presence or absence of herbivores, our results suggest that delayed reproductive maturity and reduced reproductive output could occur under abrupt environmental changes such as the introduction of native or non-native herbivores, or the increasing severity of drought conditions associated with climate change (Gosper et al. [2022;](#page-18-6) Matusick et al. [2018\)](#page-19-31). Modelling suggests that primary juvenile periods for serotinous obligate seeders (here represented by *B. prionotes*) could more than double in the study area under 2050 climate change scenarios, including lower mean annual rainfall (Gosper et al. [2022\)](#page-18-6), potentially requiring longer fire intervals to conserve vulnerable populations. In general, we sampled across a relatively narrow mean annual rainfall gradient (~150mm difference) compared to the variation present in the broader region, and in particular, our sampling of *B. prionotes* populations occurred across a very narrow range (30mm difference). It is not surprising, therefore, that we did not detect an effect of rainfall for *B. prionotes*; however, if sampling was repeated across a wider rainfall gradient (spatial or temporal), we would expect to detect slower maturity rates under low rainfall. This is a broad concern for fire-killed species which rely on post-fire recruitment from seeds for persistence, and is consistent with the concept of 'interval squeeze' where populations are vulnerable to decline with the simultaneous shortening of fire intervals and reduced seed production and post-fire recruitment associated with climate change impacts (Enright et al. [2015\)](#page-18-1). Invasive grassy weeds are also a significant threat in Banksia woodlands (Ritchie et al. [2021\)](#page-19-14), and may pose an additional limitation on population recovery if weeds reduce post-fire seedling recruitment or delay maturation and reproductive maturity. The effects of varying mean annual rainfall on flowering rate (juvenile period) provided a curious result for *B. attenuata*, where populations in high mean rainfall sites appeared to mature more slowly than populations in low mean rainfall sites. Rather than higher rainfall delaying maturation, we believe this relates to differences in the demographic structure of populations under varying rainfall regimes altering population-level calculations. In the study area, higher rainfall and longer growing seasons likely facilitate higher rates of inter-fire seedling recruitment (Miller, Enright, Fontaine et al. [2024\)](#page-19-23), although not to a level that would result in densification or canopy closure that would, in turn, preclude recruitment of shade-intolerant seedlings and probably reduce reproductive output. Flowering rates reported here are a composite of reproduction (or lack thereof) in seedlings, juveniles and adults, and therefore a higher proportion of non-reproductive seedlings and juveniles resulting from higher recruitment will lower flowering rate estimates. Canopy seed banks (closed cone counts per plant) for both *Banksia* species were very low, with *B. attenuata* generally having less than two seed-bearing cones per plant on average, and *B. prionotes* generally less than one. Low cone counts can be explained by a combination of the weakly serotinous nature of these *Banksia* species in the study area, and demographic structures with a high proportion of juvenile plants with little to no reproduction (Figures [S5](#page-20-8) and [S6](#page-20-8)). Cowling and Lamont [\(1985](#page-18-21)) reported a gradient in the degree of serotiny of *Banksia* species in the region with populations in our study area being weakly or non-serotinous, meaning that the majority of the accumulated canopy seed bank originates from the most recent seed crop minus any losses from disease and predation. Whelan and Ayre [\(2020\)](#page-20-15) likewise reported very low canopy seed bank accumulation for a serotinous *Banksia* shrub species from southeastern Australia. Both weakly serotinous *Banksia* species studied here develop multi-cohort populations, especially in the absence of fire (Hobbs and Atkins [1990;](#page-19-15) Miller, Enright, Fontaine et al. [2024](#page-19-23)). Like the effect of rainfall on *B. attenuata* flowering rate noted above, a high proportion of non-reproductive juvenile plants lowers population-level seed bank size estimates which likely underestimates the reproductive potential of mature individuals. While mature individuals have the potential to contribute much larger seed banks, weak serotiny will ultimately limit the maximum size of the canopy seed bank. This contrasts with the seed bank dynamics of highly serotinous *Banksia* species in ecosystems with more regular crown fire regimes where canopy seed banks can accumulate over many years (Enright, Lamont, and Marsula [1996\)](#page-18-9). Top-ranked models explained up to 92% of variation in the data (mean=43%, inter-quartile range=30%–51%; Table [2,](#page-6-0) Table [5\)](#page-8-2), leaving, in some cases, substantial variation unexplained by the variables considered in this study. More detailed analyses of the effects of interannual weather variation and spatially varying site variables (e.g., soil type, aspect, elevation) could explain greater variation in the data and provide a deeper understanding of the drivers of reproduction. The analysis presented here using mean annual rainfall could also be extended to quantify the effects of varying rainfall at different demographic stages—for example, during seedling establishment (1–2years post-fire), floral initiation and fruit development—to assess the sensitivity of post-fire reproduction to extreme dry climate conditions. Such analyses could help predict scenarios or sites under which fire managers may need to consider longer managed fire intervals to accommodate delayed juvenile periods under increasingly common droughts and heatwave events (Matusick et al. [2018;](#page-19-31) Ruthrof et al. [2021\)](#page-20-16). #### **4.4   |   Time Since Fire Versus Size as a Predictor of Reproduction** While we found that TSF was a clear indicator of reproduction, we also show that plant size is a much stronger predictor of reproductive capacity as also reported elsewhere by Andrus et al. [\(2020\)](#page-17-18), Gauthier, Bergeron, and Simon [\(1993](#page-18-31)) and von Takach Dukai, Lindenmayer, and Banks [\(2018\)](#page-20-3). Many plant species that inhabit fire-prone environments (especially fire-killed species in stand-replacing fire regimes) are often assumed to follow a specific post-fire trajectory where a single, post-fire seedling cohort matures and grows larger at a similar rate (Gill and McMahon [1986](#page-18-11)). However, this assumption may weaken in noncrown fire regimes, or for multi-cohort populations resulting from inter-fire recruitment, post-fire resprouting, or both. Interfire recruitment is evident for most of the species studied here (Hobbs and Atkins [1990](#page-19-15); Miller, Enright, Fontaine et al. [2024\)](#page-19-23), and therefore, population-level metrics of reproduction may be more closely related to varying demographic structure or environmental conditions rather than TSF. We acknowledge TSF and post-fire juvenile periods as simplistic yet useful indicators of post-fire reproductive maturity, but here we show that the effects of other environmental and demographic conditions can introduce substantial variation into species === p18 responses, and therefore are important to consider when making decisions about fire intervals that may impact species persistence (Gosper et al. [2022](#page-18-6)). As originally recognised, the juvenile period approach for estimating minimum tolerable fire intervals can provide rapid and low-cost guidance for fire management planning, but advances in ecological understanding and technology for measuring vegetation attributes should allow for the development of more sophisticated models for predicting variation in reproduction by including multiple environmental and demographic variables. Other metrics of species reproductive maturity and minimum tolerable fire intervals that may provide useful alternative or supplemental information for fire managers include the assessment of (1) the reproductive output (and density) of the largest individuals as the plants that contribute most to the reproductive capacity of the population and (2) average understorey plant height and litter cover as surrogates of plant growth and fuel accumulation. Ongoing advances in the mapping of vegetation structure from remote sensing data (e.g., through airborne or terrestrial laser scanning) (Moudrý et al. [2023;](#page-19-32) Turner et al. [2023](#page-20-17)) may provide an opportunity to measure plant size and density across large areas and combine with environmental and demographic data, such as that presented in this study, to calculate metrics of reproduction at a similar landscape scale to traditional fire age mapping currently used extensively in fire management planning. #### **Author Contributions** **Russell G. +#### **4 | Discussion**
+#### **4.1 | Juvenile Periods and Tolerable Fire Intervals**

+The shape of post-fire reproductive trajectories provides direct evidence of fire frequencies that permit species persistence and is critical information for the conservation and management of fire-prone ecosystems globally, especially with ongoing climate and fire regime change. We modelled reproduction in six woody plant species with a variety of fire-related traits across a range of fire ages in Banksia woodlands and found juvenile periods of 1–4 years, with little difference attributable to fire response type. Minimum tolerable fire intervals under average growing conditions based on primary juvenile periods for fire-killed species and a mix of primary and secondary juvenile periods for resprouters ranged from approximately 3–8 years and 2–9 years, respectively. Although there was some evidence of decline in reproduction in the oldest sites (>30 years since the last fire), reproductive capacity was likely still adequate for post-fire seedling recruitment after these long fire intervals. Variation in juvenile periods and reproductive output across all fire ages were associated with variation in growth forms and with changes in site productivity (rainfall) and herbivory. Taken together, our observations of rapid post-fire reproductive recovery and no fatal decline in reproduction in the long absence of fire are consistent with the suggestion that Banksia woodlands are adapted to mixed-severity fire regimes including widely varying intervals, where species have the capacity to cope with short and long fire intervals (Miller, Enright, Fontaine et al. 2024).

+The species studied here, potentially representing a larger suite of Banksia woodland species with similar growth forms, fire response and seed bank storage modes, would all likely tolerate fire intervals of 10 years under average growing conditions, and the most rapidly maturing would likely tolerate intervals as short as 5 years under average growing conditions. While juvenile period data for resprouters is important for understanding effects on reproduction from seed, which is crucial for long-term population persistence, minimum tolerable fire intervals for resprouters based on the juvenile period method disregard the often-overriding contribution of resprouting to the post-fire recovery of species with this capability. Resprouters, therefore, may be able to tolerate even shorter intervals (i.e., less than 5 years) if resprouting capacity develops rapidly post-fire. However, several repeated short fire intervals (less than 5 years) may preclude recruitment and erode adult resprouting capacity
+*Austral Ecology*, 2025 | 13 of 21

Current managed fire interval objectives of 13–33 years for risk reduction (Ritchie et al. 2021) should, therefore, support the persistence of the woody plant functional types studied here; however, continued regional warming and drying associated with climate change may pose a threat of shortening wildfire intervals, consistent with the interval squeeze concept *sensu* (Enright et al. 2015).

+Our juvenile period and minimum tolerable fire interval findings are consistent with evidence from the region on the same or similar species (Enright et al. 2014; Wilson et al. 2014). However, corresponding minimum fire interval recommendations (8–16 years) suggested by Wilson et al. (2014) are based on population-level maturity of resprouters (a combination of primary and secondary juvenile periods) which, as explained above, are not the primary focus of the juvenile period approach as they largely recover via resprouting. Instead, minimum fire intervals based on juvenile period data for fire-killed species
+14 of 21 | *Austral Ecology*, 2025
