+presented in Wilson et al. (2014) are up to 8–10 years for the most sensitive, slow-maturing species, which is consistent with our findings.

+Suggested minimum tolerable fire intervals for fire-killed serotinous species (including *B. prionotes*) in drier (less productive) shrublands north of our study region range from 10 to 15 years for high versus low post-fire winter rainfall years, respectively (Enright et al. 2014). As our minimum tolerable interval estimates (2–9 years) suggest, minimum tolerable fire intervals should be somewhat shorter in the more productive (higher rainfall) Banksia woodlands. Consistent with this hypothesis, our estimates of minimum tolerable fire intervals of around 3–5 years for fire-killed shrubs with soil seed banks are somewhat shorter than the equivalent 5–6 years reported in Enright et al. (2014). Interestingly, however, estimates for resprouting shrubs show little difference between the two regions; resprouting shrubs with canopy seed banks showed minimum tolerable intervals of around 5–7 years and resprouting shrubs with soil seed banks showed little risk of even the shortest intervals sampled (Enright et al. 2014). Post-fire growth and maturation rates of fire-killed shrubs, which regenerate from seedlings, are strongly contingent on environmental productivity (Gosper et al. 2022), whereas post-fire growth rates in resprouting shrubs may be less contingent on environmental conditions during the post-fire period as already-established plants draw on stored energy reserves for post-fire growth and reproduction (Clarke et al. 2013), acknowledging again that seedling recruitment is not the major form of post-fire recovery for resprouters. A strength of the analysis of Enright et al. (2014) is that estimates of minimum tolerable fire intervals were based on robust, direct measures of resprouter survival and seedling recruitment, and therefore we suggest that further targeted study of seed availability and subsequent post-fire seedling recruitment at various fire intervals in Banksia woodlands is warranted to confirm minimum tolerable fire intervals and further explore variation along environmental gradients.

+Additional evidence is also needed to test the assumptions of the juvenile period approach for estimating minimum intervals, including whether the 2× rule of thumb (Gill and Nicholls 1989) adequately covers natural variation in (1) seed bank accumulation rates and (2) flowering, pollination and seed set for species with different traits. At our estimated minimum tolerable fire intervals, populations had reached 22%–84% of their predicted maximum flowering output, and serotinous species had produced cones over at least 3–4 years and had reached 45%–91% of their predicted maximum canopy seed bank accumulation. Variation in post-fire reproductive attributes among species potentially indicates that the efficacy of the 2× approximation of minimum tolerable fire intervals varies between species. Perhaps species with soil-stored seed banks might be more adequately covered by the 2× approximation than those with canopy seed banks, as species with soil-stored seed may possess a residual seed bank after fire (i.e., seed banks are not completely exhausted by fire) (Auld and Denham 2006) and do not have to produce a persistent woody fruit requiring resources like serotinous species (Cramer and Midgley 2009; Tonnabel et al. 2012). Our results also demonstrate substantial variation in reproduction owing to varying environmental conditions, suggesting that, in some cases, the 2× approximation may be inadequate to account for delays in reproduction. For example, for *G. tomentosum*, the presence of herbivores and low mean annual rainfall delayed the juvenile period beyond the estimated minimum tolerable fire interval under average growing conditions.
+#### **4.2 | Post-Fire Reproduction**

+Fire-killed species are generally considered to have longer primary juvenile periods than the secondary juvenile periods of co-occurring resprouters (Gosper, Prober, and Yates 2013; Harvey et al. 2017), but we observed little difference. Similar juvenile periods for these species groups, however, do not necessarily mean that they have equivalent reproductive trajectories or would be expected to have similar fire interval responses given differences in other traits. For example, resprouters may have a much lower maximum reproductive output at peak maturity compared to co-occurring fire-killed species owing to differences in resource allocation to reproduction versus energy storage (Enright and Lamont 1989). Also, by the onset of reproductive maturity, resprouters have likely developed a strong resprouting capacity, potentially surviving through several fires before reaching a highly reproductive stage (Enright and Lamont 1992), although resprouting and reproductive capacity may be eroded by a series of short fire intervals (Enright et al. 2011; Fairman, Nitschke, and Bennett 2016). In contrast, fire-killed species may require several years after reaching reproductive maturity to develop adequate reproductive capacity for recovery after subsequent fires and therefore could be at risk of decline at the same intervals at which resprouters can readily resprout. There is an obvious advantage for fire-killed species in fire-prone habitats to reach maximum reproductive capacity as quickly as possible, and probably soon after the onset of reproduction, as indicated by our juvenile period data.

+For the fire-killed species with the longest juvenile period studied here (*B. prionotes*), some plants produced cones following the first year of flowering (4 years post-fire), and the corresponding estimated minimum tolerable fire interval (8 years) allowed populations to reach, on average, 56% of their maximum flower production and 91% of their maximum canopy seed bank size. For a related, fire-killed *Banksia* species, Enright, Lamont, and Marsula (1996) similarly showed that plants began producing cones after the first year of flowering and produced an increasing number of cones in the following few years. Despite being the slowest-maturing, fire-killed species in this study, and probably in Banksia woodlands generally, *B. prionotes* appears to have a relatively short juvenile period compared to other fire-killed species in southwestern Australia (Gosper et al. 2022; Harvey et al. 2017; Wooller, Wooller, and Brown 2002). Populations of *B. prionotes* also often occur in discrete stands such that a conservative minimum interval of 10 years, under average growing conditions, may not necessarily be relevant to apply to the entire landscape, or where fires are sufficiently patchy or of low severity to allow established individuals to survive fire (Burrows and Middleton 2016). Intervals less than 10 years are relatively rare on the Swan Coastal Plain, especially in areas with managed fire regimes, although changing climate regimes and increasing human disturbance do not necessarily preclude such intervals (Fontaine 2022).
+*Austral Ecology*, 2025 | 15 of 21
+<!-- PAGE BREAK -->

+Our findings are consistent with previous efforts from the region in quantifying post-fire seed production in the resprouting *B. attenuata* in showing that mature trees are capable of producing cones in the first year or two after fire because they can resprout epicormically (Densmore and Clingan 2019; Valentine et al. 2014). Post-fire cone production is mediated by fire severity, where there are minimal interruptions to reproduction after low severity fire, but trees may take several years to regain the same level of cone production after high severity fire (Densmore and Clingan 2019). By the time of the species-specific minimum tolerable fire interval estimated here (~9 years), Valentine et al. (2014) estimated that mature adults (>2 m tall) had accumulated, on average, approximately 6 cones per plant, which is higher than estimates presented here (~1 cone per plant). Our dataset includes smaller juvenile plants and a subset of our data on *B. attenuata* trees >2 m tall shows cone counts across a similar range of values to Valentine et al. (2014). Johnston, Stock, and Mawson (2016) and Densmore and Clingan (2019) report around 1.3 and 7 times higher estimates of *B. attenuata* mean canopy seed bank density (cones per ha), respectively, than we find here (mean 746 cones per ha; Figure S3). However, Johnston, Stock, and Mawson (2016) included higher rainfall sites on the Swan Coastal Plain and Densmore and Clingan (2019) reported on the entire crop of cones for ease of recording regardless of whether they had closed follicles or not, where, in both cases, it would be reasonable to expect higher canopy seed bank estimates. Interestingly, the much higher estimates of cones per ha reported by Densmore and Clingan (2019) can be explained by the weakly serotinous nature of *B. attenuata* in the region (Cowling and Lamont 1985), where most seeds are released from cones within two years of seed maturity, but opened cones are likely retained on the plant for many years, and could therefore give the impression of a much larger canopy seed bank. Johnston, Stock, and Mawson (2016) reported a similar trend of gradually increasing seed bank size with increasing time since fire for *B. attenuata* and a similar range of values for cones per ha for *B. prionotes*.

+We show that plants of fire-killed shrubs that regenerate via seed following fire gain reproductive capacity quickly. Likewise, Monk, Pate, and Loneragan (1981) observed that the fire-killed *A. pulchella* began producing flowers and seeds in the second year after fire, and achieved maximum seed production shortly thereafter (3–4 years post-fire). These observations differ from those for fire-killed Proteaceae shrubs from southeastern Australia where cone and seed production was not observed for a few years after first flowering, and was slower overall (Jenkins, Morrison, and Auld 2010). For fast-growing species such as *A. pulchella*, a doubling of the juvenile period as a general rule of thumb for estimating the minimum tolerable fire interval may be adequate to sustain populations under average growing conditions, even if this only allows for one or two additional years of seed production. Rapid post-fire reproductive maturity and abundant seed production are important mechanisms to cope with short fire intervals for species adapted to frequent canopy scorch, whether that be understorey shrubs scorched in all but the lowest severity fires, or trees burnt in crown fire regimes (Enright, Lamont, and Marsula 1996; Gauthier, Bergeron, and Simon 1996). Likewise, soil-stored seed banks, variable seed dormancy and residual seedbanks are traits that allow species to cope with short fire intervals. Banksia woodlands may be adapted to mixed severity fire regimes where understorey and overstorey components experience a range of low, moderate and high severity fire at widely varying intervals, potentially as short as 5–10 years in the understorey (Hobbs and Atkins 1990; Miller, Enright, Fontaine et al. 2024).

+Our findings for the resprouting shrub *A. humilis* are consistent with expectations for dioecious species in that patterns of post-fire flowering appear to be driven by the costs of male versus female reproduction (Barrett and Hough 2012; Obeso 2002). Flower and pollen production in male plants is less costly than flower, cone and seed production in female plants and so we would expect to observe precocious male flowering (Field, Pickup, and Barrett 2013). In comparison to female plants, male *A. humilis* plants had a shorter juvenile period (2.5 vs. 3.5 years on average), produced more flowers per plant on average across all fire ages (927 vs. 269) and produced more flowers on average at any given plant size.

+Wilson et al. (2014) provided an estimate of 40 years for the maximum tolerable fire interval for Banksia woodlands based on the maximum longevity of serotinous, fire-killed *Banksia* species. However, *Banksia* longevity was derived for a different species (*B. hookeriana*) from a nearby region with different climate and fire regimes, and for a species that grows as a tall shrub rather than a tree, and therefore presumably has a shorter lifespan (Cowling and Lamont 1985). We expect *Banksia* tree longevity in the range of 40–60 years for *B. prionotes* (fire-killed) and to exceed 100 years for *B. attenuata* (resprouter). Over the approximately 35-year chronosequence studied here, we found no evidence of decline in reproduction for *B. attenuata*, but some evidence for a minor decline in reproduction in *B. prionotes* which appears primarily driven by a decline in plant density of mature stages with a minor contribution from a decline in reproductive output per plant. Although *B. prionotes* can have low levels of inter-fire seedling recruitment (Miller, Enright, Fontaine et al. 2024), this input of non-reproductive individuals does not appear to have a noticeable effect on population-level reproduction (Figure S5). There is little evidence of major population senescence in *B. prionotes*, and therefore, maximum tolerable intervals are likely to exceed 40 years, which are very rare regardless (Wilson et al. 2014).
+#### **4.3 | Reproduction Under Varying Environmental and Demographic Conditions**

+Environmental productivity (mean annual rainfall) and the presence or absence of herbivory were found to be important factors associated with post-fire reproductive trajectories (Burrows, Wardell-Johnson, and Ward 2008; Gosper et al. 2022; McCaw 2008). In sites with low mean rainfall (low productivity) or herbivore presence, predicted juvenile periods were delayed by up to 3 years, and therefore minimum tolerable fire intervals by up to 6 years for fire-killed understorey shrubs (*A. pulchella* and *G. tomentosum*). Low mean rainfall also decreased flower production by up to 61% for the same species. For short-lived species, this may represent a doubling (or more) of the minimum fire-free period required for population replacement, and potentially a reduction in lifetime reproductive output.

+While these data pertain to mean rainfall and the prevailing presence or absence of herbivores, our results suggest that delayed reproductive maturity and reduced reproductive output could occur under abrupt environmental changes such as the introduction of native or non-native herbivores, or the increasing severity of drought conditions associated with climate change (Gosper et al. 2022; Matusick et al. 2018). Modelling suggests that primary juvenile periods for serotinous obligate seeders (here represented by *B. prionotes*) could more than double in the study area under 2050 climate change scenarios, including lower mean annual rainfall (Gosper et al. 2022), potentially requiring longer fire intervals to conserve vulnerable populations. In general, we sampled across a relatively narrow mean annual rainfall gradient (~150 mm difference) compared to the variation present in the broader region, and in particular, our sampling of *B. prionotes* populations occurred across a very narrow range (30 mm difference). It is not surprising, therefore, that we did not detect an effect of rainfall for *B. prionotes*; however, if sampling was repeated across a wider rainfall gradient (spatial or temporal), we would expect to detect slower maturity rates under low rainfall. This is a broad concern for fire-killed species which rely on post-fire recruitment from seeds for persistence, and is consistent with the concept of 'interval squeeze' where populations are vulnerable to decline with the simultaneous shortening of fire intervals and reduced seed production and post-fire recruitment associated with climate change impacts (Enright et al. 2015). Invasive grassy weeds are also a significant threat in Banksia woodlands (Ritchie et al. 2021), and may pose an additional limitation on population recovery if weeds reduce post-fire seedling recruitment or delay maturation and reproductive maturity.

+The effects of varying mean annual rainfall on flowering rate (juvenile period) provided a curious result for *B. attenuata*, where populations in high mean rainfall sites appeared to mature more slowly than populations in low mean rainfall sites. Rather than higher rainfall delaying maturation, we believe this relates to differences in the demographic structure of populations under varying rainfall regimes altering population-level calculations. In the study area, higher rainfall and longer growing seasons likely facilitate higher rates of inter-fire seedling recruitment (Miller, Enright, Fontaine et al. 2024), although not to a level that would result in densification or canopy closure that would, in turn, preclude recruitment of shade-intolerant seedlings and probably reduce reproductive output. Flowering rates reported here are a composite of reproduction (or lack thereof) in seedlings, juveniles and adults, and therefore a higher proportion of non-reproductive seedlings and juveniles resulting from higher recruitment will lower flowering rate estimates.

+Canopy seed banks (closed cone counts per plant) for both *Banksia* species were very low, with *B. attenuata* generally having less than two seed-bearing cones per plant on average, and *B. prionotes* generally less than one. Low cone counts can be explained by a combination of the weakly serotinous nature of these *Banksia* species in the study area, and demographic structures with a high proportion of juvenile plants with little to no reproduction (Figures S5 and S6). Cowling and Lamont (1985) reported a gradient in the degree of serotiny of *Banksia* species in the region with populations in our study area being weakly or non-serotinous, meaning that the majority of the accumulated canopy seed bank originates from the most recent seed crop minus any losses from disease and predation. Whelan and Ayre (2020) likewise reported very low canopy seed bank accumulation for a serotinous *Banksia* shrub species from southeastern Australia. Both weakly serotinous *Banksia* species studied here develop multi-cohort populations, especially in the absence of fire (Hobbs and Atkins 1990; Miller, Enright, Fontaine et al. 2024). Like the effect of rainfall on *B. attenuata* flowering rate noted above, a high proportion of non-reproductive juvenile plants lowers population-level seed bank size estimates which likely underestimates the reproductive potential of mature individuals. While mature individuals have the potential to contribute much larger seed banks, weak serotiny will ultimately limit the maximum size of the canopy seed bank. This contrasts with the seed bank dynamics of highly serotinous *Banksia* species in ecosystems with more regular crown fire regimes where canopy seed banks can accumulate over many years (Enright, Lamont, and Marsula 1996).

+Top-ranked models explained up to 92% of variation in the data (mean = 43%, inter-quartile range = 30%–51%; Table 2, Table 5), leaving, in some cases, substantial variation unexplained by the variables considered in this study. More detailed analyses of the effects of interannual weather variation and spatially varying site variables (e.g., soil type, aspect, elevation) could explain greater variation in the data and provide a deeper understanding of the drivers of reproduction. The analysis presented here using mean annual rainfall could also be extended to quantify the effects of varying rainfall at different demographic stages—for example, during seedling establishment (1–2 years post-fire), floral initiation and fruit development—to assess the sensitivity of post-fire reproduction to extreme dry climate conditions. Such analyses could help predict scenarios or sites under which fire managers may need to consider longer managed fire intervals to accommodate delayed juvenile periods under increasingly common droughts and heatwave events (Matusick et al. 2018; Ruthrof et al. 2021).
+#### **4.4 | Time Since Fire Versus Size as a Predictor of Reproduction**

+While we found that TSF was a clear indicator of reproduction, we also show that plant size is a much stronger predictor of reproductive capacity as also reported elsewhere by Andrus et al. (2020), Gauthier, Bergeron, and Simon (1993) and von Takach Dukai, Lindenmayer, and Banks (2018). Many plant species that inhabit fire-prone environments (especially fire-killed species in stand-replacing fire regimes) are often assumed to follow a specific post-fire trajectory where a single, post-fire seedling cohort matures and grows larger at a similar rate (Gill and McMahon 1986). However, this assumption may weaken in non-crown fire regimes, or for multi-cohort populations resulting from inter-fire recruitment, post-fire resprouting, or both. Inter-fire recruitment is evident for most of the species studied here (Hobbs and Atkins 1990; Miller, Enright, Fontaine et al. 2024), and therefore, population-level metrics of reproduction may be more closely related to varying demographic structure or environmental conditions rather than TSF.

+We acknowledge TSF and post-fire juvenile periods as simplistic yet useful indicators of post-fire reproductive maturity, but here we show that the effects of other environmental and demographic conditions can introduce substantial variation into species

+responses, and therefore are important to consider when making decisions about fire intervals that may impact species persistence (Gosper et al. 2022). As originally recognised, the juvenile period approach for estimating minimum tolerable fire intervals can provide rapid and low-cost guidance for fire management planning, but advances in ecological understanding and technology for measuring vegetation attributes should allow for the development of more sophisticated models for predicting variation in reproduction by including multiple environmental and demographic variables. Other metrics of species reproductive maturity and minimum tolerable fire intervals that may provide useful alternative or supplemental information for fire managers include the assessment of (1) the reproductive output (and density) of the largest individuals as the plants that contribute most to the reproductive capacity of the population and (2) average understorey plant height and litter cover as surrogates of plant growth and fuel accumulation. Ongoing advances in the mapping of vegetation structure from remote sensing data (e.g., through airborne or terrestrial laser scanning) (Moudrý et al. 2023; Turner et al. 2023) may provide an opportunity to measure plant size and density across large areas and combine with environmental and demographic data, such as that presented in this study, to calculate metrics of reproduction at a similar landscape scale to traditional fire age mapping currently used extensively in fire management planning.

1	=== p1
2	# Demography of woody plants in relation to fire: *Banksia ericifolia* **L.f. and** *Petrophile pulchella* **(Schrad) R.Br.**
3	
4	R. A, BRADSTOCK\*
5	
6	*School of Biological Sciences. Macleay Building Al 2, University of Sydney, Sydney, NSW 2006, Australia*
7	
8	M. A. O'CONNELL
9	
10	*NSW National Parks and Wildlife Service, Box Ni89 Grosvenor St. Sydney, NSW 2000, Australia*
11	
12	*Two variables accounted for the biggest changes in numbers and density between generations interspersed by fires; namely the age at which a stand is burned and the proportion of seeds which emerge as seedlings. A comparison with other similar species showed similarities in controls on emergence and establishment, lengths of primary juvenile periods and life spans.*
13	
14	#### **Abstract**
15	
16	*Plants* o/Banksia ericifolia awiiPetrophile pulchella *are sensitive to fire. Changes in population size under different fire regimes were estimated, based on measurements of post-fire seedling emergence, seedling survival, survival and seed production in established plants of differing ages, survival of seeds held in serotinous cones and seed-release in the periods between fire.*
17	
18	*Seeds were first available at 5 years in* P. pulchella *and 6 years in* B. ericifolia. *Exact replacement would be possible when burnt at these ages, if seedling establishment were very high. Low establishment would delay replacement to 13 years of age in both species. Late summer/autumn ftres of high intensity favour high establishment. Such fires at 8-10 year intervals would be tolerated without any sustained decline in numbers. Eires at 10-15 year intervals could occur regardless of season or intensity with little risk ofa population decline. Large increases in numbers and density would follow fires spaced at 15-30 years. Enough seeds would be available for replacement up to about 50 years in both species. Viable seedrelease in unburnt conditions was sufficient to compensate for deaths in stands over 20 years old, even with very low levels of establishment.*
19	
20	#### **Introduction**
21	
22	Plants which rely on seeds for regeneration after fire (obligate seeders) form a prominent part of the vegetation in many fire-prone regions of the world (Gill 1981; Keeley 1981). Some obligate seeders are serotinous as their seeds are retained in the canopy and released by fire (Lotan 1976).
23	
24	The present report presents demographic studies of two species which co-occur in fireprone vegetation in the Sydney Region of south-eastern Australia; *Banksia ericifolia* L.f. and *Petrophile pulchella* (Schrad) R.Br. These perennial woody shrubs are frequently dominant in shrublands or the understorey of woodlands. Plants of both species are usually killed by fires of most intensities. Seeds (achenes in *P. pulchella)* are stored in woody infructescences, referred to here as cones, within closed follicles *(B. ericifolia)* or bracts *(P. pulchella).* Many other species of shrubs or small trees in these local vegetation types are also serotinous obligate seeders (Beadle 1940; Clemens & Franklin 1981; Benson 1985).
25	
26	Crucial aspects of the demography of serotinous, obligate seeders are: (i) the time taken to first reproduction (primary juvenile period. Gill 1975) which determines the minimum possible interval at which fire may recur without causing extinction (Bradstock & Myerscough 1981; Bond *et al.* 1984; Gill & McMahon 1986) because seeds are usually non-dormant; (ii) seedling establishment postfire, which is determined by rainfall, tempera-
27	
28	<sup>•</sup>Present address: NSW National Parks and Wildlife Service, Box N189 Grosvenor St, Sydney, NSW 2000, Australia.
29	=== p2
30	ture, predators and the rate of release of seeds which, in turn, may be influenced by the season and intensity of fire (Bradstock & Myerscough 1981; Bond *e( al.* 1984; Cowling & Lamont 1984, 1985; McMahon 1984); (iii) the size of the pre-fire seed-bank, which is dependent on current storage plus new seeds added after each episode of seasonal fruiting minus losses of stored seeds in existing fruits (McMaster & Zedler 1981; Bond 1984; Gill & McMahon 1986); (iv) rates of survival of seedlings, juveniles and adults; (v) any subsequent establishment in unburnt conditions. Survival will be partly determined by density and age (Schlesinger & Gill 1978; Morris & Myerscough 1983, 1988). If establishment is absent in such conditions, the numbers and density in an even-aged post-fire generation will decline to low levels as the time since last fire nears the limit of longevity of the species (Specht *et al.* 1958; Ashton 1976; Gill & McMahon 1986).
31	
32	These factors can be linked in a demographic model to predict population size over successive generations subject to re-occurring fires. Such information would provide a detailed basis for the management of fire-prone plant communities. However, few studies have attempted to relate changes in population size to fire regimes (Zedler 1977; Kruger 1983). At present there is much pressure for repeated burning ofthe vegetation containing the study species at intervals of less than 10 years for the purpose of fuel reduction. Often such prescribed fires are ignited in the cool months, between April and October. If informed firemanagement is to take place it is important to know how these fire regimes and their alternatives may affect these potentially vulnerable, serotinous, obligate seeders. This study aimed to answer the following questions.
33	
34	(1) What is the shortest interval between fires (maximum fire frequency) that either species can withstand for a sustained period (e.g. about 100 years) without suffering a prolonged decrease in population size?
35	
36	(2) How is this maximum tolerable fire frequency affected by differences in the amounts of seedling emergence and survival occurring after different fires?
37	
38	(3) Are variations in seedling emergence and survival related to the seasonal timing and intensity of fires?
39	
40	(4) What are the likely trends in numbers
41	
42	and density of stands when fires occur infrequently?
43	
44	(5) How do these species compare with other serotinous obligate seeders?
45	
46	#### **Methods**
47	
48	#### *Study sites*
49	
50	The survival of plants more than 3 years of age, and the sizes of their seed-banks, were studied in seven areas situated within the Brisbane Water National Park, approximately 50 km north of Sydney, from 1980-83. These areas were last burned in 1977, 1976, 1975, 1974, 1973, 1968 and 1960 respectively, determined from fire-history maps and aerial photographs. All were located on ridge-tops of sandy earths derived from Hawkesbury Sandstone. Distance from the coast varied between 3 and 15 km. 14429993a, 1988, 4, Downloaded from https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/j.1442-9993.1988.tb00999.x by University of New South Wales, Wiley Online Library on [06/10/2026]. See the Terms and Conditions (https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/terms-and-conditions) on Wiley Online Library for rules of use; OA articles are governed by the applicable Creative Commons License
51	
52	Observations on the emergence and survival of seedlings (<3 years of age) were made in populations after four unplanned fires and in one experiment, between December 1980 and November 1982. These were located in the same area and had similar site characteristics to those populations used for the study of established plants.
53	
54	## *Seedling emergence and survival*
55	
56	The number of seedlings that emerged after each fire was counted in 40-70 quadrats (0.1 m^) for each species. The number of prefire seeds on dead plants was estimated by counting the number of cones held on branches in transects adjacent to the study quadrats, after the fire. The number of seeds per cone and the proportion of stored seeds that were intact and viable were estimated in cones taken from nearby unburnt stands. These procedures are described below.
57	
58	The fate of the seedlings was followed until mid 1983. Two alternative models of survival, the exponential and power function (Silvertown 1982) were fitted. No model is given for Bum IV in *P. pulchella* due to the small numbers of plants which emerged. Indeed, models were fitted only when data for major cohorts of 10 or more seedlings were available.
59	=== p3
60	Emergence was studied in two experiments (commenced May and November 1982) in which artificial ashbeds were prepared and known quantities of seeds sown. Quadrats (lmxlm) were prepared by removing all plant cover and litter. Heat was applied to the exposed soil using propane burners. Harvested plant material and litter were ashed and placed on the soil after the heating had ceased. Either 50 (May 1982) or 100 (November 1982) seeds of each species were scattered on the quadrats several days later. The number of emerged seedlings was counted on average every month for a year after the starting dates.
61	
62	### *Survival in established plants*
63	
64	Survival was measured in samples of 50 or more plants of both species which were tagged in late 1980-early 1981. Each sample was located within quadrats (1.0 mx 1.0 m or 0.5 mxO.5 m) on two adjacent lines randomly situated on a 20 m baseline located in thick patches of either species. All tagged plants were assumed to have arisen as seedlings after the previous fire in each area. The initial height of each plant was recorded.
65	
66	Plants of *B. ericifolia* in some areas (burned 1977, 1974) were located solely on shallow soils (depth 0.3-0.4 m) and these were stunted in height and spindly in form compared with populations located on deep soils (depth 1.0- 1.5 m; burned 1973, 1968, 1960). One area (burned 1975) contained plants on both soils. One sample was tagged in each area on each available soil type. A second was then established in each of the 1968 and 1960 areas, several hundred metres from the first.
67	
68	Plants of/", *pulchella* were not as common on shallow soils, therefore samples were tagged only on deep soils. These were separate but often close to the *B. ericifolia* samples. No sampling was done in the 1976 or 1973 areas. Two samples were tagged in each of the other areas. A fire in 1982 destroyed a single sample of each species in the 1960 area.
69	
70	Plants were checked twice yearly from the beginning of 1981 until October 1983 and the proportion of deaths was measured for each area to test for differences in mortality between soils in *B. ericifolia* and between populations of differing age in both species using G tests of independence.
71	
72	## *Seed-survival*
73	
74	Ten cones from each of four age classes (1, 5, 9 and 15 years) were harvested from each sample in 1983. These harvests were spread over three to four plants. Ages were estimated either by direct observation (1 and 5 years only) or by position and appearance (9 and 15 years). Cones of 9 and 15 years were those borne nearest the base of plants and presumed to be from the earliest cohort set in the 1968 stand and from the third oldest cohort in the 1960 stand. The latter origin was assumed because some cones in a more advanced state of degradation were found on the ground and these were assumed to be slightly older. In areas where only a single sample was available for each soil type a replicate often cones was harvested 50- 100 m from the tagged plants. Two samples of cones were also taken from *P. pulchella* plants at the same time as sampling from *B. ericifolia* in the 1973 area.
75	
76	Counts were made, in the laboratory, of total follicles or bracts and the number that was open and empty was recorded. Cones of *B. ericifolia* were heated in an oven at 200°C for 10 min to open follicles and aid seed removal. This treatment had no eflect on seed viability (Bradstock 1985). Cones of P. *pulchella* were left unheated for several weeks after which seed extraction was possible.
77	
78	Twenty unopened follicles/bracts were selected randomly and examined and the seeds within were scored as damaged by predators or intact. If intact, seeds were classified as filled, desiccated or aborted. Viability of intact, filled seeds was determined in batches of 50 by germination on filter paper in petri dishes maintained at saturation for 2-3 months. Germination occurred under optimum conditions (12:12 h day:night cycle of 15:5°C; Bradstock 1985) in an environmental cabinet.
79	
80	The relationship between the proportion of seeds per cone surviving (i.e. intact, filled, viable, unreleased seeds) and age was described using various linear and non-linear models. The preferred model was chosen via a comparison of the percentage variances (PV) accounted for. 179	
180	### *Effects of frequent fires*
181	
182	The importance of emergence and survival was reflected in the variability of the interval between fires at which stand replacement would be possible (Fig. 7). Burning at an interval close to 13 years could be done with little regard to other factors such as season or intensity of fire without risk ofa decline in numbers. The low levels of emergence and survival (Tables 1,2) used to produce this estimate were the product of a severe drought in the area (Bureau of Meteorology, pers. comm.). It is likely that fires in most years will produce at least a similar or larger number of seedlings. Survival of established plants may also be higher, for this reason.
183	
184	Fire-managers may wish to burn as often as twice a decade, hence it is necessary to know the limit to which fire frequency can be reduced below 13 years without risking a serious decline in numbers. Seasons and intensities of fire may become important in such

187	
188	circumstances as will year to year variability in rainfall.
189	
190	Bradstock (1985) found that emergence in *B. ericifolia* and *P. pulchella* varied with rainfall, soil moisture and temperature. High summer temperatures impose a form of exogenous dormancy on seeds (definition of Mott & Groves 1981), restricting emergence to the cooler months. Seeds which lie on the soil over summer lose some viability. The amount of emergence was positively correlated with the period of time the soil surface (0-1.0 cm) remains at field capacity after rain. Seed predation was minimal in burnt areas.
191	
192	Rainfall near the coast in the Sydney Region is highest, on average, from January to July (100-130 mm/month), and lowest from August to December (70-80 mm/month); however, there is great year to year variation.
193	
194	FIG. *5.* Mean number of stored viable seeds (seed-bank) per plant, under two regimes of seed production: continuous ( ), ceased at 30 years ( ).
195	
196	When evaporation is taken into account, the average period of sustained high soil moisture is May-July (early winter). Emergence may therefore be highest after fires which are timed so that most seeds are released in early winter. Seed-release will be most rapid after high intensity fires (Bradstock & Myerscough 1981; Bradstock 1985) and such fires in late summer-autumn will cause most seeds to be released by early winter. In contrast, low inten-
197	=== p10
198	FIG. 6. Estimated annual release of viable seeds per plant in samples of differing age.
199	
200	FIG. 7. Proportional changes m sizes of stands over two generations of equal length as a function of interval between fires and seedling establishment (maximum o; minimum •). Intersections of estimates with the broken line indicate intervals at which self-replacement is possible (see text).
201	
202	sity fires at this time will prolong seed-release over winter and spring. Late summer-autumn, high intensity fires will therefore, on average, yield optimum emergence. A similar fire regime giving optimum emergence in other species of serotinous Proteaceae has been observed by Specht *et al.* (1958), Specht (1981), Bond *et at.* (1984), Cowling and Lamont (1984a, 1984b, 1985), McMahon (1984). Mechanisms in each case were generally similar to those described here.
203	
204	While mortality of plants older than 100 days was due mainly to drought, younger seedlings died during both short dry spells and heavy rain (Bradstock 1985) when they were broken by raindrop impact or washed away. Bradstock (1985) concluded that the risk of death at the most vulnerable age (< 100 days; Table 2) would be minimized when seedlings emerged in early winter. This reinforced the conclusion that late summer fires are optimal in producing seedlings.
205	
206	After successive fires at 8 years, the proportional change in second generation stand size may vary from 9.8 to 0.5 in *B. ericifolia* and from 7.2 to 0.6 in *P. pulchella* (Fig. 7). The daily rainfall patterns for Sydney over 50 years (Bureau ofMeterology, pers. comm.) show that a winter containing two successive months of low soil surface moisture occurs on average once every decade whereas very wet winters in which the soil is more or less continually moist occur several times a decade (Bradstock 1985). Thus fires of optimal season and intensity occurring 8 years apart would be followed by a dry winter and a subsequent decline in postfire numbers, once every 80-100 years. More usually these fires would be followed by wet winters which would permit an increase in numbers. Hence an optimal regime in terms of season and intensity with an 8-10 year interval may cause fluctuations in numbers but is unlikely to send either species into a persistent decline if sustained over a period of up to 100 years. A 6-8 year cycle would be hazardous, due to a lower seed-bank and the increased probability of encountering dry post-fire conditions.
207	
208	Reproduction is delayed in *B. ericifolia* growing on shallow soils and such stands may decline when fires occur less than 15 years apart. Observations indicate that the primary juvenile period may extend to more than 8 years and also that the seed-bank size may be less than on deep soils.
209	
210	There are, therefore, two consecutive phases in which plants are susceptible to recurrent fires: first, during the primary juvenile period and second, the subsequent time up to the age at which exact self-replacement of stands is possible. So far most attention has been given to describing the lengths of primary juvenile periods. Values given here fell within the ranges already reported for these species (Benson 1985) and for other serotinous obligate seeders of the Proteaceae (3-11 years; Kruger 1983; Lamont 1985). Measurements of this second critical phase need to be made if serotinous obligate seeders are to be used as indicator species in fire-prone vegetation. === p1
# Demography of woody plants in relation to fire: *Banksia ericifolia* **L.f. and** *Petrophile pulchella* **(Schrad) R.Br.**

R. A, BRADSTOCK\*

*School of Biological Sciences. Macleay Building Al 2, University of Sydney, Sydney, NSW 2006, Australia*

M. A. O'CONNELL

*NSW National Parks and Wildlife Service, Box Ni89 Grosvenor St. Sydney, NSW 2000, Australia*

*Two variables accounted for the biggest changes in numbers and density between generations interspersed by fires; namely the age at which a stand is burned and the proportion of seeds which emerge as seedlings. A comparison with other similar species showed similarities in controls on emergence and establishment, lengths of primary juvenile periods and life spans.*

#### **Abstract**

*Plants* o/Banksia ericifolia awiiPetrophile pulchella *are sensitive to fire. Changes in population size under different fire regimes were estimated, based on measurements of post-fire seedling emergence, seedling survival, survival and seed production in established plants of differing ages, survival of seeds held in serotinous cones and seed-release in the periods between fire.*

*Seeds were first available at 5 years in* P. pulchella *and 6 years in* B. ericifolia. *Exact replacement would be possible when burnt at these ages, if seedling establishment were very high. Low establishment would delay replacement to 13 years of age in both species. Late summer/autumn ftres of high intensity favour high establishment. Such fires at 8-10 year intervals would be tolerated without any sustained decline in numbers. Eires at 10-15 year intervals could occur regardless of season or intensity with little risk ofa population decline. Large increases in numbers and density would follow fires spaced at 15-30 years. Enough seeds would be available for replacement up to about 50 years in both species. Viable seedrelease in unburnt conditions was sufficient to compensate for deaths in stands over 20 years old, even with very low levels of establishment.*

#### **Introduction**

Plants which rely on seeds for regeneration after fire (obligate seeders) form a prominent part of the vegetation in many fire-prone regions of the world (Gill 1981; Keeley 1981). Some obligate seeders are serotinous as their seeds are retained in the canopy and released by fire (Lotan 1976).

The present report presents demographic studies of two species which co-occur in fireprone vegetation in the Sydney Region of south-eastern Australia; *Banksia ericifolia* L.f. and *Petrophile pulchella* (Schrad) R.Br. These perennial woody shrubs are frequently dominant in shrublands or the understorey of woodlands. Plants of both species are usually killed by fires of most intensities. Seeds (achenes in *P. pulchella)* are stored in woody infructescences, referred to here as cones, within closed follicles *(B. ericifolia)* or bracts *(P. pulchella).* Many other species of shrubs or small trees in these local vegetation types are also serotinous obligate seeders (Beadle 1940; Clemens & Franklin 1981; Benson 1985).

Crucial aspects of the demography of serotinous, obligate seeders are: (i) the time taken to first reproduction (primary juvenile period. Gill 1975) which determines the minimum possible interval at which fire may recur without causing extinction (Bradstock & Myerscough 1981; Bond *et al.* 1984; Gill & McMahon 1986) because seeds are usually non-dormant; (ii) seedling establishment postfire, which is determined by rainfall, tempera-

<sup>•</sup>Present address: NSW National Parks and Wildlife Service, Box N189 Grosvenor St, Sydney, NSW 2000, Australia.
=== p2
ture, predators and the rate of release of seeds which, in turn, may be influenced by the season and intensity of fire (Bradstock & Myerscough 1981; Bond *e( al.* 1984; Cowling & Lamont 1984, 1985; McMahon 1984); (iii) the size of the pre-fire seed-bank, which is dependent on current storage plus new seeds added after each episode of seasonal fruiting minus losses of stored seeds in existing fruits (McMaster & Zedler 1981; Bond 1984; Gill & McMahon 1986); (iv) rates of survival of seedlings, juveniles and adults; (v) any subsequent establishment in unburnt conditions. Survival will be partly determined by density and age (Schlesinger & Gill 1978; Morris & Myerscough 1983, 1988). If establishment is absent in such conditions, the numbers and density in an even-aged post-fire generation will decline to low levels as the time since last fire nears the limit of longevity of the species (Specht *et al.* 1958; Ashton 1976; Gill & McMahon 1986).

These factors can be linked in a demographic model to predict population size over successive generations subject to re-occurring fires. Such information would provide a detailed basis for the management of fire-prone plant communities. However, few studies have attempted to relate changes in population size to fire regimes (Zedler 1977; Kruger 1983). At present there is much pressure for repeated burning ofthe vegetation containing the study species at intervals of less than 10 years for the purpose of fuel reduction. Often such prescribed fires are ignited in the cool months, between April and October. If informed firemanagement is to take place it is important to know how these fire regimes and their alternatives may affect these potentially vulnerable, serotinous, obligate seeders. This study aimed to answer the following questions.

(1) What is the shortest interval between fires (maximum fire frequency) that either species can withstand for a sustained period (e.g. about 100 years) without suffering a prolonged decrease in population size?

(2) How is this maximum tolerable fire frequency affected by differences in the amounts of seedling emergence and survival occurring after different fires?

(3) Are variations in seedling emergence and survival related to the seasonal timing and intensity of fires?

(4) What are the likely trends in numbers

and density of stands when fires occur infrequently?

(5) How do these species compare with other serotinous obligate seeders?

#### **Methods**

#### *Study sites*

The survival of plants more than 3 years of age, and the sizes of their seed-banks, were studied in seven areas situated within the Brisbane Water National Park, approximately 50 km north of Sydney, from 1980-83. These areas were last burned in 1977, 1976, 1975, 1974, 1973, 1968 and 1960 respectively, determined from fire-history maps and aerial photographs. All were located on ridge-tops of sandy earths derived from Hawkesbury Sandstone. Distance from the coast varied between 3 and 15 km. 14429993a, 1988, 4, Downloaded from https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/j.1442-9993.1988.tb00999.x by University of New South Wales, Wiley Online Library on [06/10/2026]. See the Terms and Conditions (https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/terms-and-conditions) on Wiley Online Library for rules of use; OA articles are governed by the applicable Creative Commons License

Observations on the emergence and survival of seedlings (<3 years of age) were made in populations after four unplanned fires and in one experiment, between December 1980 and November 1982. These were located in the same area and had similar site characteristics to those populations used for the study of established plants.

## *Seedling emergence and survival*

The number of seedlings that emerged after each fire was counted in 40-70 quadrats (0.1 m^) for each species. The number of prefire seeds on dead plants was estimated by counting the number of cones held on branches in transects adjacent to the study quadrats, after the fire. The number of seeds per cone and the proportion of stored seeds that were intact and viable were estimated in cones taken from nearby unburnt stands. These procedures are described below.

The fate of the seedlings was followed until mid 1983. Two alternative models of survival, the exponential and power function (Silvertown 1982) were fitted. No model is given for Bum IV in *P. pulchella* due to the small numbers of plants which emerged. Indeed, models were fitted only when data for major cohorts of 10 or more seedlings were available.
=== p3
Emergence was studied in two experiments (commenced May and November 1982) in which artificial ashbeds were prepared and known quantities of seeds sown. Quadrats (lmxlm) were prepared by removing all plant cover and litter. Heat was applied to the exposed soil using propane burners. Harvested plant material and litter were ashed and placed on the soil after the heating had ceased. Either 50 (May 1982) or 100 (November 1982) seeds of each species were scattered on the quadrats several days later. The number of emerged seedlings was counted on average every month for a year after the starting dates.

### *Survival in established plants*

Survival was measured in samples of 50 or more plants of both species which were tagged in late 1980-early 1981. Each sample was located within quadrats (1.0 mx 1.0 m or 0.5 mxO.5 m) on two adjacent lines randomly situated on a 20 m baseline located in thick patches of either species. All tagged plants were assumed to have arisen as seedlings after the previous fire in each area. The initial height of each plant was recorded.

Plants of *B. ericifolia* in some areas (burned 1977, 1974) were located solely on shallow soils (depth 0.3-0.4 m) and these were stunted in height and spindly in form compared with populations located on deep soils (depth 1.0- 1.5 m; burned 1973, 1968, 1960). One area (burned 1975) contained plants on both soils. One sample was tagged in each area on each available soil type. A second was then established in each of the 1968 and 1960 areas, several hundred metres from the first.

Plants of/", *pulchella* were not as common on shallow soils, therefore samples were tagged only on deep soils. These were separate but often close to the *B. ericifolia* samples. No sampling was done in the 1976 or 1973 areas. Two samples were tagged in each of the other areas. A fire in 1982 destroyed a single sample of each species in the 1960 area.

Plants were checked twice yearly from the beginning of 1981 until October 1983 and the proportion of deaths was measured for each area to test for differences in mortality between soils in *B. ericifolia* and between populations of differing age in both species using G tests of independence.

## *Seed-survival*

Ten cones from each of four age classes (1, 5, 9 and 15 years) were harvested from each sample in 1983. These harvests were spread over three to four plants. Ages were estimated either by direct observation (1 and 5 years only) or by position and appearance (9 and 15 years). Cones of 9 and 15 years were those borne nearest the base of plants and presumed to be from the earliest cohort set in the 1968 stand and from the third oldest cohort in the 1960 stand. The latter origin was assumed because some cones in a more advanced state of degradation were found on the ground and these were assumed to be slightly older. In areas where only a single sample was available for each soil type a replicate often cones was harvested 50- 100 m from the tagged plants. Two samples of cones were also taken from *P. pulchella* plants at the same time as sampling from *B. ericifolia* in the 1973 area.

Counts were made, in the laboratory, of total follicles or bracts and the number that was open and empty was recorded. Cones of *B. ericifolia* were heated in an oven at 200°C for 10 min to open follicles and aid seed removal. This treatment had no eflect on seed viability (Bradstock 1985). Cones of P. *pulchella* were left unheated for several weeks after which seed extraction was possible.

Twenty unopened follicles/bracts were selected randomly and examined and the seeds within were scored as damaged by predators or intact. If intact, seeds were classified as filled, desiccated or aborted. Viability of intact, filled seeds was determined in batches of 50 by germination on filter paper in petri dishes maintained at saturation for 2-3 months. Germination occurred under optimum conditions (12:12 h day:night cycle of 15:5°C; Bradstock 1985) in an environmental cabinet.

The relationship between the proportion of seeds per cone surviving (i.e. intact, filled, viable, unreleased seeds) and age was described using various linear and non-linear models. The preferred model was chosen via a comparison of the percentage variances (PV) accounted for. These PV were the differences between the residual and total mean squares expressed as a percentage of the total mean square.
=== p4
#### *Seed-bank estimation*

All new cones set in the samples during the study were counted. Cone production during 1984-85 in the 1960 stands was also measured. Collections of 10 cones produced in two flowering seasons between 1981 and 1983 were made from each sample to determine seed-set per cone. A further 10 cones were harvested in areas with only one sample per soil-depth tested. Mean total annual seed production per plant was thus calculated and then described as a function of age by various linear and nonlinear models from which a preferred model was chosen by a comparison of PV.

Seed-bank at any given age (per plant) was predicted by estimating the number of seeds (one seed per follicle or bract) set in each of the successive annual cohorts produced up to that age, using the preferred seed production model. In each cohort survival was then calculated using the preferred survival model for each species. The numbers of surviving seeds from each cohort at a given age were then summed to give an estimate of total stored viable seeds for that age. This was repeated for all ages between the time of first reproduction and 40 years. The estimates above 2 5 years were therefore extrapolations beyond the age limit of the samples. Allowance was made for the time between flowering and fruit maturity which is about one year in both species.

A further, alternative estimate of seed-bank was made. Seed production was stopped at age 30 years and the attrition of existing seeds was predicted up to an age of 100 years.

#### *Seed-release between fires*

The mean number of viable seeds released annually (per plant) in each sample in unburnt conditions was estimated. Samples of cones of four difl"erent ages were marked in the 1968 and 1960 samples in mid 1981. Two age classes of cones (1 and 5 years in 1981, method of ageing similar to that described above) were marked in all other samples. The oldest cones in each sample were also marked and in 1981 these were estimated to be 7 and 13 years old. Follicles *{B. ericifolia)* or bracts *{P. pulchella)* which were open and empty were marked. Cones were rechecked after 2 years and the number of follicles/bracts was counted along

with those which had opened and shed seeds. Rates of seed-release were compared between samples and cone ages using analysis of variance.

All cones set before 1981 were counted in each sample. The mean number of seeds released per plant was then estimated from the product of the measured annual rate of release per cone age class and the mean number of cones in each class. Cones set before 1981 were allocated to the nearest age class and a correction was made for viability.

# *The effect of frequent fires*

The effect of three successive fires, separated by intervals of identical length, on the number of plants in a hypothetical stand of each species was estimated. Plants living in the first interval were called first generation and in the second, second generation. The first generation immediate pre-fire number was set at 50 and model stands were assumed to be similar to the sample stands in other respects, such as density. #### *The effect of frequent fires*

The alternative values of E were set at 0.5 and 0.05. These bounded the range observed in the field (Table 1). #### **Discussion**

### *Effects of frequent fires*

The importance of emergence and survival was reflected in the variability of the interval between fires at which stand replacement would be possible (Fig. 7). Burning at an interval close to 13 years could be done with little regard to other factors such as season or intensity of fire without risk ofa decline in numbers. The low levels of emergence and survival (Tables 1,2) used to produce this estimate were the product of a severe drought in the area (Bureau of Meteorology, pers. comm.). It is likely that fires in most years will produce at least a similar or larger number of seedlings. Survival of established plants may also be higher, for this reason.

Fire-managers may wish to burn as often as twice a decade, hence it is necessary to know the limit to which fire frequency can be reduced below 13 years without risking a serious decline in numbers. Seasons and intensities of fire may become important in such

circumstances as will year to year variability in rainfall.

Bradstock (1985) found that emergence in *B. ericifolia* and *P. pulchella* varied with rainfall, soil moisture and temperature. High summer temperatures impose a form of exogenous dormancy on seeds (definition of Mott & Groves 1981), restricting emergence to the cooler months. Seeds which lie on the soil over summer lose some viability. The amount of emergence was positively correlated with the period of time the soil surface (0-1.0 cm) remains at field capacity after rain. Seed predation was minimal in burnt areas.

Rainfall near the coast in the Sydney Region is highest, on average, from January to July (100-130 mm/month), and lowest from August to December (70-80 mm/month); however, there is great year to year variation.

FIG. *5.* Mean number of stored viable seeds (seed-bank) per plant, under two regimes of seed production: continuous ( ), ceased at 30 years ( ).

When evaporation is taken into account, the average period of sustained high soil moisture is May-July (early winter). Emergence may therefore be highest after fires which are timed so that most seeds are released in early winter. Seed-release will be most rapid after high intensity fires (Bradstock & Myerscough 1981; Bradstock 1985) and such fires in late summer-autumn will cause most seeds to be released by early winter. In contrast, low inten-
=== p10
FIG. 6. Estimated annual release of viable seeds per plant in samples of differing age.

FIG. 7. Proportional changes m sizes of stands over two generations of equal length as a function of interval between fires and seedling establishment (maximum o; minimum •). Intersections of estimates with the broken line indicate intervals at which self-replacement is possible (see text).

sity fires at this time will prolong seed-release over winter and spring. Late summer-autumn, high intensity fires will therefore, on average, yield optimum emergence. A similar fire regime giving optimum emergence in other species of serotinous Proteaceae has been observed by Specht *et al.* (1958), Specht (1981), Bond *et at.* (1984), Cowling and Lamont (1984a, 1984b, 1985), McMahon (1984). Mechanisms in each case were generally similar to those described here.

While mortality of plants older than 100 days was due mainly to drought, younger seedlings died during both short dry spells and heavy rain (Bradstock 1985) when they were broken by raindrop impact or washed away. Bradstock (1985) concluded that the risk of death at the most vulnerable age (< 100 days; Table 2) would be minimized when seedlings emerged in early winter. This reinforced the conclusion that late summer fires are optimal in producing seedlings.

After successive fires at 8 years, the proportional change in second generation stand size may vary from 9.8 to 0.5 in *B. ericifolia* and from 7.2 to 0.6 in *P. pulchella* (Fig. 7). The daily rainfall patterns for Sydney over 50 years (Bureau ofMeterology, pers. comm.) show that a winter containing two successive months of low soil surface moisture occurs on average once every decade whereas very wet winters in which the soil is more or less continually moist occur several times a decade (Bradstock 1985). Thus fires of optimal season and intensity occurring 8 years apart would be followed by a dry winter and a subsequent decline in postfire numbers, once every 80-100 years. More usually these fires would be followed by wet winters which would permit an increase in numbers. Hence an optimal regime in terms of season and intensity with an 8-10 year interval may cause fluctuations in numbers but is unlikely to send either species into a persistent decline if sustained over a period of up to 100 years. A 6-8 year cycle would be hazardous, due to a lower seed-bank and the increased probability of encountering dry post-fire conditions.

Reproduction is delayed in *B. ericifolia* growing on shallow soils and such stands may decline when fires occur less than 15 years apart. Observations indicate that the primary juvenile period may extend to more than 8 years and also that the seed-bank size may be less than on deep soils.

There are, therefore, two consecutive phases in which plants are susceptible to recurrent fires: first, during the primary juvenile period and second, the subsequent time up to the age at which exact self-replacement of stands is possible. So far most attention has been given to describing the lengths of primary juvenile periods. Values given here fell within the ranges already reported for these species (Benson 1985) and for other serotinous obligate seeders of the Proteaceae (3-11 years; Kruger 1983; Lamont 1985). Measurements of this second critical phase need to be made if serotinous obligate seeders are to be used as indicator species in fire-prone vegetation. Replacement ages for the study species were similar, despite differences in seedling-survival, early rates of development of seed-bank and primary juvenile period. Gill and McMahon (1986) reported that in *Banksia ornata.* a serotinous obligate seeder, common in parts of southern Australia, stand replacement may be likely after 16 years of age if postfire emergence took place from 20% of available seeds. Seeds first become available at about 6 years in *B. ornata* (Gill & McMahon 1986), a figure comparable to that in *B. ericifolia* and *P. pulchella.* Despite this similarity, populations *of B. ornata* may decline under some repeated cycles of fire less than 15 years apart, whilst *B. ericifolia* and *P. pulchella* populations may increase or remain stable. This difference was primarily due to a slower rate of accumulation of seed-bank in *B. ornata.* though other possible differences in projected survival rate were also present. Similarly, Kruger and Bigalke (1984) reported that in *Protea repens,* a shrub of the South African fynbos, the primary juvenile period may be 4-5 years (ripe seeds first available), but replacement age may be 10-12 years. It is most prudent to conclude that there is little current evidence of any consistent linkage between these key events. Further demographic studies amongst a wider range of species are needed to confirm this.

## *Effects of infrequent fires*

The present study was hampered by a lack of old populations (>25 years). This prevented direct measurements of life span and seed-production in very old plants. It was necessary to extrapolate trends from younger populations and anecdotal evidence to describe what happens when fire is excluded for long periods.

In the seed-bank models (Fig. 5) seed-production was arbitrarily set to cease at 30 years. However, Bradstock and Myerscough (1981) observed the occurrence of stands of *B. ericifolia* older than this (these also contained *P. pulchella)* in which seeds were still being produced. The modeled storages will therefore

underestimate the trend in real stands. Nevertheless, these suggested that enough seeds would be available for replacement for up to about 45 years in *B. ericifolia* and 90 years in *P. pulchella.* The life spans of these species are more likely to be less than 50 years (Bradstock & Myerscough 1981), hence in reality, senescence will hasten the decline of the seed-bank through the death of plants and replacement ages may be much nearer 30 years. The fall of viable seeds onto the litter and soil will increase as a consequence and, if seed-production occurs beyond 30 years, this pool of released seeds will be very large. If these assumptions are correct, changes in number and seedbank may be quite similar in their pattern to those described by Gill and McMahon 1986 for *B. ornata.* Kruger and Bigalke (1984) also reported a similar decline in numbers after 30 years in some serotinous obligate seeders from South African shrublands, and suggested that life spans for dominant species of this kind fell within the range 20-50 years.

In samples that are more than 20 years of age the number of viable seeds released each year (Fig. 6) greatly exceeded the number of plants that died annually (Figs 1, 2). Bradstock (1985) found that the heavy cover of plants and seedling predators restricted establishment from this pool of available seeds. However, a few seedlings are likely to survive in both species. A rough calculation can be done to estimate the number which may establish in a stand of 50 plants. Average conditions of soil moisture in any year will usually be adequate to give 10% emergence of available seeds. If 5% of these survive for 3 years (about eight times lower survival than in burnt conditions; Table 2), then 21-24 year old stands would produce two *{B. ericifolia)* and 12 *{P. pulchella)* seedlings annually. Such recruits would join the ranks of small suppressed plants which are subject to high mortality and would probably have little chance of reproducing (Bradstock 1985).

At greater ages, when seed-release and mortality may be high, gaps in the canopy caused by senescence of dominants may appear. Seedling predators may become satiated as a result (e.g. Bond 1984a; O'Dowd & Gill 1984) and these conditions may promote the emergence, growth and reproduction of new plants. The relative abilities of *B. ericifolia. P. pulchella* 
=== p12
and other species to exploit gaps and openings may determine whether self-perpetuation in large numbers is possible in the absence of fire. More work is needed to determine regeneration processes in older stands and their scarcity means that some effort needs to be made to preserve unburnt areas in the future.

Fires, 20-30 years apart, will create very high density stands and the absence of these in the study area may be due to a history of burning at a higher frequency.

### *Effects of density*

Fire regimes may be used to increase or decrease the density of stands. For instance, if the relationships in Figs 1-7 hold true for much of the potential range of densities, then it may be possible, for example, to thin very dense stands and then hold them in this state. Several adverse fire-cycles (e.g. low intensity spring fires, less than 10 years apart) followed by a 10 year cycle of high intensity autumn fires would achieve this result.

The density of a stand will change with age as plants die and the chronosequence in Table 3 may indicate the approximate trend. Bradstock (1985) found that density had no effect on the survival of seedlings older than 100 days. There were also no obvious effects of density on survival at older ages in either species, including the 1975 samples in *P. pulchella* (Fig. 2; Table 3), although dead plants tended to be small suppressed individuals in both species. Morris and Myerscough (1983, 1988) found evidence for density-dependent mortality in *B. ericifolia* stands of very high density (initial sample: 140 plants m^-) between the ages of 4 and 9 years.

In both *B. ericifolia* and *P. pulchella,* the proportion of plants that continues to produce cones declined with age (Bradstock 1985) so that over time the increase in reproductive effort (Fig. 4) came from a small number of dominant individuals (Bradstock 1985). This pattern of reproduction amongst individuals may affect the relationship between density and seed-bank if the survival of dominant reproductive plants is unaffected by the number of suppressed individuals. The number of plants which reproduce and the amount of seeds produced may then be fixed above a moderate threshold of density, as indicated by

experimental studies in other single-species populations (Harper 1977; Silvertown 1982). Further evidence of Morris and Myerscough (1988) showed that *B. ericifolia* plants at densities of 27.5 plants m~2 had set a mean of 345 ± 92 seeds m~2 at 8 years whereas high density plants (142 m-2) produced 225 ± 80 seeds m~^. If seed-bank size is fixed across the upper range of densities then its prime determinant will be stand age. The perpetuation of very dense stands would then be possible only after longer fire-free intervals than those described here for lower density samples.

Density and numbers may also be influenced by pollinators. Paton and Turner (1985) found that introduced bees may double the numbers of seeds set in *B. ericifolia* cones. The introduction of exotic bees may therefore have caused a massive increase in density and numbers in stands containing this species without any concurrent change in fire frequency. Other changes in species composition may have followed.

All components of fire regime can influence a change in numbers and density, between generations, of *B. ericifolia* and *P. pulchella.* However, the largest change was due to differences in the age at which stands were burnt and the proportion of seeds which emerged as seedlings. Seasonal controls on seedling establishment, lengths of primary juvenile periods, effects of seed or seedling predators in unburnt conditions, and changes in structure of old stands and life spans, are generally similar in southern hemisphere species, particularly within the family, Proteaceae. However, demographic behaviour of fire-prone species cannot be predicted solely from any single characteristic such as survival, degree of serotiny (seed-survival in cones), seed-bank size or success of emergence.
