20	## **Flowering, seed dispersal, seed predation and seedling recruitment in two pyrogenic flowering resprouters**
21	
22	*Andrew J*. *Denham*<sup>A</sup> *and Tony D*. *Auld*
23	
24	Biodiversity Research Group, NSW National Parks and Wildlife Service, PO Box 1967, Hurstville, NSW 2220, Australia.
25	
26	ACorresponding author; email: andrew.denham@npws.nsw.gov.au
27	
28	*Abstract.* A few resprouting plants in fire-prone environments have no local seed bank (soil or canopy) when a fire occurs. These species rely on post-fire flowering and the production of non-dormant seeds to exploit favourable post-fire establishment and growth conditions. For two such pyrogenic flowering species (*Doryanthes excelsa* Correa and *Telopea speciosissima* (Smith) R.Br.), we examined the timing of seed release, patterns of fruit production, seed dispersal, seed predation and seedling establishment following a fire in the Sydney region of southeastern Australia. Both species took some 19 months after the fire to flower and the first seeds were released 2 years after the fire. *D*. *excelsa* flowered and fruited only once after the fire. For *T*. *speciosissima*, plants also flowered at least once more in the subsequent 5 years, but produced seed in only the first three post-fire flowering years. Fruit production differed between species, with fruiting individuals of *D*. *excelsa* producing fewer infructescences, similar numbers of follicles, but many more seeds per follicle than fruiting individuals of *T*. *speciosissima*. Ultimately, *D*. *excelsa* produced approximately six times as many seeds per m2 and four times as many seeds per adult in one flowering season than *T*. *speciosissima* did after four flowering (three successful fruiting) seasons.
29	
30	Seeds were passively dispersed from fruits borne 3–4 m (*D*. *excelsa*) or 1–2 m (*T*. *speciosissima*) above the ground. Most seeds were found within 5 m (*D*. *excelsa*) or 3 m (*T*. *speciosissima*) of parent plants. The primary seed shadow of both species was a poor predictor of the distribution of seedlings, with more seedlings occurring further from the adults than expected from the distribution of seeds. Seed loss to predators was high in both species in exclusion experiments where mammals had access to clumps of seeds (77–88%). It was variable and generally lower (8–65%) in experiments where seeds were not locally clumped. However, for *T*. *speciosissima*, at one site, some 65% of seeds were lost to mammals and invertebrates in these latter experiments. At this site, these losses appeared to influence subsequent recruitment levels, as very low seedling densities were observed.
31	
32	For both species, germination of seedlings first occurred some 2.5–3 years after the passage of the fire. The percentage of seeds produced to seedlings successfully established was low in *D*. *excelsa* (2–3%) and more variable across sites and years in *T*. *speciosissima* (0–18%). Resultant post-fire seedling densities of *D*. *excelsa* (two sites) and *T*. *speciosissima* at one site were similar, but they were much lower at the *T*. *speciosissima* site that had high levels of seed predation. Both *D*. *excelsa* and *T*. *speciosissima* are amongst the slowest woody resprouting species to recruit seedlings after fire in south-eastern Australia and lag years behind species with soil or canopy seed banks.
33	
34	#### **Introduction**
35	
36	In fire-prone habitats, recruitment in plant species is frequently linked to the passage of a fire (Tyler 1995). This results from at least two main mechanisms. First, in species with soil seed banks, seed dormancy may be broken by the passage of fires (e.g. via heat, smoke, charred wood: Keeley 1991; Brown 1993; or interactions of these factors: Keith 1997; Morris 2000). Examples include many legumes (Jeffery *et al.* 1988; Auld and O'Connell 1991) and nonleguminous species (Brown 1993; Dixon *et al.* 1995). Second, in species with canopy seed banks, fires result in the mass opening of fruits and the release of seeds (Bond *et al.* 1984; Lamont *et al.* 1991).
37	
38	However, a number of species have no available seed storage in either the soil or canopy at the time of the passage of a fire (Keith 1996). A few may rely on dispersal from unburnt areas, but most have mechanisms that allow established plants to survive fire via buried lignotubers, rhizomes or buds (protected meristems). These species usually flower soon after fire and then release seeds (Gill 1981; Frost 1984; Johnson *et al.* 1994; Bond and van Wilgen 1996; Carrington 1999). For species dependant on post-fire flowering for recruitment (pyrogenic flowering resprouters), 
39	=== p3
40	the timing and magnitude of this flowering will influence opportunities for post-fire seedling establishment. The longer the interval between the passage of a fire and seedling recruitment, the more of the available resources such as light, nutrients and space, are likely to have been captured by other resprouting species or by those species with soil or canopy seed banks that can recruit in the immediate post-fire period.
41	
42	Many individuals of pyrogenic flowering resprouting species in south-eastern Australia appear to have a single post-fire flowering (e.g. *Angophora hispida*, Auld 1986; *Blandfordia nobilis*, Johnson *et al.* 1994; *Lomatia silaifolia*, Denham and Whelan 2000; *Xanthorrhoea australis*, Gill and Ingwersen 1976, but see; *X*. *fulva*, Taylor *et al.* 1998). In such cases, this represents the only opportunity for recruitment between fires. For other species, flowering may extend over several years following a fire (e.g. *T*. *speciosissima*, Pyke 1983; Bradstock 1995; Goldingay 2000; *Xanthorrhoea australis*, Curtis 1998). However, the timing of recruitment in pyrogenic flowering resprouting species has been little studied and the degree to which each post-fire flowering event contributes to recruitment is unexplored.
43	
44	In the post-fire environment, the impact of seed predation may be reduced due to lower predator abundance and also via predator satiation, in the case of serotinous seed release (Whelan 1995; Bond and van Wilgen 1996; Myerscough *et al.* 2000). However, the seeds of pyrogenic flowering resprouters are likely to be released after most seeds from serotinous species have germinated and, consequently, would not benefit from any predator satiation effects from serotinous seed release. In addition, populations of predators may have recovered by this time. All pyrogenic flowering resprouters are thought to release seeds in a non-dormant state (Bell *et al.* 1993; Bond and van Wilgen 1996) and hence form transient soil seed banks (*sensu* Parker and Kelly 1989).
45	
46	In this study, we assessed post-fire reproduction and the patterns of seedling recruitment after a wildfire in 1994, in two resprouting species reliant on post-fire flowering for seed production (*Doryanthes excelsa* and *Telopea speciosissima*), from the Sydney area of south-eastern Australia. We examined (i) the timing of flowering and magnitude of seed production over 5 years after the fire; (ii) the pattern of seed and seedling dispersal; (iii) the level of post-dispersal seed predation; and (iv) the proportion of seeds released that resulted in successful establishment of new plants.
47	
48	#### **Methods**
49	
50	#### *Study species*
51	
52	*Doryanthes excelsa* Correa (Gymea lily—Doryanthaceae) is a large perennial rosette plant with a bulbous rhizome and long broad linear leaves up to 3 m long. It is apparently capable of asexual reproduction by branching of the rhizome (Nash 1996). It grows in dry sclerophyll forests and woodlands on soils derived from sandstone containing some clay and is restricted to the Sydney Basin in south-eastern Australia, with three outlying populations in northern New South Wales (Harden 1990–1993). The species survives fire by having apical buds protected in underground leaf bases. It flowers in a large, red inflorescence held up to 5 m above the foliage of the plant (Harden 1990–1993). Fire appears to stimulate flowering, although sporadic flowering does occur in the absence of fire (Nash 1996). The mechanism determining flowering is unknown (Beeh 1996; Nash 1996).
53	
54	*Telopea speciosissima* (Smith) R.Br. (waratah—Proteaceae) is a tall shrub, generally 2–4 m, which is also known for its striking red blooms that emerge above the resprouting shrubby vegetation in the post-fire environment. It is common in dry sclerophyll forest and woodlands on the central coast and central and southern tablelands of New South Wales (Harden 1990–1993). The species survives fire by having dormant buds protected in an underground lignotuber (Bradstock 1995). Aerial stems are completely regrown after each fire.
55	
56	#### *Sites*
57	
58	Three sample sites within a 10-km radius were chosen in Royal National Park, about 35 km south of Sydney (34°03′S, 151°03′E). All sites occurred on soils derived from the Triassic Hawkesbury Sandstone Formation, although Site 1 (with an ironstone influence) and Site 2 (with an alluvial influence) were on soils slightly more fertile than Site 3. At Site 1, both study species occurred in ironstone woodland vegetation (D. Keith and M. Tozer, unpubl. data), with an overstorey of *Eucalyptus sieberi*, *Corymbia gummifera*, *Banksia serrata*, *Xylomelum pyriforme* and *Ceratopetalum gummiferum*. The shrubby understorey included *Grevillea diffusa*, *Banksia spinulosa*, *Lissanthe strigosa*, *Prostanthera* sp., *Isopogon anemonifolius*, *Acacia myrtifolia*, *Xanthorrhoea media*, *Lomandra* spp. and *Dianella* sp. The vegetation at Site 2 (*D*. *excelsa* only) is Sandstone Gully Forest (D. Keith and M. Tozer, unpubl. data), with an overstorey of *Angophora costata*, *Banksia serrata*, *Ceratopetalum gummiferum*, *Eucalyptus piperita* and *E*. *sieberi* and a shrubby understorey that included *Boronia pinnata*, *Grevillea mucronulata*, *Acacia terminalis*, *Lomandra longifolia* and *Caustis flexuosa*. At Site 3 (*T*. *speciosissima* only) the vegetation is Sandstone Heath (D. Keith and M. Tozer, unpubl. data), with a short overstorey of *Corymbia gummifera*, *Eucalyptus obstans*, *E*. *sclerophylla* and *Banksia serrata* and a shrubby understorey that included *Lambertia formosa*, *Lissanthe strigosa* and sedges including *Xanthorrhoea media*, *Restio dimorpha* and *Cyathochaeta diandra*. Plant nomenclature follows Harden (1990–1993).
59	
60	All sites were burnt in January 1994. Before 1994, there was variation in fire history across sites. The eastern part of Site 1 (sampled for *D*. *excelsa*) and Site 3 were burnt in 1988. The western part of Site 1, separated by a road from the eastern part (sampled for both study species), and Site 2 were burnt in the early 1980s (NPWS fire records; D. Keith, pers. comm.).
61	
62	#### *Timing of flowering and seed release*
63	
64	The three study sites were monitored to observe flowering after the January 1994 fire for both species up until December 2000. As both *D*. *excelsa* and *T*. *speciosissima* flower in July–October, this involved seven potential flowering seasons (1994–2000). General observations were also made throughout Royal National Park to determine whether the pattern of the study sites was representative of the general response of the study species to fire in this area. The timing of fruit development and seed release was recorded for the first four flowering seasons after the 1994 fire.
65	
66	#### *Estimates of seed production and seedling establishment*
67	
68	Six 30 × 30-m plots were established as follows: *D*. *excelsa*, two plots at each of Sites 1 and 2; *T*. *speciosissima*, one plot at each of Sites 1 and 3. For both study species, within each plot at each site, the numbers of infructescences and follicles on all plants were scored each year (1994–2000). To estimate the number of seeds per follicle, intact
69	=== p4
70	follicles were collected in autumn 1996, prior to dehiscence, for each species from each site. For *T*. *speciosissima*, samples of 23 and 25 follicles were collected from Sites 1 and 3, respectively, while for *D*. *excelsa*, samples of 15 and 29 follicles were collected from Sites 1 and 2, respectively. Seeds within these follicles were scored after dehiscence in the laboratory. For *T*. *speciosissima*, only those seeds judged as 'filled' (i.e. likely to be viable) were included in this assessment (see also Bradstock 1995; Denham and Whelan 2000). For *D*. *excelsa*, no assessment was made, although Nash (1996) found that the average viability of seeds collected from a number of locations (not including Royal National Park) was 86% (±6.2 s.e.). The individuals used to estimate numbers of seeds per follicle were sampled from outside the plots to avoid impacts on primary seed dispersal and seedling recruitment. The density of seeds per plot was estimated by multiplying the number of intact follicles by the estimate of the mean number of seeds per follicle and dividing this value by the area of each plot (900 m2 ).
71	
72	To estimate the magnitude of post-fire seedling recruitment for both study species, five randomly allocated transects each 1 × 30 m were searched for seedlings in spring 1998, within each of the 30 × 30-m plots. For *T*. *speciosissima*, we assessed the probable fruiting year from which seedlings were established, by comparisons with other seedlings of known age within the sites.
73	
74	#### *Primary seed dispersal*
75	
76	The seeds of *D*. *excelsa* are disc-like, about 15 mm in diameter, 2 mm thick, have a dry spongy texture and weigh approximately 43 mg (Westoby *et al.* 1990; Nash 1996; A. J. Denham, pers. obs.). The seeds of *T*. *speciosissima* are winged and weigh approximately 72 mg (Westoby *et al.* 1990). Westoby *et al.* (1990) considered *T*. *speciosissima* to be adapted for wind dispersal, but could only suggest that the spongy texture of *D*. *excelsa* seed could serve for wind or water dispersal. Initial seed fall from dehisced follicles in both species is passive and movement in the air appears likely to be the main means of dispersal away from the infructescence.
77	
78	The spatial pattern of initial seed fall was estimated by counting seeds found on the ground in four orthogonal transects along compass bearings from each of five isolated plants at Site 1 for *D*. *excelsa* and Sites 1 and 3 for *T*. *speciosissima*. Because of time constraints, this was not done at Site 2 for *D*. *excelsa*. Searches were done in June–August of 1996, when most seeds had fallen from the follicles. Some further redistribution of seeds along the soil surface by wind and rain after this time is likely (Lamont *et al.* 1993; Hammill *et al.* 1998). The transects for *D*. *excelsa* started approximately 0.25 m from the centre of each clump, because of the space occupied by the leaf bases of the plants. Counts of numbers of seeds were made every 0.1 m along each transect. Transects were 0.5 m wide and limited to 7.25 m long as there were no seeds seen in initial searches beyond 7.15 m. For *T*. *speciosissima*, the area occupied by the stems was included in the transects. In preliminary searches around *T*. *speciosissima* adults, no seeds were found more than 3 m from adults at Site 1 and 2 m from adults at Site 3, so the transect lengths were reduced to 3.5 and 2.5 m, respectively.
79	
80	#### *Seed predation*
81	
82	The fates of recently released seeds on the ground were examined during the initial seed release after the 1994 fire (i.e. in 1996), in two trials. First, an exclusion experiment was used to investigate the agents responsible for and the degree of post-dispersal predation at each site. It was assumed that no secondary dispersal of seeds by invertebrates such as ants was likely, since neither species have lipid bodies attached to their seeds. Westoby *et al.* (1990) suggested that neither species is myrmecochorous and field observations supported this. A block design was used with two treatments and 10 seeds per treatment per block. This experiment was set up for *D*. *excelsa* at Sites 1 and 2 and for *T*. *speciosissima* at Sites 1 and 3 as follows:
83	
84	(a) caged: cages (15 × 15 cm × 5 cm high with 1-cm<sup>2</sup> mesh size) were used to exclude vertebrate predators, while still allowing access to most invertebrates. To prevent seeds from washing away in heavy rain, a PVC ring sawn from pipe 10 cm in diameter and about 1 cm tall was placed on the ground. This ring was pushed into the soil leaving only the top 0.5 cm protruding. The cage was placed over the ring and fastened down with wire stakes.
85	
86	(b) uncaged: where only the PVC ring was used. This allowed access to both invertebrates and vertebrates.
87	
88	Ten blocks consisting of a caged and an uncaged treatment, were used for each species, at each site. The blocks were placed about 5 m apart along a transect through the site, with separate transects for each species at Site 1.
89	
90	The number of seeds remaining in each treatment block was recorded every day for the first week and approximately every second day for the following 10 weeks. Additionally, any information concerning the condition of seeds (such as whether chewed or germinated) or the presence of testa remains was recorded at each visit.
91	
92	Second, for both study species, a trial was established to examine the level of predation on seeds that were placed singly at random locations throughout the plots, rather than clumped as above (see Auld and Denham 1999, 2001). These trials were established for *D*. *excelsa* in two plots at Site 1 and in one plot at Site 2 and for *T*. *speciosissima* in one plot at each of Sites 1 and 3. A single seed was placed at each of 10 randomly located positions according to the 30 × 30-m grid established at each site, with the location marked by a steel stake 0.2 m away. Additional batches of 10 seeds were similarly placed in new random locations each week for the following 3 weeks. The fate of these seeds was followed for the next 10 weeks, with details recorded as for the exclusion experiment. Only 'filled' seeds were used in these experiments.
93	
94	#### *Seedling dispersal*
95	
96	The following two different estimates were made of the dispersal pattern of seedlings around adult plants:
97	
98	(a) the ground was searched for seedlings up to a distance of 10 m from fruiting plants around five isolated plants of *D*. *excelsa* at Site 1. The distance of each seedling from the centre of the adult was measured. The adults included two of those used to sample primary seed dispersal. Sufficient seedlings were not available at the other three adults sampled for primary seed dispersal. For *T*. *speciosissima*, this technique was not used as adults continued to flower after the first year.
99	
100	(b) for *D*. *excelsa* at Sites 1 and 2 and *T*. *speciosissima* at Sites 1 and 3, the distance of each seedling from the centre of the nearest parent was measured for all seedlings observed in the transects used for estimating seedling establishment (above). Because of the overall low number of seedlings observed for *T*. *speciosissima* at Site 3, the entire 30 × 30-m plot was surveyed. This estimate included overlapping seed shadows from adult plants, as typically occurs in the field.
101	
102	#### *Analyses*
103	
104	To test the hypothesis that fruit and seed production varied across sites and years within the study area, estimates of infructescence and follicle production per fruiting plant were compared in *D*. *excelsa* by a nested 2-factor ANOVA with plots nested within sites and in *T*. *speciosissima* across sites and years when fruit was produced, by a 2-factor ANOVA without replication. Estimates of seed production per m2 were compared in *D*. *excelsa* across sites by a 1-factor ANOVA with plots as replicates and in *T*. *speciosissima* across sites and fruiting years by a 2-factor ANOVA without replication (Zar 1996).
105	
106	To test the hypothesis that vertebrate seed predators had an impact on the number of seeds available for germination (the seed predation 
107	=== p5
108	exclusion experiment), the proportions of seeds remaining in each replicate treatment within the 10 blocks after 75 days were compared by a 3-factor ANOVA (factors were treatment, site and block, with blocks nested within sites) for each species separately. The hypothesis that the two species suffered different levels of predation at Site 1, where both *D*. *excelsa* and *T*. *speciosissima* were sampled, was tested by a 3-factor ANOVA with species and caging treatment (with blocks nested within species) as factors.
109	
110	At lower seed densities than in the seed predation exclusion experiment (the single seeds trial) we tested the hypothesis that predation varied across sites. For *T*. *speciosissima*, the proportions of seeds remaining in each weekly cohort of 10 seeds at the end of the study (after 9 weeks) were compared across sites by a 1-factor ANOVA. Data for *D*. *excelsa* were similarly analysed, using both plots at Site 1 and the single plot at Site 2 as three levels in a 'location' factor. Again, it was possible to test the hypothesis that the two species suffered different levels of predation at Site 1 at this lower seed density. Here, only the western of the two *D*. *excelsa* plots was used, as it was adjacent to the *T*. *speciosissima* plot (1-factor ANOVA).
111	
112	We tested the hypothesis that seedling establishment varied across sites in both species and across years for *T*. *speciosissima*. In *D*. *excelsa*, the number of seedlings per transect was compared across sites by a nested 2-factor ANOVA with plots nested in sites. For *T*. *speciosissima*, the number of seedlings per transect was compared across sites and fruiting year of origin by a 2-factor ANOVA.
113	
114	For each ANOVA, homogeneity of variances was tested by Cochran's test. Where variances were significantly heterogeneous an arcsine transformation was applied to proportion data and a square-root transformation was applied to count data. If variances were still heterogeneous, the analysis was carried out on the raw data with a conservative approach to rejection of the null hypothesis (Underwood 1981).
115	
116	To test the hypothesis that the distributions of seedlings around plants were the same as the distributions of seeds around plants, a number of Kolmogorov–Smirnov goodness-of-fit tests were done.
117	
118	(i) For *D*. *excelsa* at Site 1, seed and seedling data from the isolated plants were placed into 0.1-m classes and frequency counts of seeds or seedlings were obtained from each distance class for all five individuals. The proportions of seeds or seedlings per distance class were then determined. Seedling data for distances less than 0.25 m from the adult were omitted, since data for seed distribution were not obtained at this distance, due to the occupation of most of the available space by the parent plants. Similarly, seedling distances greater than 7.15 m were omitted since this was distance of the furthest observed seed. A Kolmogorov–Smirnov test was used to determine the goodnessof-fit of the seedling distribution (observed) with the seed distribution (predicted) (Zar 1996).
119	
120	(ii) For *D*. *excelsa* at Site 1 and *T*. *speciosissima* at Sites 1 and 3, estimations were made of the goodness-of-fit of the seedling distributions from the plot transect sampling (observed) with the seed distributions from the isolated individuals (expected). Restriction of seedling data to the greatest distance observed for seeds (7.15 m) was as above for *D*. *excelsa*, and to 3.75 m for *T*. *speciosissima*. There was no restriction on the least distance for *T*. *speciosissima*. This test enabled the determination of whether the distribution of seeds around isolated adults adequately explained the distribution of seedlings around adults that were contagiously distributed (a more typical situation) and thus had overlapping seed shadows.
121	
122	(iii) For *D*. *excelsa* at Site 1, the seedling distribution from the five isolated plants ('expected') was compared with that obtained from the plot transect sampling ('observed'). This test assessed how well the distribution of seedlings around isolated plants of *D*. *excelsa* represented the more typical situation of contagiously distributed individuals.
123	
124	#### **Results**
125	
126	#### *Timing of flowering and seed release*
127	
128	For both *D*. *excelsa* and *T*. *speciosissima*, the first flowering after the January 1994 fires occurred in late winter (August) of 1995, some 19 months after the January 1994 fire. This pattern was found at all study sites and more generally across Royal National Park. Fruits matured in the following autumn (March–June 1996), with *D*. *excelsa* first releasing seeds in March 1996 and *T*. *speciosissima* in April 1996. Consequently, seeds were not released into the post-fire habitat until some 25–26 months after the passage of the January 1994 fire. Seed fall was quite prolonged with some seeds still in fruits in June (both species). *D. excelsa* plants in the study plots did not flower in any of the subsequent 5 years, while most *T*. *speciosissima* individuals flowered again the following year and a few in three of the subsequent 4 years (Table 1), with a similar timing of flowering and fruiting to that observed in 1995–1996.
129	
130	#### *Fruit and seed production*
131	
132	In *D*. *excelsa*, the number, and hence density, of flowering plants varied considerably between plots within sites, ranging from six at Site 1, plot 1 (0.2 m–2) to 39 at Site 2, plot 2 (1.3 m–2) (Table 1). There were no significant differences between sites in the mean numbers of infructescences (*F*1,2 = 0.86, *P* = 0.45) or follicles (*F*1,2 = 9.94, *P* = 0.09) produced per fruiting plant, although there were almost twice as many follicles produced at Site 1, plot 1, than at Site 2, plot 2 (Table 1). For *T*. *speciosissima*, the total number of individuals that flowered between 1995 and 2000 varied from 14 at Site 1 to 24 at Site 3 (Table 1). There was no significant difference in the mean number of infructescences (*F*1,2 = 0.4, *P* = 0.59) or follicles (*F*1,2 = 0.003, *P* = 0.96) per fruiting plant between sites across the 1995–1997 flowering seasons. *D. excelsa* had greater seed production per follicle than *T*. *speciosissima* (104, 105 *v.* 11 seeds per follicle, respectively, Table 2). There were no significant differences in the number of seeds per follicle between sites for *T*. *speciosissima* (*F*1,46 = 0.43, *P* = 0.52) or *D*. *excelsa* (*F*1,42 = 0.08, *P* = 0.93) (Table 2). The estimated density of seeds produced by *D*. *excelsa* varied greatly, although not significantly (*F*1,2 = 4.76, *P* = 0.16) across sites, with Site 1 producing 9.9 (±0.4 s.e.) seeds per m<sup>2</sup> and Site 2 producing 17.7 (±3.6 s.e.) (Table 3). The lack of significance in this comparison is likely to be a result of the considerable variation between plots at Site 2, with one plot producing approximately 1.5 times as many seeds as the other. This in turn was largely because of the much higher density of flowering and fruiting plants in plot 2 than in plot 1 of Site 2 (Table 1). There were no significant differences in seed density of *T*. *speciosissima* between sites (*F*1,2 = 1.11, *P* = 0.40) or among years (*F*2,2 = 4.19, *P* = 0.19). In the first post-fire fruiting year (1996), the estimated density of seeds
133	=== p6
134	produced was 1.1 seeds per m<sup>2</sup> at both sites (Table 3). Seed production was higher in the second fruiting year at Site 2, but lower at Site 1. Despite the lack of significance of a year effect in the analysis, at both sites seed production declined dramatically by the third fruiting year (1997) and no seeds were produced in subsequent years (Table 1). ## **Flowering, seed dispersal, seed predation and seedling recruitment in two pyrogenic flowering resprouters**

*Andrew J*. *Denham*<sup>A</sup> *and Tony D*. *Auld*

Biodiversity Research Group, NSW National Parks and Wildlife Service, PO Box 1967, Hurstville, NSW 2220, Australia.

ACorresponding author; email: andrew.denham@npws.nsw.gov.au

*Abstract.* A few resprouting plants in fire-prone environments have no local seed bank (soil or canopy) when a fire occurs. These species rely on post-fire flowering and the production of non-dormant seeds to exploit favourable post-fire establishment and growth conditions. For two such pyrogenic flowering species (*Doryanthes excelsa* Correa and *Telopea speciosissima* (Smith) R.Br.), we examined the timing of seed release, patterns of fruit production, seed dispersal, seed predation and seedling establishment following a fire in the Sydney region of southeastern Australia. Both species took some 19 months after the fire to flower and the first seeds were released 2 years after the fire. *D*. *excelsa* flowered and fruited only once after the fire. For *T*. *speciosissima*, plants also flowered at least once more in the subsequent 5 years, but produced seed in only the first three post-fire flowering years. Fruit production differed between species, with fruiting individuals of *D*. *excelsa* producing fewer infructescences, similar numbers of follicles, but many more seeds per follicle than fruiting individuals of *T*. *speciosissima*. Ultimately, *D*. *excelsa* produced approximately six times as many seeds per m2 and four times as many seeds per adult in one flowering season than *T*. *speciosissima* did after four flowering (three successful fruiting) seasons.

Seeds were passively dispersed from fruits borne 3–4 m (*D*. *excelsa*) or 1–2 m (*T*. *speciosissima*) above the ground. Most seeds were found within 5 m (*D*. *excelsa*) or 3 m (*T*. *speciosissima*) of parent plants. The primary seed shadow of both species was a poor predictor of the distribution of seedlings, with more seedlings occurring further from the adults than expected from the distribution of seeds. Seed loss to predators was high in both species in exclusion experiments where mammals had access to clumps of seeds (77–88%). It was variable and generally lower (8–65%) in experiments where seeds were not locally clumped. However, for *T*. *speciosissima*, at one site, some 65% of seeds were lost to mammals and invertebrates in these latter experiments. At this site, these losses appeared to influence subsequent recruitment levels, as very low seedling densities were observed.

For both species, germination of seedlings first occurred some 2.5–3 years after the passage of the fire. The percentage of seeds produced to seedlings successfully established was low in *D*. *excelsa* (2–3%) and more variable across sites and years in *T*. *speciosissima* (0–18%). Resultant post-fire seedling densities of *D*. *excelsa* (two sites) and *T*. *speciosissima* at one site were similar, but they were much lower at the *T*. *speciosissima* site that had high levels of seed predation. Both *D*. *excelsa* and *T*. *speciosissima* are amongst the slowest woody resprouting species to recruit seedlings after fire in south-eastern Australia and lag years behind species with soil or canopy seed banks.

#### **Introduction**

In fire-prone habitats, recruitment in plant species is frequently linked to the passage of a fire (Tyler 1995). This results from at least two main mechanisms. First, in species with soil seed banks, seed dormancy may be broken by the passage of fires (e.g. via heat, smoke, charred wood: Keeley 1991; Brown 1993; or interactions of these factors: Keith 1997; Morris 2000). Examples include many legumes (Jeffery *et al.* 1988; Auld and O'Connell 1991) and nonleguminous species (Brown 1993; Dixon *et al.* 1995). Second, in species with canopy seed banks, fires result in the mass opening of fruits and the release of seeds (Bond *et al.* 1984; Lamont *et al.* 1991).

However, a number of species have no available seed storage in either the soil or canopy at the time of the passage of a fire (Keith 1996). A few may rely on dispersal from unburnt areas, but most have mechanisms that allow established plants to survive fire via buried lignotubers, rhizomes or buds (protected meristems). These species usually flower soon after fire and then release seeds (Gill 1981; Frost 1984; Johnson *et al.* 1994; Bond and van Wilgen 1996; Carrington 1999). For species dependant on post-fire flowering for recruitment (pyrogenic flowering resprouters), 
=== p3
the timing and magnitude of this flowering will influence opportunities for post-fire seedling establishment. The longer the interval between the passage of a fire and seedling recruitment, the more of the available resources such as light, nutrients and space, are likely to have been captured by other resprouting species or by those species with soil or canopy seed banks that can recruit in the immediate post-fire period.

Many individuals of pyrogenic flowering resprouting species in south-eastern Australia appear to have a single post-fire flowering (e.g. *Angophora hispida*, Auld 1986; *Blandfordia nobilis*, Johnson *et al.* 1994; *Lomatia silaifolia*, Denham and Whelan 2000; *Xanthorrhoea australis*, Gill and Ingwersen 1976, but see; *X*. *fulva*, Taylor *et al.* 1998). In such cases, this represents the only opportunity for recruitment between fires. For other species, flowering may extend over several years following a fire (e.g. *T*. *speciosissima*, Pyke 1983; Bradstock 1995; Goldingay 2000; *Xanthorrhoea australis*, Curtis 1998). However, the timing of recruitment in pyrogenic flowering resprouting species has been little studied and the degree to which each post-fire flowering event contributes to recruitment is unexplored.

In the post-fire environment, the impact of seed predation may be reduced due to lower predator abundance and also via predator satiation, in the case of serotinous seed release (Whelan 1995; Bond and van Wilgen 1996; Myerscough *et al.* 2000). However, the seeds of pyrogenic flowering resprouters are likely to be released after most seeds from serotinous species have germinated and, consequently, would not benefit from any predator satiation effects from serotinous seed release. In addition, populations of predators may have recovered by this time. All pyrogenic flowering resprouters are thought to release seeds in a non-dormant state (Bell *et al.* 1993; Bond and van Wilgen 1996) and hence form transient soil seed banks (*sensu* Parker and Kelly 1989).

In this study, we assessed post-fire reproduction and the patterns of seedling recruitment after a wildfire in 1994, in two resprouting species reliant on post-fire flowering for seed production (*Doryanthes excelsa* and *Telopea speciosissima*), from the Sydney area of south-eastern Australia. We examined (i) the timing of flowering and magnitude of seed production over 5 years after the fire; (ii) the pattern of seed and seedling dispersal; (iii) the level of post-dispersal seed predation; and (iv) the proportion of seeds released that resulted in successful establishment of new plants.

#### **Methods**

#### *Study species*

*Doryanthes excelsa* Correa (Gymea lily—Doryanthaceae) is a large perennial rosette plant with a bulbous rhizome and long broad linear leaves up to 3 m long. It is apparently capable of asexual reproduction by branching of the rhizome (Nash 1996). It grows in dry sclerophyll forests and woodlands on soils derived from sandstone containing some clay and is restricted to the Sydney Basin in south-eastern Australia, with three outlying populations in northern New South Wales (Harden 1990–1993). The species survives fire by having apical buds protected in underground leaf bases. It flowers in a large, red inflorescence held up to 5 m above the foliage of the plant (Harden 1990–1993). Fire appears to stimulate flowering, although sporadic flowering does occur in the absence of fire (Nash 1996). The mechanism determining flowering is unknown (Beeh 1996; Nash 1996).

*Telopea speciosissima* (Smith) R.Br. (waratah—Proteaceae) is a tall shrub, generally 2–4 m, which is also known for its striking red blooms that emerge above the resprouting shrubby vegetation in the post-fire environment. It is common in dry sclerophyll forest and woodlands on the central coast and central and southern tablelands of New South Wales (Harden 1990–1993). The species survives fire by having dormant buds protected in an underground lignotuber (Bradstock 1995). Aerial stems are completely regrown after each fire.

#### *Sites*

Three sample sites within a 10-km radius were chosen in Royal National Park, about 35 km south of Sydney (34°03′S, 151°03′E). All sites occurred on soils derived from the Triassic Hawkesbury Sandstone Formation, although Site 1 (with an ironstone influence) and Site 2 (with an alluvial influence) were on soils slightly more fertile than Site 3. At Site 1, both study species occurred in ironstone woodland vegetation (D. Keith and M. Tozer, unpubl. data), with an overstorey of *Eucalyptus sieberi*, *Corymbia gummifera*, *Banksia serrata*, *Xylomelum pyriforme* and *Ceratopetalum gummiferum*. The shrubby understorey included *Grevillea diffusa*, *Banksia spinulosa*, *Lissanthe strigosa*, *Prostanthera* sp., *Isopogon anemonifolius*, *Acacia myrtifolia*, *Xanthorrhoea media*, *Lomandra* spp. and *Dianella* sp. The vegetation at Site 2 (*D*. *excelsa* only) is Sandstone Gully Forest (D. Keith and M. Tozer, unpubl. data), with an overstorey of *Angophora costata*, *Banksia serrata*, *Ceratopetalum gummiferum*, *Eucalyptus piperita* and *E*. *sieberi* and a shrubby understorey that included *Boronia pinnata*, *Grevillea mucronulata*, *Acacia terminalis*, *Lomandra longifolia* and *Caustis flexuosa*. At Site 3 (*T*. *speciosissima* only) the vegetation is Sandstone Heath (D. Keith and M. Tozer, unpubl. data), with a short overstorey of *Corymbia gummifera*, *Eucalyptus obstans*, *E*. *sclerophylla* and *Banksia serrata* and a shrubby understorey that included *Lambertia formosa*, *Lissanthe strigosa* and sedges including *Xanthorrhoea media*, *Restio dimorpha* and *Cyathochaeta diandra*. Plant nomenclature follows Harden (1990–1993).

All sites were burnt in January 1994. Before 1994, there was variation in fire history across sites. The eastern part of Site 1 (sampled for *D*. *excelsa*) and Site 3 were burnt in 1988. The western part of Site 1, separated by a road from the eastern part (sampled for both study species), and Site 2 were burnt in the early 1980s (NPWS fire records; D. Keith, pers. comm.).

#### *Timing of flowering and seed release*

The three study sites were monitored to observe flowering after the January 1994 fire for both species up until December 2000. As both *D*. *excelsa* and *T*. *speciosissima* flower in July–October, this involved seven potential flowering seasons (1994–2000). General observations were also made throughout Royal National Park to determine whether the pattern of the study sites was representative of the general response of the study species to fire in this area. The timing of fruit development and seed release was recorded for the first four flowering seasons after the 1994 fire.

#### *Estimates of seed production and seedling establishment*

Six 30 × 30-m plots were established as follows: *D*. *excelsa*, two plots at each of Sites 1 and 2; *T*. *speciosissima*, one plot at each of Sites 1 and 3. For both study species, within each plot at each site, the numbers of infructescences and follicles on all plants were scored each year (1994–2000). To estimate the number of seeds per follicle, intact
=== p4
follicles were collected in autumn 1996, prior to dehiscence, for each species from each site. For *T*. *speciosissima*, samples of 23 and 25 follicles were collected from Sites 1 and 3, respectively, while for *D*. *excelsa*, samples of 15 and 29 follicles were collected from Sites 1 and 2, respectively. Seeds within these follicles were scored after dehiscence in the laboratory. For *T*. *speciosissima*, only those seeds judged as 'filled' (i.e. likely to be viable) were included in this assessment (see also Bradstock 1995; Denham and Whelan 2000). For *D*. *excelsa*, no assessment was made, although Nash (1996) found that the average viability of seeds collected from a number of locations (not including Royal National Park) was 86% (±6.2 s.e.). The individuals used to estimate numbers of seeds per follicle were sampled from outside the plots to avoid impacts on primary seed dispersal and seedling recruitment. The density of seeds per plot was estimated by multiplying the number of intact follicles by the estimate of the mean number of seeds per follicle and dividing this value by the area of each plot (900 m2 ).

To estimate the magnitude of post-fire seedling recruitment for both study species, five randomly allocated transects each 1 × 30 m were searched for seedlings in spring 1998, within each of the 30 × 30-m plots. For *T*. *speciosissima*, we assessed the probable fruiting year from which seedlings were established, by comparisons with other seedlings of known age within the sites.

#### *Primary seed dispersal*

The seeds of *D*. *excelsa* are disc-like, about 15 mm in diameter, 2 mm thick, have a dry spongy texture and weigh approximately 43 mg (Westoby *et al.* 1990; Nash 1996; A. J. Denham, pers. obs.). The seeds of *T*. *speciosissima* are winged and weigh approximately 72 mg (Westoby *et al.* 1990). Westoby *et al.* (1990) considered *T*. *speciosissima* to be adapted for wind dispersal, but could only suggest that the spongy texture of *D*. *excelsa* seed could serve for wind or water dispersal. Initial seed fall from dehisced follicles in both species is passive and movement in the air appears likely to be the main means of dispersal away from the infructescence.

The spatial pattern of initial seed fall was estimated by counting seeds found on the ground in four orthogonal transects along compass bearings from each of five isolated plants at Site 1 for *D*. *excelsa* and Sites 1 and 3 for *T*. *speciosissima*. Because of time constraints, this was not done at Site 2 for *D*. *excelsa*. Searches were done in June–August of 1996, when most seeds had fallen from the follicles. Some further redistribution of seeds along the soil surface by wind and rain after this time is likely (Lamont *et al.* 1993; Hammill *et al.* 1998). The transects for *D*. *excelsa* started approximately 0.25 m from the centre of each clump, because of the space occupied by the leaf bases of the plants. Counts of numbers of seeds were made every 0.1 m along each transect. Transects were 0.5 m wide and limited to 7.25 m long as there were no seeds seen in initial searches beyond 7.15 m. For *T*. *speciosissima*, the area occupied by the stems was included in the transects. In preliminary searches around *T*. *speciosissima* adults, no seeds were found more than 3 m from adults at Site 1 and 2 m from adults at Site 3, so the transect lengths were reduced to 3.5 and 2.5 m, respectively.

#### *Seed predation*

The fates of recently released seeds on the ground were examined during the initial seed release after the 1994 fire (i.e. in 1996), in two trials. First, an exclusion experiment was used to investigate the agents responsible for and the degree of post-dispersal predation at each site. It was assumed that no secondary dispersal of seeds by invertebrates such as ants was likely, since neither species have lipid bodies attached to their seeds. Westoby *et al.* (1990) suggested that neither species is myrmecochorous and field observations supported this. A block design was used with two treatments and 10 seeds per treatment per block. This experiment was set up for *D*. *excelsa* at Sites 1 and 2 and for *T*. *speciosissima* at Sites 1 and 3 as follows:

(a) caged: cages (15 × 15 cm × 5 cm high with 1-cm<sup>2</sup> mesh size) were used to exclude vertebrate predators, while still allowing access to most invertebrates. To prevent seeds from washing away in heavy rain, a PVC ring sawn from pipe 10 cm in diameter and about 1 cm tall was placed on the ground. This ring was pushed into the soil leaving only the top 0.5 cm protruding. The cage was placed over the ring and fastened down with wire stakes.

(b) uncaged: where only the PVC ring was used. This allowed access to both invertebrates and vertebrates.

Ten blocks consisting of a caged and an uncaged treatment, were used for each species, at each site. The blocks were placed about 5 m apart along a transect through the site, with separate transects for each species at Site 1.

The number of seeds remaining in each treatment block was recorded every day for the first week and approximately every second day for the following 10 weeks. Additionally, any information concerning the condition of seeds (such as whether chewed or germinated) or the presence of testa remains was recorded at each visit.

Second, for both study species, a trial was established to examine the level of predation on seeds that were placed singly at random locations throughout the plots, rather than clumped as above (see Auld and Denham 1999, 2001). These trials were established for *D*. *excelsa* in two plots at Site 1 and in one plot at Site 2 and for *T*. *speciosissima* in one plot at each of Sites 1 and 3. A single seed was placed at each of 10 randomly located positions according to the 30 × 30-m grid established at each site, with the location marked by a steel stake 0.2 m away. Additional batches of 10 seeds were similarly placed in new random locations each week for the following 3 weeks. The fate of these seeds was followed for the next 10 weeks, with details recorded as for the exclusion experiment. Only 'filled' seeds were used in these experiments.

#### *Seedling dispersal*

The following two different estimates were made of the dispersal pattern of seedlings around adult plants:

(a) the ground was searched for seedlings up to a distance of 10 m from fruiting plants around five isolated plants of *D*. *excelsa* at Site 1. The distance of each seedling from the centre of the adult was measured. The adults included two of those used to sample primary seed dispersal. Sufficient seedlings were not available at the other three adults sampled for primary seed dispersal. For *T*. *speciosissima*, this technique was not used as adults continued to flower after the first year.

(b) for *D*. *excelsa* at Sites 1 and 2 and *T*. *speciosissima* at Sites 1 and 3, the distance of each seedling from the centre of the nearest parent was measured for all seedlings observed in the transects used for estimating seedling establishment (above). Because of the overall low number of seedlings observed for *T*. *speciosissima* at Site 3, the entire 30 × 30-m plot was surveyed. This estimate included overlapping seed shadows from adult plants, as typically occurs in the field.

#### *Analyses*

To test the hypothesis that fruit and seed production varied across sites and years within the study area, estimates of infructescence and follicle production per fruiting plant were compared in *D*. *excelsa* by a nested 2-factor ANOVA with plots nested within sites and in *T*. *speciosissima* across sites and years when fruit was produced, by a 2-factor ANOVA without replication. Estimates of seed production per m2 were compared in *D*. *excelsa* across sites by a 1-factor ANOVA with plots as replicates and in *T*. *speciosissima* across sites and fruiting years by a 2-factor ANOVA without replication (Zar 1996).

To test the hypothesis that vertebrate seed predators had an impact on the number of seeds available for germination (the seed predation 
=== p5
exclusion experiment), the proportions of seeds remaining in each replicate treatment within the 10 blocks after 75 days were compared by a 3-factor ANOVA (factors were treatment, site and block, with blocks nested within sites) for each species separately. The hypothesis that the two species suffered different levels of predation at Site 1, where both *D*. *excelsa* and *T*. *speciosissima* were sampled, was tested by a 3-factor ANOVA with species and caging treatment (with blocks nested within species) as factors.

At lower seed densities than in the seed predation exclusion experiment (the single seeds trial) we tested the hypothesis that predation varied across sites. For *T*. *speciosissima*, the proportions of seeds remaining in each weekly cohort of 10 seeds at the end of the study (after 9 weeks) were compared across sites by a 1-factor ANOVA. Data for *D*. *excelsa* were similarly analysed, using both plots at Site 1 and the single plot at Site 2 as three levels in a 'location' factor. Again, it was possible to test the hypothesis that the two species suffered different levels of predation at Site 1 at this lower seed density. Here, only the western of the two *D*. *excelsa* plots was used, as it was adjacent to the *T*. *speciosissima* plot (1-factor ANOVA).

We tested the hypothesis that seedling establishment varied across sites in both species and across years for *T*. *speciosissima*. In *D*. *excelsa*, the number of seedlings per transect was compared across sites by a nested 2-factor ANOVA with plots nested in sites. For *T*. *speciosissima*, the number of seedlings per transect was compared across sites and fruiting year of origin by a 2-factor ANOVA.

For each ANOVA, homogeneity of variances was tested by Cochran's test. Where variances were significantly heterogeneous an arcsine transformation was applied to proportion data and a square-root transformation was applied to count data. If variances were still heterogeneous, the analysis was carried out on the raw data with a conservative approach to rejection of the null hypothesis (Underwood 1981).

To test the hypothesis that the distributions of seedlings around plants were the same as the distributions of seeds around plants, a number of Kolmogorov–Smirnov goodness-of-fit tests were done.

(i) For *D*. *excelsa* at Site 1, seed and seedling data from the isolated plants were placed into 0.1-m classes and frequency counts of seeds or seedlings were obtained from each distance class for all five individuals. The proportions of seeds or seedlings per distance class were then determined. Seedling data for distances less than 0.25 m from the adult were omitted, since data for seed distribution were not obtained at this distance, due to the occupation of most of the available space by the parent plants. Similarly, seedling distances greater than 7.15 m were omitted since this was distance of the furthest observed seed. A Kolmogorov–Smirnov test was used to determine the goodnessof-fit of the seedling distribution (observed) with the seed distribution (predicted) (Zar 1996).

(ii) For *D*. *excelsa* at Site 1 and *T*. *speciosissima* at Sites 1 and 3, estimations were made of the goodness-of-fit of the seedling distributions from the plot transect sampling (observed) with the seed distributions from the isolated individuals (expected). Restriction of seedling data to the greatest distance observed for seeds (7.15 m) was as above for *D*. *excelsa*, and to 3.75 m for *T*. *speciosissima*. There was no restriction on the least distance for *T*. *speciosissima*. This test enabled the determination of whether the distribution of seeds around isolated adults adequately explained the distribution of seedlings around adults that were contagiously distributed (a more typical situation) and thus had overlapping seed shadows.

(iii) For *D*. *excelsa* at Site 1, the seedling distribution from the five isolated plants ('expected') was compared with that obtained from the plot transect sampling ('observed'). This test assessed how well the distribution of seedlings around isolated plants of *D*. *excelsa* represented the more typical situation of contagiously distributed individuals.

#### **Results**

#### *Timing of flowering and seed release*

For both *D*. *excelsa* and *T*. *speciosissima*, the first flowering after the January 1994 fires occurred in late winter (August) of 1995, some 19 months after the January 1994 fire. This pattern was found at all study sites and more generally across Royal National Park. Fruits matured in the following autumn (March–June 1996), with *D*. *excelsa* first releasing seeds in March 1996 and *T*. *speciosissima* in April 1996. Consequently, seeds were not released into the post-fire habitat until some 25–26 months after the passage of the January 1994 fire. Seed fall was quite prolonged with some seeds still in fruits in June (both species). *D. excelsa* plants in the study plots did not flower in any of the subsequent 5 years, while most *T*. *speciosissima* individuals flowered again the following year and a few in three of the subsequent 4 years (Table 1), with a similar timing of flowering and fruiting to that observed in 1995–1996.

#### *Fruit and seed production*

In *D*. *excelsa*, the number, and hence density, of flowering plants varied considerably between plots within sites, ranging from six at Site 1, plot 1 (0.2 m–2) to 39 at Site 2, plot 2 (1.3 m–2) (Table 1). There were no significant differences between sites in the mean numbers of infructescences (*F*1,2 = 0.86, *P* = 0.45) or follicles (*F*1,2 = 9.94, *P* = 0.09) produced per fruiting plant, although there were almost twice as many follicles produced at Site 1, plot 1, than at Site 2, plot 2 (Table 1). For *T*. *speciosissima*, the total number of individuals that flowered between 1995 and 2000 varied from 14 at Site 1 to 24 at Site 3 (Table 1). There was no significant difference in the mean number of infructescences (*F*1,2 = 0.4, *P* = 0.59) or follicles (*F*1,2 = 0.003, *P* = 0.96) per fruiting plant between sites across the 1995–1997 flowering seasons. *D. excelsa* had greater seed production per follicle than *T*. *speciosissima* (104, 105 *v.* 11 seeds per follicle, respectively, Table 2). There were no significant differences in the number of seeds per follicle between sites for *T*. *speciosissima* (*F*1,46 = 0.43, *P* = 0.52) or *D*. *excelsa* (*F*1,42 = 0.08, *P* = 0.93) (Table 2). The estimated density of seeds produced by *D*. *excelsa* varied greatly, although not significantly (*F*1,2 = 4.76, *P* = 0.16) across sites, with Site 1 producing 9.9 (±0.4 s.e.) seeds per m<sup>2</sup> and Site 2 producing 17.7 (±3.6 s.e.) (Table 3). The lack of significance in this comparison is likely to be a result of the considerable variation between plots at Site 2, with one plot producing approximately 1.5 times as many seeds as the other. This in turn was largely because of the much higher density of flowering and fruiting plants in plot 2 than in plot 1 of Site 2 (Table 1). There were no significant differences in seed density of *T*. *speciosissima* between sites (*F*1,2 = 1.11, *P* = 0.40) or among years (*F*2,2 = 4.19, *P* = 0.19). In the first post-fire fruiting year (1996), the estimated density of seeds
=== p6
produced was 1.1 seeds per m<sup>2</sup> at both sites (Table 3). Seed production was higher in the second fruiting year at Site 2, but lower at Site 1. Despite the lack of significance of a year effect in the analysis, at both sites seed production declined dramatically by the third fruiting year (1997) and no seeds were produced in subsequent years (Table 1). Total post-fire seed production by *D*. *excelsa* was considerably greater than by *T*. *speciosissima* (e.g. 9.9 *v*. 2.0 seeds per m<sup>2</sup> , 2350 *v*. 430 seeds per flowering plant for *D*. *excelsa* and *T*. *speciosissima*, respectively, at Site 1) (Table 3).

Seed dispersal approximated an exponential decay curve (see also Janzen 1970; Okubo and Levin 1989; Willson 1992). Most seeds fell within 5 m of adults for *D*. *excelsa* and within 3 m of adults for *T*. *speciosissima* (Fig. 1).

lines: +# CSIRO **Publishing**
+# AUSTRALIAN JOURNAL *of* BOTANY
+Volume 50, 2002 © CSIRO 2002
+An international journal for the publication of original research in plant science
+**All enquiries and manuscripts should be directed to:**
+*Australian Journal of Botany* CSIRO Publishing PO Box 1139 (150 Oxford St) Collingwood, Vic. 3066, Australia
+Telephone: +61 3 9662 7613 Fax: +61 3 9662 7611 Email: publishing.ajb@csiro.au
+Published by CSIRO Publishing for CSIRO and the Australian Academy of Science
+www.publish.csiro.au/journals/ajb
+<!-- PAGE BREAK -->
+## **Flowering, seed dispersal, seed predation and seedling recruitment in two pyrogenic flowering resprouters**
+*Andrew J. Denham*<sup>A</sup> *and Tony D. Auld*
+Biodiversity Research Group, NSW National Parks and Wildlife Service, PO Box 1967, Hurstville, NSW 2220, Australia.
+<sup>A</sup>Corresponding author; email: andrew.denham@npws.nsw.gov.au

+*Abstract.* A few resprouting plants in fire-prone environments have no local seed bank (soil or canopy) when a fire occurs. These species rely on post-fire flowering and the production of non-dormant seeds to exploit favourable post-fire establishment and growth conditions. For two such pyrogenic flowering species (*Doryanthes excelsa* Correa and *Telopea speciosissima* (Smith) R.Br.), we examined the timing of seed release, patterns of fruit production, seed dispersal, seed predation and seedling establishment following a fire in the Sydney region of southeastern Australia. Both species took some 19 months after the fire to flower and the first seeds were released 2 years after the fire. *D. excelsa* flowered and fruited only once after the fire. For *T. speciosissima*, plants also flowered at least once more in the subsequent 5 years, but produced seed in only the first three post-fire flowering years. Fruit production differed between species, with fruiting individuals of *D. excelsa* producing fewer infructescences, similar numbers of follicles, but many more seeds per follicle than fruiting individuals of *T. speciosissima*. Ultimately, *D. excelsa* produced approximately six times as many seeds per m<sup>2</sup> and four times as many seeds per adult in one flowering season than *T. speciosissima* did after four flowering (three successful fruiting) seasons.

+Seeds were passively dispersed from fruits borne 3–4 m (*D. excelsa*) or 1–2 m (*T. speciosissima*) above the ground. Most seeds were found within 5 m (*D. excelsa*) or 3 m (*T. speciosissima*) of parent plants. The primary seed shadow of both species was a poor predictor of the distribution of seedlings, with more seedlings occurring further from the adults than expected from the distribution of seeds. Seed loss to predators was high in both species in exclusion experiments where mammals had access to clumps of seeds (77–88%). It was variable and generally lower (8–65%) in experiments where seeds were not locally clumped. However, for *T. speciosissima*, at one site, some 65% of seeds were lost to mammals and invertebrates in these latter experiments. At this site, these losses appeared to influence subsequent recruitment levels, as very low seedling densities were observed.

+For both species, germination of seedlings first occurred some 2.5–3 years after the passage of the fire. The percentage of seeds produced to seedlings successfully established was low in *D. excelsa* (2–3%) and more variable across sites and years in *T. speciosissima* (0–18%). Resultant post-fire seedling densities of *D. excelsa* (two sites) and *T. speciosissima* at one site were similar, but they were much lower at the *T. speciosissima* site that had high levels of seed predation. Both *D. excelsa* and *T. speciosissima* are amongst the slowest woody resprouting species to recruit seedlings after fire in south-eastern Australia and lag years behind species with soil or canopy seed banks.
+#### **Introduction**

+In fire-prone habitats, recruitment in plant species is frequently linked to the passage of a fire (Tyler 1995). This results from at least two main mechanisms. First, in species with soil seed banks, seed dormancy may be broken by the passage of fires (e.g. via heat, smoke, charred wood: Keeley 1991; Brown 1993; or interactions of these factors: Keith 1997; Morris 2000). Examples include many legumes (Jeffery *et al.* 1988; Auld and O'Connell 1991) and non-leguminous species (Brown 1993; Dixon *et al.* 1995). Second, in species with canopy seed banks, fires result in the mass opening of fruits and the release of seeds (Bond *et al.* 1984; Lamont *et al.* 1991).

+However, a number of species have no available seed storage in either the soil or canopy at the time of the passage of a fire (Keith 1996). A few may rely on dispersal from unburnt areas, but most have mechanisms that allow established plants to survive fire via buried lignotubers, rhizomes or buds (protected meristems). These species usually flower soon after fire and then release seeds (Gill 1981; Frost 1984; Johnson *et al.* 1994; Bond and van Wilgen 1996; Carrington 1999). For species dependant on post-fire flowering for recruitment (pyrogenic flowering resprouters),
+<!-- PAGE BREAK -->
+546 A. J. Denham and T. D. Auld

+the timing and magnitude of this flowering will influence opportunities for post-fire seedling establishment. The longer the interval between the passage of a fire and seedling recruitment, the more of the available resources such as light, nutrients and space, are likely to have been captured by other resprouting species or by those species with soil or canopy seed banks that can recruit in the immediate post-fire period.

+Many individuals of pyrogenic flowering resprouting species in south-eastern Australia appear to have a single post-fire flowering (e.g. *Angophora hispida*, Auld 1986; *Blandfordia nobilis*, Johnson *et al.* 1994; *Lomatia silaifolia*, Denham and Whelan 2000; *Xanthorrhoea australis*, Gill and Ingwersen 1976, but see; *X. fulva*, Taylor *et al.* 1998). In such cases, this represents the only opportunity for recruitment between fires. For other species, flowering may extend over several years following a fire (e.g. *T. speciosissima*, Pyke 1983; Bradstock 1995; Goldingay 2000; *Xanthorrhoea australis*, Curtis 1998). However, the timing of recruitment in pyrogenic flowering resprouting species has been little studied and the degree to which each post-fire flowering event contributes to recruitment is unexplored.

+In the post-fire environment, the impact of seed predation may be reduced due to lower predator abundance and also via predator satiation, in the case of serotinous seed release (Whelan 1995; Bond and van Wilgen 1996; Myerscough *et al.* 2000). However, the seeds of pyrogenic flowering resprouters are likely to be released after most seeds from serotinous species have germinated and, consequently, would not benefit from any predator satiation effects from serotinous seed release. In addition, populations of predators may have recovered by this time. All pyrogenic flowering resprouters are thought to release seeds in a non-dormant state (Bell *et al.* 1993; Bond and van Wilgen 1996) and hence form transient soil seed banks (*sensu* Parker and Kelly 1989).

+In this study, we assessed post-fire reproduction and the patterns of seedling recruitment after a wildfire in 1994, in two resprouting species reliant on post-fire flowering for seed production (*Doryanthes excelsa* and *Telopea speciosissima*), from the Sydney area of south-eastern Australia. We examined (i) the timing of flowering and magnitude of seed production over 5 years after the fire; (ii) the pattern of seed and seedling dispersal; (iii) the level of post-dispersal seed predation; and (iv) the proportion of seeds released that resulted in successful establishment of new plants.
+#### **Methods**
+#### *Study species*

+*Doryanthes excelsa* Correa (Gymea lily—Doryanthaceae) is a large perennial rosette plant with a bulbous rhizome and long broad linear leaves up to 3 m long. It is apparently capable of asexual reproduction by branching of the rhizome (Nash 1996). It grows in dry sclerophyll forests and woodlands on soils derived from sandstone containing some clay and is restricted to the Sydney Basin in south-eastern Australia, with three outlying populations in northern New South Wales (Harden 1990–1993). The species survives fire by having apical buds protected in underground leaf bases. It flowers in a large, red inflorescence held up to 5 m above the foliage of the plant (Harden 1990–1993). Fire appears to stimulate flowering, although sporadic flowering does occur in the absence of fire (Nash 1996). The mechanism determining flowering is unknown (Beeh 1996; Nash 1996).

+*Telopea speciosissima* (Smith) R.Br. (waratah—Proteaceae) is a tall shrub, generally 2–4 m, which is also known for its striking red blooms that emerge above the resprouting shrubby vegetation in the post-fire environment. It is common in dry sclerophyll forest and woodlands on the central coast and central and southern tablelands of New South Wales (Harden 1990–1993). The species survives fire by having dormant buds protected in an underground lignotuber (Bradstock 1995). Aerial stems are completely regrown after each fire.
+#### *Sites*

+Three sample sites within a 10-km radius were chosen in Royal National Park, about 35 km south of Sydney (34°03′S, 151°03′E). All sites occurred on soils derived from the Triassic Hawkesbury Sandstone Formation, although Site 1 (with an ironstone influence) and Site 2 (with an alluvial influence) were on soils slightly more fertile than Site 3. At Site 1, both study species occurred in ironstone woodland vegetation (D. Keith and M. Tozer, unpubl. data), with an overstorey of *Eucalyptus sieberi*, *Corymbia gummifera*, *Banksia serrata*, *Xylomelum pyriforme* and *Ceratopetalum gummiferum*. The shrubby understorey included *Grevillea diffusa*, *Banksia spinulosa*, *Lissanthe strigosa*, *Prostanthera* sp., *Isopogon anemonifolius*, *Acacia myrtifolia*, *Xanthorrhoea media*, *Lomandra* spp. and *Dianella* sp. The vegetation at Site 2 (*D. excelsa* only) is Sandstone Gully Forest (D. Keith and M. Tozer, unpubl. data), with an overstorey of *Angophora costata*, *Banksia serrata*, *Ceratopetalum gummiferum*, *Eucalyptus piperita* and *E. sieberi* and a shrubby understorey that included *Boronia pinnata*, *Grevillea mucronulata*, *Acacia terminalis*, *Lomandra longifolia* and *Caustis flexuosa*. At Site 3 (*T. speciosissima* only) the vegetation is Sandstone Heath (D. Keith and M. Tozer, unpubl. data), with a short overstorey of *Corymbia gummifera*, *Eucalyptus obstans*, *E. sclerophylla* and *Banksia serrata* and a shrubby understorey that included *Lambertia formosa*, *Lissanthe strigosa* and sedges including *Xanthorrhoea media*, *Restio dimorpha* and *Cyathochaeta diandra*. Plant nomenclature follows Harden (1990–1993).

+All sites were burnt in January 1994. Before 1994, there was variation in fire history across sites. The eastern part of Site 1 (sampled for *D. excelsa*) and Site 3 were burnt in 1988. The western part of Site 1, separated by a road from the eastern part (sampled for both study species), and Site 2 were burnt in the early 1980s (NPWS fire records; D. Keith, pers. comm.).
+#### *Timing of flowering and seed release*

+The three study sites were monitored to observe flowering after the January 1994 fire for both species up until December 2000. As both *D. excelsa* and *T. speciosissima* flower in July–October, this involved seven potential flowering seasons (1994–2000). General observations were also made throughout Royal National Park to determine whether the pattern of the study sites was representative of the general response of the study species to fire in this area. The timing of fruit development and seed release was recorded for the first four flowering seasons after the 1994 fire.
+#### *Estimates of seed production and seedling establishment*

+Six 30 × 30-m plots were established as follows: *D. excelsa*, two plots at each of Sites 1 and 2; *T. speciosissima*, one plot at each of Sites 1 and 3. For both study species, within each plot at each site, the numbers of infructescences and follicles on all plants were scored each year (1994–2000). To estimate the number of seeds per follicle, intact
+<!-- PAGE BREAK -->
+Reproduction in two pyrogenic flowerers 547

+follicles were collected in autumn 1996, prior to dehiscence, for each species from each site. For *T. speciosissima*, samples of 23 and 25 follicles were collected from Sites 1 and 3, respectively, while for *D. excelsa*, samples of 15 and 29 follicles were collected from Sites 1 and 2, respectively. Seeds within these follicles were scored after dehiscence in the laboratory. For *T. speciosissima*, only those seeds judged as 'filled' (i.e. likely to be viable) were included in this assessment (see also Bradstock 1995; Denham and Whelan 2000). For *D. excelsa*, no assessment was made, although Nash (1996) found that the average viability of seeds collected from a number of locations (not including Royal National Park) was 86% (±6.2 s.e.). The individuals used to estimate numbers of seeds per follicle were sampled from outside the plots to avoid impacts on primary seed dispersal and seedling recruitment. The density of seeds per plot was estimated by multiplying the number of intact follicles by the estimate of the mean number of seeds per follicle and dividing this value by the area of each plot (900 m<sup>2</sup>).

+To estimate the magnitude of post-fire seedling recruitment for both study species, five randomly allocated transects each 1 × 30 m were searched for seedlings in spring 1998, within each of the 30 × 30-m plots. For *T. speciosissima*, we assessed the probable fruiting year from which seedlings were established, by comparisons with other seedlings of known age within the sites.
+#### *Primary seed dispersal*

+The seeds of *D. excelsa* are disc-like, about 15 mm in diameter, 2 mm thick, have a dry spongy texture and weigh approximately 43 mg (Westoby *et al.* 1990; Nash 1996; A. J. Denham, pers. obs.). The seeds of *T. speciosissima* are winged and weigh approximately 72 mg (Westoby *et al.* 1990). Westoby *et al.* (1990) considered *T. speciosissima* to be adapted for wind dispersal, but could only suggest that the spongy texture of *D. excelsa* seed could serve for wind or water dispersal. Initial seed fall from dehisced follicles in both species is passive and movement in the air appears likely to be the main means of dispersal away from the infructescence.

+The spatial pattern of initial seed fall was estimated by counting seeds found on the ground in four orthogonal transects along compass bearings from each of five isolated plants at Site 1 for *D. excelsa* and Sites 1 and 3 for *T. speciosissima*. Because of time constraints, this was not done at Site 2 for *D. excelsa*. Searches were done in June–August of 1996, when most seeds had fallen from the follicles. Some further redistribution of seeds along the soil surface by wind and rain after this time is likely (Lamont *et al.* 1993; Hammill *et al.* 1998). The transects for *D. excelsa* started approximately 0.25 m from the centre of each clump, because of the space occupied by the leaf bases of the plants. Counts of numbers of seeds were made every 0.1 m along each transect. Transects were 0.5 m wide and limited to 7.25 m long as there were no seeds seen in initial searches beyond 7.15 m. For *T. speciosissima*, the area occupied by the stems was included in the transects. In preliminary searches around *T. speciosissima* adults, no seeds were found more than 3 m from adults at Site 1 and 2 m from adults at Site 3, so the transect lengths were reduced to 3.5 and 2.5 m, respectively.
+#### *Seed predation*

+The fates of recently released seeds on the ground were examined during the initial seed release after the 1994 fire (i.e. in 1996), in two trials. First, an exclusion experiment was used to investigate the agents responsible for and the degree of post-dispersal predation at each site. It was assumed that no secondary dispersal of seeds by invertebrates such as ants was likely, since neither species have lipid bodies attached to their seeds. Westoby *et al.* (1990) suggested that neither species is myrmecochorous and field observations supported this. A block design was used with two treatments and 10 seeds per treatment per block. This experiment was set up for *D. excelsa* at Sites 1 and 2 and for *T. speciosissima* at Sites 1 and 3 as follows:

+(a) caged: cages (15 × 15 cm × 5 cm high with 1-cm<sup>2</sup> mesh size) were used to exclude vertebrate predators, while still allowing access to most invertebrates. To prevent seeds from washing away in heavy rain, a PVC ring sawn from pipe 10 cm in diameter and about 1 cm tall was placed on the ground. This ring was pushed into the soil leaving only the top 0.5 cm protruding. The cage was placed over the ring and fastened down with wire stakes.
+(b) uncaged: where only the PVC ring was used. This allowed access to both invertebrates and vertebrates.

+Ten blocks consisting of a caged and an uncaged treatment, were used for each species, at each site. The blocks were placed about 5 m apart along a transect through the site, with separate transects for each species at Site 1.

+The number of seeds remaining in each treatment block was recorded every day for the first week and approximately every second day for the following 10 weeks. Additionally, any information concerning the condition of seeds (such as whether chewed or germinated) or the presence of testa remains was recorded at each visit.

+Second, for both study species, a trial was established to examine the level of predation on seeds that were placed singly at random locations throughout the plots, rather than clumped as above (see Auld and Denham 1999, 2001). These trials were established for *D. excelsa* in two plots at Site 1 and in one plot at Site 2 and for *T. speciosissima* in one plot at each of Sites 1 and 3. A single seed was placed at each of 10 randomly located positions according to the 30 × 30-m grid established at each site, with the location marked by a steel stake 0.2 m away. Additional batches of 10 seeds were similarly placed in new random locations each week for the following 3 weeks. The fate of these seeds was followed for the next 10 weeks, with details recorded as for the exclusion experiment. Only 'filled' seeds were used in these experiments.
+#### *Seedling dispersal*
+The following two different estimates were made of the dispersal pattern of seedlings around adult plants:

+(a) the ground was searched for seedlings up to a distance of 10 m from fruiting plants around five isolated plants of *D. excelsa* at Site 1. The distance of each seedling from the centre of the adult was measured. The adults included two of those used to sample primary seed dispersal. Sufficient seedlings were not available at the other three adults sampled for primary seed dispersal. For *T. speciosissima*, this technique was not used as adults continued to flower after the first year.

+(b) for *D. excelsa* at Sites 1 and 2 and *T. speciosissima* at Sites 1 and 3, the distance of each seedling from the centre of the nearest parent was measured for all seedlings observed in the transects used for estimating seedling establishment (above). Because of the overall low number of seedlings observed for *T. speciosissima* at Site 3, the entire 30 × 30-m plot was surveyed. This estimate included overlapping seed shadows from adult plants, as typically occurs in the field.
+#### *Analyses*

+To test the hypothesis that fruit and seed production varied across sites and years within the study area, estimates of infructescence and follicle production per fruiting plant were compared in *D. excelsa* by a nested 2-factor ANOVA with plots nested within sites and in *T. speciosissima* across sites and years when fruit was produced, by a 2-factor ANOVA without replication. Estimates of seed production per m<sup>2</sup> were compared in *D. excelsa* across sites by a 1-factor ANOVA with plots as replicates and in *T. speciosissima* across sites and fruiting years by a 2-factor ANOVA without replication (Zar 1996).
+To test the hypothesis that vertebrate seed predators had an impact on the number of seeds available for germination (the seed predation
+<!-- PAGE BREAK -->
+548 A. J. Denham and T. D. Auld

+exclusion experiment), the proportions of seeds remaining in each replicate treatment within the 10 blocks after 75 days were compared by a 3-factor ANOVA (factors were treatment, site and block, with blocks nested within sites) for each species separately. The hypothesis that the two species suffered different levels of predation at Site 1, where both *D. excelsa* and *T. speciosissima* were sampled, was tested by a 3-factor ANOVA with species and caging treatment (with blocks nested within species) as factors.

+At lower seed densities than in the seed predation exclusion experiment (the single seeds trial) we tested the hypothesis that predation varied across sites. For *T. speciosissima*, the proportions of seeds remaining in each weekly cohort of 10 seeds at the end of the study (after 9 weeks) were compared across sites by a 1-factor ANOVA. Data for *D. excelsa* were similarly analysed, using both plots at Site 1 and the single plot at Site 2 as three levels in a 'location' factor. Again, it was possible to test the hypothesis that the two species suffered different levels of predation at Site 1 at this lower seed density. Here, only the western of the two *D. excelsa* plots was used, as it was adjacent to the *T. speciosissima* plot (1-factor ANOVA).

+We tested the hypothesis that seedling establishment varied across sites in both species and across years for *T. speciosissima*. In *D. excelsa*, the number of seedlings per transect was compared across sites by a nested 2-factor ANOVA with plots nested in sites. For *T. speciosissima*, the number of seedlings per transect was compared across sites and fruiting year of origin by a 2-factor ANOVA.

+For each ANOVA, homogeneity of variances was tested by Cochran's test. Where variances were significantly heterogeneous an arcsine transformation was applied to proportion data and a square-root transformation was applied to count data. If variances were still heterogeneous, the analysis was carried out on the raw data with a conservative approach to rejection of the null hypothesis (Underwood 1981).
+To test the hypothesis that the distributions of seedlings around plants were the same as the distributions of seeds around plants, a number of Kolmogorov–Smirnov goodness-of-fit tests were done.
