This decline in the rate of establishment concurs with the accepted wisdom that conditions for recruitment decline with time since fire in these environments (Whelan 1995). 61 62 The distribution of seedlings in this study was not solely influenced by the shape of the seed shadow. There is a pattern for the seeds nearest to adults to have a relatively lower chance of successful establishment as seedlings. This pattern was most evident in *D*. *excelsa* (Fig. 1 *v*. 5*a*) and *T*. *speciosissima* at Site 1 (Fig. 1 *v*. 5*b*). Hutchings (1986) suggested that there are a number of factors that determine the final spatial distribution of seedlings, including the behaviour of seed predators and herbivores (Janzen 1970) and the distribution of safe sites, while Schupp and Fuentes (1995) warned that the correspondence of distributions or their lack cannot say much about what determines the ultimate distribution of adults. The distribution of safe sites is affected by competitive influences of adult plants (Sarukhan *et al.* 1985; Hutchings 1986; Crawley 1990; Le Maitre and Midgely 1992; Morgan 1995; Tozer and Bradstock 1997) and possibly allelopathy (Muller *et al.* 1968; Crawley 1986, 1990; Hutchings 1986). For *D*. *excelsa*, the leaves of adults protrude beyond the basal rosette and may reduce light and rainfall at the soil surface within the first 0.5 m of the rosette. For *T*. *speciosissima*, the lignotubers of adult plants extend beyond the aerial stems and result in reduced soil depth adjacent to the base of plants. Nevertheless, some seedlings were observed growing from the base of *D*. *excelsa* and from within the area of the lignotuber of *T*. *speciosissima*, although these seedlings may not persist. It is also apparent that our estimates of the seed shadow of plants did not detect some seeds that successfully germinated and became recruits well away from potential parents. These rarer, long-distance-dispersed seedlings may have greater significance for the species for colonisation of new habitat or recolonisation after adult mortality (Portnoy and Willson 1993). The distribution patterns observed here may change again after further mortality occurs, especially in relation to survival during future fires. 63 64 In this study, after just one fire, it is apparent that significant recruitment by *D*. *excelsa* and *T*. *speciosissima* occurred despite the long time between the fire and the release of seeds into the environment. The strategy of a single or few post-fire flowering events has the advantage that adults of these species may then redirect all their resources to surviving and flowering after the next fire. 65 66 Because of their spectacular inflorescences, some pyrogenic, flowering resprouters are subject to harvesting for the cut-flower market (e.g. *Blandfordia* spp., *D*. *excelsa*, *Telopea* spp. and *Xanthorrhoea* spp., NSW National Parks and Wildlife 2002). In NSW, south-eastern Australia, despite licensing requirements under the NSW National Parks and Wildlife Act 1987, little is known of the impact of 67 === p13 68 inflorescence-harvesting on the viability of populations of these species. The percentage of the seeds released that established as seedlings varied between species, sites and years. For *D*. *excelsa*, both sites had low establishment percentages (1.6–3.1%) (Table 3). For *T*. *speciosissima* at Site 3, the percentage seedling establishment was low (0–1.9%), but comparable to *D*. *excelsa*, while at Site 1 percentage seedling establishment was higher (11.2–20.6%) (Table 3). The resultant seedling densities per m2 were similar for both species, except for *T*. *speciosissima* at Site 3, where they were an order of magnitude lower (Table 3). For *T*. *speciosissima*, these seedling densities reflected an accumulation of cohorts of seedlings from 3 years of postfire fruiting, compared with 1 year for *D*. *excelsa*. In terms of seedlings per flowering plant there was more variation, with results for *D*. *excelsa* ranging from 64.5 seedlings per flowering adult at Site 1, plot 1 to 6 at Site 2, plot 2. For *T*. *speciosissima* for the three fruiting seasons combined, the range was from 22.7 seedlings per flowering adult at Site 1 to 0.1 at Site 3. ## *Seedling distribution* The distribution of seedlings around adults differed significantly from that of seeds (Table 4). In all cases, a greater proportion of seedlings occurred further from the adult than suggested by the seed distributions. When the distribution of seeds was compared with that of seedlings around isolated individuals of *D*. *excelsa* at Site 1, there was a difference in the shape of the respective distributions, with the distribution of seedlings fairly uniform up to about 7 m from an adult (Fig. 4). In contrast to the distribution of seeds (Fig. 1*a*), there was not a large proportion of seedlings near adults. These data suggest that seedlings had a similar likelihood of occurring anywhere up to 7 m from their parent. Where there were overlapping seed shadows from parent plants in *D*. *excelsa*, the distribution of seedlings (Fig. 5*a*) was uneven, but more or less uniform in density up to 4 m from a parent plant, with a decline further away. For *T*. *speciosissima*, the overall shape of the distributions of seeds and seedlings was similar, despite the significant difference in the distributions. The greatest proportion of seedlings occurred further from the adult than for seeds and the tail extended further from the adult (Figs 1*b*, 5*b*). The maximum difference in distributions tended to occur within 2 m from adults, suggesting that there is some interaction between adults and seedling recruitment that leads to reduced recruitment less than 2 m from adults. This effect appeared to be most pronounced in *T*. *speciosissima* at Site 1. In both species, recruits were located well beyond the limit of seeds detected in the seed-distribution surveys, suggesting either occasional long-distance dispersal directly from the infructescence or later (i.e. after our survey) dispersal occurring at ground level (Harper 1977; Hammill *et al.* 1998). #### **Discussion** Both pyrogenic flowering, resprouting species took some 19 months to flower after the January 1994 fire. For *D*. *excelsa*, this represented the only post-fire flowering event, although sporadic flowering in the absence of fire does occur in the species (Nash 1996). A single post-fire flowering event has been observed in several other local taxa that are pyrogenic flowering resprouters (Auld 1986; Denham and Whelan 2000), as well as from elsewhere, although most are herbaceous or geophytes (Frost 1984; Johnson *et al.* 1994; Bond and van Wilgen 1996). In *D*. *excelsa*, following the senescence of the flowering spike, individuals undergo subterranean branching, which may result in asexual reproduction (Beeh 1996; Nash 1996). In *T*. *speciosissima*, there was further flowering in some individuals over the next 4 years after the fire, although no seeds were produced following flowering in 1998 (4.5 years post-fire) or later in our study plots. In *T*. *speciosissima*, there was a trend for the highest seed production in the first two post-fire fruiting seasons, followed by a marked decline in the third. Bradstock (1995) and Pyke (1983) observed a similar trend; however, Pyke (1987) suggested that temporal patterns of flowering may depend on other, unknown factors. Goldingay (2000) presented data indicating that for plants in one population of *T*. *speciosissima*, flowering was prolific for up to 8 years after fire, before declining subsequently. The temporal pattern of post-fire flowering in *T*. *speciosissima* clearly varies with location. Despite flowering only once after the 1994 fire, *D*. *excelsa* was very successful in producing seed, releasing nearly five times as many seeds as *T*. *speciosissima* at Site 1 where they co-occurred. Both species took some 2.5 years after the fire to establish seedlings. Other species either cohabiting with *D*. *excelsa* and *T*. *speciosissima*, or from other fire-prone habitats, established seedlings much sooner. In general, those species with a soil seed bank mostly establish seedlings within the first year after a fire, while those with a canopy seed bank mostly release seed in the first 6 months (Lamont and Barker 1988; Lamont *et al.* 1991) and establish seedlings in the first year (Table 5). Even other species that rely on post-fire flowering for seedling establishment appear to be 0.5–1.5 years quicker than *D*. *excelsa* and *T*. *speciosissima* in establishing seedlings post-fire (Table 5). Among other Australian species, Auld (1986) found that for the shrub *Angophora hispida*, establishment occurred within about 18 months, while seedlings of shrubby *Xanthorrhoea* spp. were observed 18 months to 2 years after fire (Benwell 1998; Curtis 1998; Taylor *et al.* 1998). This is also the case in other fire-prone areas of the world, including Californian sage scrub, Florida sand pine scrub and South African fynbos (Table 5). By the time seedlings of *D*. *excelsa* and *T*. *speciosissima* are becoming established, much of the space, light and nutrients made available by the fire may have been captured by other species (both resprouting plants and seedlings). This will be particularly the case for seedlings from the second and third fruit crops post-fire in *T*. *speciosissima*. In other vegetation types, resprouting species may be able to continue recruiting new seedlings several years after fire (e.g. *Garberia heterophylla* in Florida, Abrahamson and Abrahamson 1996). Curtis (1998) observed seedlings of the arborescent monocot, *X*. *australis*, at sites unburnt for about 100 years. However, such inter-fire recruitment has rarely been observed in the post-fire environment of *D*. *excelsa* and *T*. *speciosissima*. Thus, despite the tolerance of their adults to fire, the persistence of these species may in part be due to their large seed size, which ensures that seedlings have sufficient reserves to establish (Westoby *et al.* 1992; Lamont and Groom 1998), although the relative proportions of different nutrients in these seeds has not been determined (Lamont and Groom 1998; Myerscough *et al.* 2000). Primary seed dispersal for both species produced a high concentration of seeds adjacent to the adult and an exponential decay of seed density with distance. This pattern is typical of a broad range of other plant species (Janzen 1970; Auld 1986; Willson 1992; Hammill *et al.* 1998). However, Hammill *et al.* (1998) found that seeds from species with canopy seed banks were dispersed at considerably greater distances than found here for *D*. *excelsa* or *T*. *speciosissima*. Differences in dispersal distances between our study species and between sites for *T*. *speciosissima* in this study are probably related to the height of the infructescences and the height and density of the surrounding vegetation (Hammill *et al.* 1998). Infructescences of *D*. *excelsa* at Site 1 were on average 3.9 m (±0.15 s.e.) tall. For *T*. *speciosissima* at Site 1, infructescences were relatively shorter at 1.85 m (±0.08 s.e.), while *T*. *speciosissima* at Site 3 had the shortest infructescences at 0.95 m (±0.08 s.e.). The surrounding vegetation at Site 3 appeared to be denser than at Site 1 and this may have further contributed to the shorter dispersal distances. Dispersal along the ground by wind or water in heavy rains may also have contributed to these dispersal patterns (Harper 1977; Hammill *et al.* 1998). For serotinous species that release seeds shortly after fire, the understorey would be relatively open at the time of seed release, while for *D*. *excelsa* and *T*. *speciosissima*, considerable post-fire regrowth would have increased the density of the understorey. This may act to limit seed dispersal in *D*. *excelsa* and *T*. *speciosissima*. The exclosure experiment indicated that seed losses to mammals and invertebrates occurred in the field (Fig. 2), as has been found for other large-seeded species in similar habitats (e.g. *Banksia* spp., *Isopogon anemonifolius* and *Petrophile pulchella*, Bradstock 1991; *Protea neriifolia*, Botha and Le Maitre 1992; *Grevillea* spp., Auld and Denham 1999, 2001; *Hakea sericea* and *P*. *pulchella*, R. J. Whelan and J. York*,* unpubl. data). Generally, other studies have found greatly reduced predation in burnt sites (Bradstock 1991; Botha and le Maitre 1992), while R. J. Whelan and J. York (unpubl. data) found that survival of seeds among exclusion treatments was extremely variable among fires and sites. The high level of losses observed in this study is more comparable to that found at unburnt sites (e.g. 100% losses, Bradstock 1991; 75–100% Botha and Le Maitre 1992; 82–95%, Auld and Denham 1999), and to that of recently burnt sites for *Grevillea caleyi* (Auld and Denham 2001). Most seed losses were presumably caused by mammals rather than invertebrates, on the basis of the patterns of seed removal and *in situ* damage. Losses were high for clumped seeds, but generally lower for seeds placed singly, implying that local seed density may affect the ability of seed predators to find === p12 and subsequently eat seeds. Differences in seed losses between study species at Site 1 for low-density seeds may reflect a difference in palatability of seeds or degree of predator satiation, given the much greater seed production in *D*. *excelsa* (Table 1). At Site 3 for *T*. *speciosissima*, losses were high for seeds at high and low densities. While predator satiation may occur in the immediate post-fire period when species with canopy seed banks release seeds, it appears that such effects are less important by the time *D*. *excelsa* and *T*. *speciosissima* release seeds. Consequently, if recruitment is not limited by a lack of safe sites, then seed losses to predators are likely to have had an impact on the magnitude of seedling recruitment, particularly for *T*. *speciosissima* at Site 3. Seedling recruitment was observed at all sites, but generally only a small percentage of the seeds released successfully established (≤4%, Table 3). The exception was at Site 1 for *T*. *speciosissima* where about 14% of all seeds released post-fire were established as seedlings. However, seedling densities by 1998 were comparable between *D*. *excelsa* and *T*. *speciosissima* at Site 1 (0.3 per m2 , Table 3), resulting from the much greater seed production of *D*. *excelsa* at this site (Table 1). In contrast, for *T*. *speciosissima* at Site 3, seedling densities were an order of magnitude lower (0.03 per m2 , Table 3), even though there was no significant difference in seed production to *T*. *speciosissima* at Site 1. The highest levels of seedling recruitment in relation to the available seeds observed here (*T*. *speciosissima* at Site 1) were comparable to some estimates from local species with canopy seed banks, such as *Banksia serrata* (11–21% over 3 years) and *Isopogon anemonifolius* (6–18%) (Bradstock 1990), and from previous work on *T*. *speciosissima* (7–9%) (Bradstock 1995), while levels for *D*. *excelsa* and *T*. *speciosissima* (Site 3) were lower than those in these previous studies. In terms of individual plant fitness, the number of seedlings per flowering plant was more variable. For *T*. *speciosissima* at Site 1, the number of seedlings per flowering plant (22.7) was slightly greater than that found by Bradstock (1995) (range 1–9.7), while at Site 3 it was much lower (0.1). For *D*. *excelsa*, at three plots the number of seedlings per flowering plant (6–16.8) was comparable to that found by Bradstock (1995) for *T*. *speciosissima*, but at Site 1 plot 1 it was much greater (64.5). The impact of low recruitment from one episode of postfire reproduction depends on the ability of the recruits to survive to fire resistance (primary juvenile phase) and on the ability of the existing adults to survive future fires and produce additional seed crops (Bradstock 1990). Bradstock (1995) showed that less than 25% of *T*. *speciosissima* seedlings are resistant to fire at 8–10 years old. Further demographic studies should establish the length of the primary juvenile period of these species. Reduction in recruitment levels over the three sampled fruiting seasons in *T*. *speciosissima* in this study may be explained by variation in seed predation, environmental conditions or the availability of suitable sites for germination and establishment. This decline in the rate of establishment concurs with the accepted wisdom that conditions for recruitment decline with time since fire in these environments (Whelan 1995). The distribution of seedlings in this study was not solely influenced by the shape of the seed shadow. There is a pattern for the seeds nearest to adults to have a relatively lower chance of successful establishment as seedlings. This pattern was most evident in *D*. *excelsa* (Fig. 1 *v*. 5*a*) and *T*. *speciosissima* at Site 1 (Fig. 1 *v*. 5*b*). Hutchings (1986) suggested that there are a number of factors that determine the final spatial distribution of seedlings, including the behaviour of seed predators and herbivores (Janzen 1970) and the distribution of safe sites, while Schupp and Fuentes (1995) warned that the correspondence of distributions or their lack cannot say much about what determines the ultimate distribution of adults. The distribution of safe sites is affected by competitive influences of adult plants (Sarukhan *et al.* 1985; Hutchings 1986; Crawley 1990; Le Maitre and Midgely 1992; Morgan 1995; Tozer and Bradstock 1997) and possibly allelopathy (Muller *et al.* 1968; Crawley 1986, 1990; Hutchings 1986). For *D*. *excelsa*, the leaves of adults protrude beyond the basal rosette and may reduce light and rainfall at the soil surface within the first 0.5 m of the rosette. For *T*. *speciosissima*, the lignotubers of adult plants extend beyond the aerial stems and result in reduced soil depth adjacent to the base of plants. Nevertheless, some seedlings were observed growing from the base of *D*. *excelsa* and from within the area of the lignotuber of *T*. *speciosissima*, although these seedlings may not persist. It is also apparent that our estimates of the seed shadow of plants did not detect some seeds that successfully germinated and became recruits well away from potential parents. These rarer, long-distance-dispersed seedlings may have greater significance for the species for colonisation of new habitat or recolonisation after adult mortality (Portnoy and Willson 1993). The distribution patterns observed here may change again after further mortality occurs, especially in relation to survival during future fires. In this study, after just one fire, it is apparent that significant recruitment by *D*. *excelsa* and *T*. *speciosissima* occurred despite the long time between the fire and the release of seeds into the environment. The strategy of a single or few post-fire flowering events has the advantage that adults of these species may then redirect all their resources to surviving and flowering after the next fire. Because of their spectacular inflorescences, some pyrogenic, flowering resprouters are subject to harvesting for the cut-flower market (e.g. *Blandfordia* spp., *D*. *excelsa*, *Telopea* spp. and *Xanthorrhoea* spp., NSW National Parks and Wildlife 2002). In NSW, south-eastern Australia, despite licensing requirements under the NSW National Parks and Wildlife Act 1987, little is known of the impact of === p13 inflorescence-harvesting on the viability of populations of these species. +#### *Seedling distribution*

+The distribution of seedlings around adults differed significantly from that of seeds (Table 4). In all cases, a greater proportion of seedlings occurred further from the adult than suggested by the seed distributions. When the distribution of seeds was compared with that of seedlings around isolated individuals of *D. excelsa* at Site 1, there was a difference in the shape of the respective distributions, with the distribution of seedlings fairly uniform up to about 7 m from an adult (Fig. 4). In contrast to the distribution of seeds (Fig. 1*a*), there was not a large proportion of seedlings near adults. These data suggest that seedlings had a similar likelihood of occurring anywhere up to 7 m from their parent. Where there were overlapping seed shadows from parent plants in *D. excelsa*, the distribution of seedlings (Fig. 5*a*) was uneven, but more or less uniform in density up to 4 m from a parent plant, with a decline further away. For *T. speciosissima*, the overall shape of the distributions of seeds and seedlings was similar, despite the significant difference in the distributions. The greatest proportion of seedlings occurred further from the adult than for seeds and the tail extended further from the adult (Figs 1*b*, 5*b*). The maximum difference in distributions tended to occur within 2 m from adults, suggesting that there is some interaction between adults and seedling recruitment that leads to reduced recruitment less than 2 m from adults. This effect appeared to be most pronounced in *T. speciosissima* at Site 1. In both species, recruits were located well beyond the limit of seeds detected in the seed-distribution surveys, suggesting either occasional long-distance dispersal directly from the infructescence or later (i.e. after our survey) dispersal occurring at ground level (Harper 1977; Hammill *et al.* 1998).
+#### **Discussion**

+Both pyrogenic flowering, resprouting species took some 19 months to flower after the January 1994 fire. For *D. excelsa*, this represented the only post-fire flowering event, although sporadic flowering in the absence of fire does occur in the species (Nash 1996). A single post-fire flowering event has been observed in several other local taxa that are pyrogenic flowering resprouters (Auld 1986; Denham and Whelan 2000), as well as from elsewhere, although most are herbaceous or geophytes (Frost 1984; Johnson *et al.* 1994; Bond and van Wilgen 1996). In *D. excelsa*, following the senescence of the flowering spike, individuals undergo subterranean branching, which may result in asexual reproduction (Beeh 1996; Nash 1996). This additional resource expenditure may explain the single post-
+<!-- PAGE BREAK -->
+554 A. J. Denham and T. D. Auld

+fire flowering event in *D. excelsa*. In *T. speciosissima*, there was further flowering in some individuals over the next 4 years after the fire, although no seeds were produced following flowering in 1998 (4.5 years post-fire) or later in our study plots. In *T. speciosissima*, there was a trend for the highest seed production in the first two post-fire fruiting seasons, followed by a marked decline in the third. Bradstock (1995) and Pyke (1983) observed a similar trend; however, Pyke (1987) suggested that temporal patterns of flowering may depend on other, unknown factors. Goldingay (2000) presented data indicating that for plants in one population of *T. speciosissima*, flowering was prolific for up to 8 years after fire, before declining subsequently. The temporal pattern of post-fire flowering in *T. speciosissima* clearly varies with location. Despite flowering only once after the 1994 fire, *D. excelsa* was very successful in producing seed, releasing nearly five times as many seeds as *T. speciosissima* at Site 1 where they co-occurred.

+Both species took some 2.5 years after the fire to establish seedlings. Other species either cohabiting with *D. excelsa* and *T. speciosissima*, or from other fire-prone habitats, established seedlings much sooner. In general, those species with a soil seed bank mostly establish seedlings within the first year after a fire, while those with a canopy seed bank mostly release seed in the first 6 months (Lamont and Barker 1988; Lamont *et al.* 1991) and establish seedlings in the first year (Table 5). Even other species that rely on post-fire flowering for seedling establishment appear to be 0.5–1.5 years quicker than *D. excelsa* and *T. speciosissima* in establishing seedlings post-fire (Table 5). Among other Australian species, Auld (1986) found that for the shrub *Angophora hispida*, establishment occurred within about 18 months, while seedlings of shrubby *Xanthorrhoea* spp. were observed 18 months to 2 years after fire (Benwell 1998; Curtis 1998; Taylor *et al.* 1998). This is also the case in other fire-prone areas of the world, including Californian sage scrub, Florida sand pine scrub and South African fynbos (Table 5). By the time seedlings of *D. excelsa* and *T. speciosissima* are becoming established, much of the space, light and nutrients made available by the fire may have been captured by other species (both resprouting plants and seedlings). This will be particularly the case for seedlings from the second and third fruit crops post-fire in *T. speciosissima*. In other vegetation types, resprouting species may be able to continue recruiting new seedlings several years after fire (e.g. *Garberia heterophylla* in Florida, Abrahamson and Abrahamson 1996). Curtis (1998) observed seedlings of the arborescent monocot, *X. australis*, at sites unburnt for about 100 years. However, such inter-fire recruitment has rarely been observed in the post-fire environment of *D. excelsa* and *T. speciosissima*. Thus, despite the tolerance of their adults to fire, the persistence of these species may in part be due to their large seed size, which ensures that seedlings have sufficient reserves to establish (Westoby *et al.* 1992; Lamont and Groom 1998), although the relative proportions of different nutrients in these seeds has not been determined (Lamont and Groom 1998; Myerscough *et al.* 2000).

+Primary seed dispersal for both species produced a high concentration of seeds adjacent to the adult and an exponential decay of seed density with distance. This pattern is typical of a broad range of other plant species (Janzen 1970; Auld 1986; Willson 1992; Hammill *et al.* 1998). However, Hammill *et al.* (1998) found that seeds from species with canopy seed banks were dispersed at considerably greater distances than found here for *D. excelsa* or *T. speciosissima*. Differences in dispersal distances between our study species and between sites for *T. speciosissima* in this study are probably related to the height of the infructescences and the height and density of the surrounding vegetation (Hammill *et al.* 1998). Infructescences of *D. excelsa* at Site 1 were on average 3.9 m (±0.15 s.e.) tall. For *T. speciosissima* at Site 1, infructescences were relatively shorter at 1.85 m (±0.08 s.e.), while *T. speciosissima* at Site 3 had the shortest infructescences at 0.95 m (±0.08 s.e.). The surrounding vegetation at Site 3 appeared to be denser than at Site 1 and this may have further contributed to the shorter dispersal distances. Dispersal along the ground by wind or water in heavy rains may also have contributed to these dispersal patterns (Harper 1977; Hammill *et al.* 1998). For serotinous species that release seeds shortly after fire, the understorey would be relatively open at the time of seed release, while for *D. excelsa* and *T. speciosissima*, considerable post-fire regrowth would have increased the density of the understorey. This may act to limit seed dispersal in *D. excelsa* and *T. speciosissima*.

+The exclosure experiment indicated that seed losses to mammals and invertebrates occurred in the field (Fig. 2), as has been found for other large-seeded species in similar habitats (e.g. *Banksia* spp., *Isopogon anemonifolius* and *Petrophile pulchella*, Bradstock 1991; *Protea neriifolia*, Botha and Le Maitre 1992; *Grevillea* spp., Auld and Denham 1999, 2001; *Hakea sericea* and *P. pulchella*, R. J. Whelan and J. York*,* unpubl. data). Generally, other studies have found greatly reduced predation in burnt sites (Bradstock 1991; Botha and le Maitre 1992), while R. J. Whelan and J. York (unpubl. data) found that survival of seeds among exclusion treatments was extremely variable among fires and sites. The high level of losses observed in this study is more comparable to that found at unburnt sites (e.g. 100% losses, Bradstock 1991; 75–100% Botha and Le Maitre 1992; 82–95%, Auld and Denham 1999), and to that of recently burnt sites for *Grevillea caleyi* (Auld and Denham 2001). Most seed losses were presumably caused by mammals rather than invertebrates, on the basis of the patterns of seed removal and *in situ* damage. Losses were high for clumped seeds, but generally lower for seeds placed singly, implying that local seed density may affect the ability of seed predators to find

+Reproduction in two pyrogenic flowerers 555

+and subsequently eat seeds. Differences in seed losses between study species at Site 1 for low-density seeds may reflect a difference in palatability of seeds or degree of predator satiation, given the much greater seed production in *D. excelsa* (Table 1). At Site 3 for *T. speciosissima*, losses were high for seeds at high and low densities. While predator satiation may occur in the immediate post-fire period when species with canopy seed banks release seeds, it appears that such effects are less important by the time *D. excelsa* and *T. speciosissima* release seeds. Consequently, if recruitment is not limited by a lack of safe sites, then seed losses to predators are likely to have had an impact on the magnitude of seedling recruitment, particularly for *T. speciosissima* at Site 3.

+Seedling recruitment was observed at all sites, but generally only a small percentage of the seeds released successfully established (≤4%, Table 3). The exception was at Site 1 for *T. speciosissima* where about 14% of all seeds released post-fire were established as seedlings. However, seedling densities by 1998 were comparable between *D. excelsa* and *T. speciosissima* at Site 1 (0.3 per m<sup>2</sup>, Table 3), resulting from the much greater seed production of *D. excelsa* at this site (Table 1). In contrast, for *T. speciosissima* at Site 3, seedling densities were an order of magnitude lower (0.03 per m<sup>2</sup>, Table 3), even though there was no significant difference in seed production to *T. speciosissima* at Site 1.

+The highest levels of seedling recruitment in relation to the available seeds observed here (*T. speciosissima* at Site 1) were comparable to some estimates from local species with canopy seed banks, such as *Banksia serrata* (11–21% over 3 years) and *Isopogon anemonifolius* (6–18%) (Bradstock 1990), and from previous work on *T. speciosissima* (7–9%) (Bradstock 1995), while levels for *D. excelsa* and *T. speciosissima* (Site 3) were lower than those in these previous studies. In terms of individual plant fitness, the number of seedlings per flowering plant was more variable. For *T. speciosissima* at Site 1, the number of seedlings per flowering plant (22.7) was slightly greater than that found by Bradstock (1995) (range 1–9.7), while at Site 3 it was much lower (0.1). For *D. excelsa*, at three plots the number of seedlings per flowering plant (6–16.8) was comparable to that found by Bradstock (1995) for *T. speciosissima*, but at Site 1 plot 1 it was much greater (64.5).

+The impact of low recruitment from one episode of post-fire reproduction depends on the ability of the recruits to survive to fire resistance (primary juvenile phase) and on the ability of the existing adults to survive future fires and produce additional seed crops (Bradstock 1990). Bradstock (1995) showed that less than 25% of *T. speciosissima* seedlings are resistant to fire at 8–10 years old. Further demographic studies should establish the length of the primary juvenile period of these species. Reduction in recruitment levels over the three sampled fruiting seasons in *T. speciosissima* in this study may be explained by variation in seed predation, environmental conditions or the availability of suitable sites for germination and establishment. This decline in the rate of establishment concurs with the accepted wisdom that conditions for recruitment decline with time since fire in these environments (Whelan 1995).

+The distribution of seedlings in this study was not solely influenced by the shape of the seed shadow. There is a pattern for the seeds nearest to adults to have a relatively lower chance of successful establishment as seedlings. This pattern was most evident in *D. excelsa* (Fig. 1 *v*. 5*a*) and *T. speciosissima* at Site 1 (Fig. 1 *v*. 5*b*). Hutchings (1986) suggested that there are a number of factors that determine the final spatial distribution of seedlings, including the behaviour of seed predators and herbivores (Janzen 1970) and the distribution of safe sites, while Schupp and Fuentes (1995) warned that the correspondence of distributions or their lack cannot say much about what determines the ultimate distribution of adults. The distribution of safe sites is affected by competitive influences of adult plants (Sarukhan *et al.* 1985; Hutchings 1986; Crawley 1990; Le Maitre and Midgely 1992; Morgan 1995; Tozer and Bradstock 1997) and possibly allelopathy (Muller *et al.* 1968; Crawley 1986, 1990; Hutchings 1986). For *D. excelsa*, the leaves of adults protrude beyond the basal rosette and may reduce light and rainfall at the soil surface within the first 0.5 m of the rosette. For *T. speciosissima*, the lignotubers of adult plants extend beyond the aerial stems and result in reduced soil depth adjacent to the base of plants. Nevertheless, some seedlings were observed growing from the base of *D. excelsa* and from within the area of the lignotuber of *T. speciosissima*, although these seedlings may not persist. It is also apparent that our estimates of the seed shadow of plants did not detect some seeds that successfully germinated and became recruits well away from potential parents. These rarer, long-distance-dispersed seedlings may have greater significance for the species for colonisation of new habitat or recolonisation after adult mortality (Portnoy and Willson 1993). The distribution patterns observed here may change again after further mortality occurs, especially in relation to survival during future fires.

+In this study, after just one fire, it is apparent that significant recruitment by *D. excelsa* and *T. speciosissima* occurred despite the long time between the fire and the release of seeds into the environment. The strategy of a single or few post-fire flowering events has the advantage that adults of these species may then redirect all their resources to surviving and flowering after the next fire.

+Because of their spectacular inflorescences, some pyrogenic, flowering resprouters are subject to harvesting for the cut-flower market (e.g. *Blandfordia* spp., *D. excelsa*, *Telopea* spp. and *Xanthorrhoea* spp., NSW National Parks and Wildlife 2002). In NSW, south-eastern Australia, despite licensing requirements under the NSW National Parks and Wildlife Act 1987, little is known of the impact of
+<!-- PAGE BREAK -->
+556 A. J. Denham and T. D. Auld

+inflorescence-harvesting on the viability of populations of these species. Where harvesting of inflorescences of *D. excelsa* or *T. speciosissima* occurs in populations in the wild, such harvests may compound the impacts of seed predation and possibly limit seedling recruitment. Such populations may be at risk of decline if subject to excessive harvesting. Studies of other species subject to floral harvesting have indicated excessive harvesting leads to reduced seed production or seed-bank size (e.g. *Banksia hookeriana*, Witkowski *et al.* 1994: *Leucodendron* spp. and *Protea* spp., Mustart and Cowling 1992; Maze and Bond 1996), ultimately reducing the potential for the species to persist (Lamont *et al.* 2001). However, these are all fire-sensitive serotinous species, whose response may be quite different from pyrogenic flowering, resprouting species.

lines: +### **Relationship between Time Since the Last Fire and Flowering in** *Telopea speciosissima* **R. Br. and** *Lambertia formosa* **Sm.**
+*Graham H. Pyke*
+The Australian Museum, 6-8 College St, Sydney, N.S.W., 2000.
+#### *Abstract*

+For *Telopea speciosissima* the percentage (or density) of plants in flower, the average number of flowers per inflorescence and the average number of fruits per inflorescence all appear to peak 2 years after a summer fire and decline thereafter. On the other hand, the average height of the inflorescences above the ground increases with time since the last fire. For *Lambertia formosa* the density of inflorescences appears to reach a peak 2 or 3 years after a summer fire.
+#### **Introduction**

+The effects of fire on the Australian flora are many and are increasingly well studied (see Gill *et al.* 1981). There appears, however, to be little quantitative information on the relationships between time since the last fire and flowering of Australian plants (Gill 1981; Specht 1981). Only for *Xanthorrhoea australis* is there a well established relationship (Specht *et al.* 1958; Garnet 1971; Gill and Ingwersen 1976; Gill 1981): in some places this species flowers only rarely in the absence of fire (Specht *et al.* 1958; Garnet 1971).

+The aim of this paper is to analyse spatial and temporal variation in flowering of *Telopea speciosissima* (waratah) and *Lambertia formosa* with respect to time since the last fire. This analysis is possible as a result of studies on the pollination biology of these plants and the foraging ecology of honeyeaters that visit them for nectar (Pyke 1980, 1981*a*, 1981*b*).
+#### **Methods**

+The data presented were collected between December 1979 and December 1981 in the Brisbane Water National Park (lat. 33°32′22″S., long. 151°16′56″E.; elevation 170 m above sea level) and Ku-ring-gai Chase National Park (lat. 33°36′18″S., long. 151°16′16″E.; elevation 145 m above sea level). In each region, study sites are located in plateau-type, low open-forest (Benson and Fallding 1981) dominated by *Eucalyptus gummifera* (Gaertn.) Hochr., *E. haemastoma* Sm. and *E. oblonga* DC., with a shrub understory composed mainly of *Lambertia formosa* Sm. Both regions are located on plateau tops and hence all study sites have the same aspect. In both regions soils are deep, yellow and earthy (Benson and Fallding 1981) with no apparent differences between the study sites.

+The Brisbane Water study site contains two areas in terms of fire history: one area last burnt in December 1976, the other in December 1979. The two areas are separated by a vehicle trail which stopped the more recent fire from spreading further. There are no apparent differences between the two areas in terms of soil or vegetation. The entire Ku-ring-gai Chase study site last burnt in 1965.

+Flowering in *Telopea speciosissima* has been recorded in two ways. In the 1976 burn study area in Brisbane Water National Park, the total number of flowering plants was recorded for the spring flowering periods of 1979, 1980 and 1981. For each inflorescence
+<!-- PAGE BREAK -->
+294 G. H. Pyke

+the total number of flowers, height above the ground and number of fruits were also recorded. In each year peak flowering occurred about mid September with high synchrony among plants. In this area and in the other two study areas, permanent circular plots of 20 m radius were established and the numbers of flowering plants within these circles counted every 3 weeks during spring 1981. The numbers of non-flowering plants in each circle were also recorded for spring 1981. Flowering in *Lambertia formosa* was recorded by counting the number of inflorescences in each circle during spring 1981 and in two of the present Brisbane Water circles during spring 1980. During spring 1981, there were four circles in the Brisbane Water area of the 1976 fire, two in the area of the 1979 fire and two in the Ku-ring-gai Chase area.
+#### **Results**
+#### *Flowering of* Telopea *in Successive Years*
+In the Brisbane Water area which last burnt in December 1976, the total number of flowering *Telopea* plants has declined dramatically since spring 1979 (Table 1). Since spring
+**Table 1. Flowering of** ***Telopea speciosissima*** **in areas of 1976 and 1979 fires during successive years**
+| Area | Flowering time | Total No. of flowering plants | Mean No. of flowers per inflorescence | Mean inflorescence ht (cm) | Mean No. of fruit per inflorescence |
+| | | Sample size | | | |

+1979 there have also been decreases in the average number of flowers per inflorescence and in the average number of fruit per inflorescence and increases in the average inflorescence height. The differences between 1979 and 1980 are all significant (*P*<0·05, *t*-test); for 1980 and 1981 only the difference in mean inflorescence height is significant (*P*<0·05, *t*-test). During spring 1981 in the circles in the 1979 fire area (see Table 1), the inflorescence height averaged less than for any of the flowering periods in the 1976 fire area (*P*<0·05, *t*-test) while the numbers of flowers and fruits per inflorescence averaged more (*P*<0·05, *t*-test).
+#### *Flowering of* Telopea *in Different Places*

+During spring 1981 the density of flowering plants (i.e. number of flowering plants per circle) and the percentage of plants in flower declined with increases in the time since an area last burnt (Table 2). The differences in the percentage of flowering are significant between the 1979 and 1976 (or 1965) burn areas (*P*<0·05, *t*-test based on Normal approximation to binomial) but not between the 1965 and 1976 burn areas (*P*>0·05, *t*-test based on Normal approximation to binomial).
+#### *Flowering of* Lambertia

+During spring 1981 the peak density of *Lambertia* inflorescences declined with increases in the time since an area last burnt (Table 3). The differences between the areas are significantly different (*P*<0·05 for comparisons between 1979 and 1976 burn areas and between 1976 and 1965 burn areas, *t*-test).
+For two circles in the 1976 burn area, the peak numbers of *Lambertia* inflorescences declined significantly from spring 1980 to spring 1981 (*P*<0·05, *t*-test) (Table 3).
+<!-- PAGE BREAK -->
+Fire and Flowering in *Telopea* and *Lambertia* 295
+#### **Discussion**

+There appear to be strong relationships between flowering and time since the last fire for both *Telopea* and *Lambertia*. In the case of *Telopea*, the percentage (or density) of plants in flower, the average number of flowers per inflorescence and the average number of fruits per inflorescence all peak 2 years after a summer fire and decline thereafter (Tables 1 and 2). On the other hand, the average height of the inflorescences above the ground appears to increase with increases in time since the last fire (Table 1). This undoubtedly reflects the continual growth of the plants, starting from a rhizome, following a fire. The density of *Lambertia* inflorescences reaches a peak 2 or 3 years after a summer fire (Table 3). No information is currently available on either the cause or the adaptive significance of these relationships.
+**Table 2. Flowering of** ***Telopea speciosissima*** **in different areas during spring 1981**

National Parks and Wildlife Service. Two anonymous referees provided many helpful comments on an earlier version of this paper.

1 === p1 2 # **Secondary Succession in Post-fire Scrub Dominated by** *Acacia verticillata* **(L'HCrit.) Willd. at Wilsons Promontory, Victoria** 3 4 *David H. Ash ton and Jennifer A. Chappill* 5 6 School of Botany, University of Melbourne, Parkville, Vic. **3052.** 7 8 #### *Abstract* 9 10 Senescence and death of 30-year-old post-fire *Acacia verticillata* scrub in areas originally supporting sclerophyll eucalypt forest were studied over a 6-year period at Wilsons Promontory, Victoria. The potential for eucalypt regeneration was also examined. On drier sites, *A. verticillata* has been replaced by drought-resistant *Kunzea ambigua* while on wet sites it has been replaced by waterlogging-tolerant *Melaleuca ericifolia.* In mid slopes *A. verticillata* is regenerating from soil seed in gaps in the field layer of *Pteridium esculentum* and *Goodenia ovata* and forming a patchy, uneven-aged stand. The composition of the mid-slope community is determined by the relative resistance of species to browsing and grazing. The failure of eucalypts to reclaim the scrub areas at this critical time has been due to poor seed crops, seed harvesting by ants and intense selective browsing. Exclosure plots have demonstrated the importance of herbivory in modifying this vegetation and indicate potential means of reafforestation without the intervention of fire. 11 12 ### **Introduction** 13 14 In the moist areas of Victoria, large areas of high forest have been converted to scrub of varying height, density and species composition by the fire regimes of the last century (Ashton 1981). Such dramatic changes have been ascribed to the fire sensitivity of the fast growing eucalypt overstorey and its relatively long non-flowering period. Thus, repeated fires at short intervals, even those of low intensity, will kill regeneration before seed has been produced. Alternatively, a similar result will be achieved if severe fires occur at a time of negligible seed storage in the crowns, or if severe drought or intense selective browsing removes or severely damages eucalypt regeneration. 15 16 The total area of potential sclerophyll forest on Wilsons Promontory (Fig. 1) is estimated to be 95 km2 and includes a wide range of structure from dry to wet sclerophyll forest (Ashton 1981; Gill 1981). Much of the present forest is intermediate between these extremes and conforms to the 'damp sclerophyll' type as described by Opie *et al.* (1984). At Wilsons Promontory (Fig. 1) approximately 14% of the tall forests of *Eucalyptus obliqua* L'Htrit., *E. muelleriana* and *E. regnans\** have been destroyed in the last 60 years by numerous fires. 17 18 Only 2.4% of the forested area currently consists of the tall open forest formation with tall and dense understoreys of shrubs, ferns and tree ferns. Of the forested areas converted to scrub, about 68% (9.0 km2) are dominated by *Acacia verticillata* in damp sclerophyll areas and 32% (4.3 km2) is dominated by *Pomaderris aspera, Bedfordia arborescens, Olearia argophylla* and *0. phlogopappa* in the wetter areas. Although 19 === p2 20 **Fig. 1.** The distribution of open forest (10-40 m) and tall open forest (140 m) together with fire-induced scrub at Wilsons Promontory. For simplicity, scrub of wet sclerophyll species (Pornaderris, Bedfordia) has not been distinguished from damp sclerophyll (Acacia verticillata, Coprosma). 21 === p3 22 E. obliqua is usually regarded as relatively fire resistant by virtue of its thick bark, it may be rendered susceptible if bark is depleted by repeated burning. Widespread introgression of this species with the thinner-barked E. regnans has resulted in trees with deciduous bark on the trunk and main branches; hence in many of the wetter sites, *E.* obliqua behaves as a fire-sensitive species (Smith 1970; Ashton 1981). Recent fires in the area (1927, 1939 and 1951) have produced a mosaic pattern of regeneration of the eucalypts and could have led to the development of scrub where the fires overlapped within the early non-flowering stage of the eucalypts, or where eucalypt death occurred at a time of meagre storage of capsules in the canopy, such as has occurred at Tidal River at times during the decade 1975-85. Extremely dense regeneration of *A.* verticillata in Lilly Pilly Gully followed the fires of 1951. Four years later this scrub was 2-3 m tall and virtually impenetrable. The ground stratum was almost devoid of 23 24 **Fig.** 2. The study site spur (L.H.S.) along Lilly Pilly valley looking towards Mt LaTrobe. (a) Dense Acacia verticillata in flower October 1967; *(b)* Same site 1986 when the scrub community had degenerated into a hummocky canopy of Melaleuca, Banksia and Kunzea; (c) Fenced and unfenced plots at commencement of experiment in 1980. 25 26 cover apart from mosses, sparse Viola hederacea, occasional clumps Goodenia ovata and rank Tetrarrhena juncea. After 10 years *A.* verticillata was mature and 4-5 m tall (Fig. 2a), but after 20 years it had begun to senesce (Fig. 2b). Death of stands commenced on the lower slopes and warmer aspects and by 1979-80 most stands were dead (Fig. 2c). The stems of the degenerating acacias were infested with numerous wood boring beetles, including Notoceresium elongata McKeown, Pentarthrium australe McKeown and Menephilus coerulescens Haag. It is possible that these and other insects have been responsible for the hastened decline of this even-aged generation. In 1978, regeneration from soil-stored seed of *A.* verticillata and G. ovata was occurring in open areas between patches of G. ovata, Pteridium esculentum and T. juncea. By 1979, browsing and grazing of vegetation was severe in certain areas due to an abundance of 27 === p4 28 samples. **Fig. 3.** Map of study area from aerial photography showing location of fenced plots and quadrat 29 30 **Fig. 4. (a)** Dendrogram of classification into six groups (I-VI); (b) Ordination of groups (I-VI) indicating the proportion of forest and scrub quadrats in each. The two species with the highest correlation coefficients for axes 1 and **2** are indicated. The dimensions of the third axis are indicated by the size of circle. 31 === p5 32 herbivores such as swamp wallabies (Wallabia bicolor Desmarest), wombats (Vombatus ursinus Shaw) and brushtail possums (Trichosurus vulpecula Kerr). 33 34 On the upper slopes, shrubs of Kunzea ambigua had invaded much of the degenerate scrub, whilst on the lower slopes the dominant, root-suckering species of the swamps, Melaleuca ericifolia, was invading much of the scrub area. The area chosen for detailed study in 1980, showed both these types of replacement. Eucalypt establishment without the intervention of fire in these communities is extremely rare. 35 36 A detailed assessment of the regeneration of the scrub began in 1979 (Chappill 1980) with the aim of predicting the future development of vegetation in these areas. The study site was near Tidal River, adjacent to the Lilly Pilly Gully walking track. The site location and the distribution of vegetation types as determined from aerial photography is indicated in Fig. 3. The study included description of the structure and species composition of the scrub, a field trial examining the possible survival of eucalypt seedlings and a survey of other species regenerating at that time. 37 38 ## **Materials and Methods** 39 40 #### Vegetation Structure and Composition 41 42 Floristic composition was assessed in 1983 by gathering data from 78 quadrats (10 by 2 m) along three transects from the edge of the Tidal River swamp to the *K.* ambigua-dominated scrub on the upper slopes of Mt Bishop. The pattern in these data was revealed with the aid of the computer-based hierarchical agglomerative classification program MACINF with presence and absence data (Lance and Williams 1967) and principal coordinates analysis (PCOA) of the data matrix produced by MACINF. The programs were accessed in the CSIRO TAXON package (Ross 1983). 43 44 Profiles were drawn in three representative areas to display the structure of the vegetation. 45 46 The relative areas occupied by light (<25%), medium (25-75%) and heavy (75-100%) cover classes of the field layer were assessed from intercepts on 16 lines 10 m long on the lower slopes of the degenerate scrub in 1983. 47 48 #### Regeneration of Eucalypts in the Scrub 49 50 An experimental plot 200 m2 was chosen in a homogeneous area of typical degenerate scrub on the lower slopes (Fig. 3). It was divided into four 10 by 5 m subplots, two of which were fenced with 4 cm wire-mesh netting to a height of I m. The fences excluded wallabies and wombats but not possums. Seventy-two seedlings of each of the three eucalypt species which grow nearby, i. e. E. obliqua and E. muelleriana\* in the moister areas and E. baxteri in the drier areas, were planted in December 1979 in **a** random block design in three cover classes of vegetation: natural vegetation, vegetation clipped to 15 cm height in a radius of 15 cm around the seedlings and areas completely cleared of vegetation to a radius of 15 cm around the seedlings. At each spot the seedlings were assigned randomly at three points of a triangle, 10 cm apart. This resulted in 12 replications of each treatment and species combination. Seedlings were first measured on 31 / 12/ 1979 and the changes in height, growth and survival were recorded at approximately monthly intervals until mid September 1980, and then at approximately yearly intervals until 1986. 51 52 Additional plantings were made of E. obliqua seedlings 1-1.5 m tall in the dense vegetation surrounding the experimental plots to determine whether larger plants would be better able to establish in the scrub. Seeds of the three eucalypts were sown separately in 10 small microsites of disturbed soil 30 cm in diameter outside the plots, to evaluate the level of predation by insects or mammals on very young stages and the success of germination. All seed was lightly covered by soil, as it had been shown by **A.** N. Andersen (personal communication) in nearby sites that insect predation by, for example, the ants Rhytidoponera victoreae Andre and Chelaner sculpturatus Clark. could account for losses of 33-8390 of the seed placed on the soil surface within 2 weeks. 53 54 #### Regeneration of A. verticillata and Other Species in the Scrub 55 56 A number of *A.* verticillata seedlings in the fenced and unfenced plots of the eucalypt field trial was \*Seed of E. obliqua and E. muelleriana was obtained from similar environments at Neerim and Yarram respectively, owing to a lack of seed at Wilsons Promontory in 1979. 57 === p6 58 **Table 1. As the seedlings were not of a uniform age at the first measurement, the percentage increase in height from the first measurement rather than mean heights was calculated. 63 64 The vegetation cover and density in the fenced and unfenced plots was assessed by vertical point quadrats using pins 1.5 mm diameter and 2 m tall. These analyses were repeated at 1-2 year intervals from 1980 until 1986. The density of the major shrub species was also assessed outside the plots by counting numbers of individuals in 16 10 by 2 m quadrats in the lower mid-slope area in 1982 and 1983. 65 66 In early January 1980, five plots in the scrub, each 1 m2, were cleared of vegetation and litter with minimal disturbance to the topsoil. In June, July and September of the same year the identifiable seedlings in a central square, 30 by 30 cm, were counted and removed. In early February, soil was collected from 10 random plots in the same community for examination of seed germination under more favourable conditions of moisture and protection in seed trays placed in the open on a rooftop at the University of Melbourne. Three depths of soil were sampled; 0-1 cm, 1-2 cm and 2-3 cm. The soil was sieved and spread to a depth of 1 cm over sterile coarse sand in seed trays 28 by 32 cm. === p1 # **Secondary Succession in Post-fire Scrub Dominated by** *Acacia verticillata* **(L'HCrit.) Willd. at Wilsons Promontory, Victoria** *David H. Ash ton and Jennifer A. Chappill* School of Botany, University of Melbourne, Parkville, Vic. **3052.** #### *Abstract* Senescence and death of 30-year-old post-fire *Acacia verticillata* scrub in areas originally supporting sclerophyll eucalypt forest were studied over a 6-year period at Wilsons Promontory, Victoria. The potential for eucalypt regeneration was also examined. On drier sites, *A. verticillata* has been replaced by drought-resistant *Kunzea ambigua* while on wet sites it has been replaced by waterlogging-tolerant *Melaleuca ericifolia.* In mid slopes *A. verticillata* is regenerating from soil seed in gaps in the field layer of *Pteridium esculentum* and *Goodenia ovata* and forming a patchy, uneven-aged stand. The composition of the mid-slope community is determined by the relative resistance of species to browsing and grazing. The failure of eucalypts to reclaim the scrub areas at this critical time has been due to poor seed crops, seed harvesting by ants and intense selective browsing. Exclosure plots have demonstrated the importance of herbivory in modifying this vegetation and indicate potential means of reafforestation without the intervention of fire. ### **Introduction** In the moist areas of Victoria, large areas of high forest have been converted to scrub of varying height, density and species composition by the fire regimes of the last century (Ashton 1981). Such dramatic changes have been ascribed to the fire sensitivity of the fast growing eucalypt overstorey and its relatively long non-flowering period. Thus, repeated fires at short intervals, even those of low intensity, will kill regeneration before seed has been produced. Alternatively, a similar result will be achieved if severe fires occur at a time of negligible seed storage in the crowns, or if severe drought or intense selective browsing removes or severely damages eucalypt regeneration. The total area of potential sclerophyll forest on Wilsons Promontory (Fig. 1) is estimated to be 95 km2 and includes a wide range of structure from dry to wet sclerophyll forest (Ashton 1981; Gill 1981). Much of the present forest is intermediate between these extremes and conforms to the 'damp sclerophyll' type as described by Opie *et al.* (1984). At Wilsons Promontory (Fig. 1) approximately 14% of the tall forests of *Eucalyptus obliqua* L'Htrit., *E. muelleriana* and *E. regnans\** have been destroyed in the last 60 years by numerous fires. Only 2.4% of the forested area currently consists of the tall open forest formation with tall and dense understoreys of shrubs, ferns and tree ferns. Of the forested areas converted to scrub, about 68% (9.0 km2) are dominated by *Acacia verticillata* in damp sclerophyll areas and 32% (4.3 km2) is dominated by *Pomaderris aspera, Bedfordia arborescens, Olearia argophylla* and *0. phlogopappa* in the wetter areas. Recent fires in the area (1927, 1939 and 1951) have produced a mosaic pattern of regeneration of the eucalypts and could have led to the development of scrub where the fires overlapped within the early non-flowering stage of the eucalypts, or where eucalypt death occurred at a time of meagre storage of capsules in the canopy, such as has occurred at Tidal River at times during the decade 1975-85. === p10 the data of all microhabitats because of the low survival in the lighter cover classes. Two-way analyses of variance were performed after logarithmic transformation of each set of measurements. No significant differences between species were observed. However, in 1986 the tallest of the dominant-crowned individuals of E. *muelleriana* (400 cm) far exceeded the tallest E. *obliqua* (256 cm) and E. *baxteri* (285 cm). A longer-term study may show that E. *muelleriana* will come to dominate the site in future years. The effect of the fencing treatment was significant by April 1980, when all species showed greater height growth (at P = 0.05) in the fenced than unfenced plots. Height growth of the eucalypt species in the fenced plots increased markedly in the second and third years, in spite of the severe drought of 1982 (Fig. 8). The difference in survival between different species of eucalypt during the 6 years of the study were marked. E. *muelleriana* showed consistently higher survival rates than the other species after the first year and E. *obliqua* had the fewest seedlings surviving. After 12 months, only about 20% of the unfenced plants had survived, and after 2 years one plant of *E, muelleriana* remained, and that specimen remained only for an **Fig. 9.** Percentage survival of all eucalypts in fenced and unfenced plots 1980-86. additional few months. The survival of plants in the fenced plots declined steadily to about 20% over the ensuing 3 years. The pooled data for all species in fenced and unfenced plots are shown in Fig. 9. E. *obliqua* was more severely attacked by groups of sawfly larvae than the other species, and E. *muelleriana* maintained large and horizontally displayed juvenile foliage for at least the second growing season. The fate of large eucalypt seedlings planted at random in thick scrub and ground stratum in the mid-slope area indicated that plants 1-2 m tall could be located, pulled down and severely browsed, most probably by wallabies. After 3 years, all plants had been destroyed, even those in thick regrowth of M. *ericifolia* and *G. ovata.* The last surviving plant, 2 m tall in 1985, had disappeared without trace 1 year later. Seeds of the three eucalypt species sown outside fences in mid to late autumn, germinated within 2 weeks and reached the 2-leaf stage and heights of 2-8 cm by the following spring. By December, browsing was evident in four out of 21 plants. By the following autumn all plants had disappeared. === p11 # *Regeneration of* A, verticillata *and Other Species in the Scrub* The development of the ground stratum in response to the exclusion of the larger herbivores from the fenced areas was dramatic (Table 2). The most conspicuous effect in the first 2 years was the increase in cover and height of the scrambling grass, T. *juncea* and the raspwort, *Gonocarpus teucrioides.* Both of these species declined sharply during the drought year of 1982 and only the former recovered its prior vigour (Fig. 10). P. *esculentum* behaved similarly to T. *juncea,* but *G. ovata* declined steadily as its associates increased. The cover repetition of species sensitive to browsing tended to be higher in the fenced plots, although *Coprosma quadrifida* did not conform, due to its development of compact, intricate spiny branches under heavy browsing (Table 2). Species diversity was greater in the fenced plots (26 species) than the unfenced plots (20 species). In 1986 the increasing cover of eucalypts in the fenced plots appears to have reduced the vigour of the field layer. In the unfenced plots T. *juncea* decreased markedly, probably as a result of wombat grazing. The field layer, therefore, became increasingly dominated by non-grazed P. *esculentum* and *G. ovata* and with scattered spiny bushes of C. *quadrifida* and *A. verticillata.* K. *ambigua* and *M. ericifolia* which are increasing in density in these areas are scarcely browsed, although occasionally killed by woodboring insects on the lower stems. The density of natural regeneration of the major woody species in the mid-slope area of the scrub in 1982 and 1983 is shown in Table 3. M. *ericifolia* is regenerating vigorously from root suckers and A. *verticillata* is also regenerating well from soil-stored seed. The later species flowered and set seed abundantly in 1984 and thus further replenishment of the soil seed bank is likely to have occurred in 1985. The reduction of height and density of A. *verticillata* in the presence of browsing was evident in 1986. The observed germination of soil-stored seed in the field and in seed trays is given in Table 4. The number of seedlings germinating from the seed trays was greatest from the upper 1 cm sample, but the species composition was similar for each depth; therefore, the results were pooled and adjusted to show numbers of germinated seedlings per square metre of soil to a depth of 3 cm. Most species showed greater germination in the trays than in the field, with the exception of *Hydrocotyle hirta* and *V. hederacea.* Some species such as *Bulbine bulbosa, Calystegia marginata* and *Schoenus apogon* appeared in the trays but were not observed in the natural vegetation. The notable absence of T. *juncea,* may be due to heavy grazing preventing normal flowering, since this species is normally present as soil seed in wet forests in central Victoria (Ashwell 1981). The species subject to grazing and browsing are indicated in Table 5. Scat analysis indicates that black-tailed wallabies and the common wombat are the major herbivores and differ in their relative abundance along the topographic gradient. This will affect the proportion of grazing and browsing in different sites. Brushtail possums were present, and may have been responsible for minor browsing of eucalypt seedlings in 1980 within the fenced plots. Hog deer *(Axis porcinus)* are present in the area but do not appear to be as important as the marsupials at this time. It is clear that the species which are most successful in the regeneration in this area have means of resistance to grazing pressure. Thus, both C. *quadr\$da* and *A, verticillata* are protected to some extent by spines, whilst G. *ovata,* K. *ambigua* and *M. ericifolia* appear to be unpalatable to the mammals in the area, although insect attack may occur. In many places it is evident that the greatest amount of damage occurred in the vicinity of animal runs and in more open spaces between the denser vegetation. Dicotyledonous herbs, such as V. *hederacea, Stellaria flaccida* and *G. teucrioides* were severely grazed, but P. *esculentum* and *G. ovata* were conspicuously undamaged, although minor insect attack was evident. === p12 === p13 === p14 The effects of herbivore exclusion are complex, due to relative growth and competition of existing species. Thus, the demise of G. *teucrioides* in 1985-86 in fenced plots may have been due to competition. Diversity was initially higher in the fenced plots in the early stages of exclusion, but the number of species declined as the density of the more vigorous species increased. **Fig. 10.** Cover values of major understorey species in fenced and unfenced plots 1980-86. **Table 3. ## **Discussion** Purdie and Slatyer (1976) have pointed out that a single model of secondary succession is unlikely to describe adequately a given sere, and this is true for the post-fire scrubs at Wilsons Promontory. The development of sclerophyll open forests is the product of site quality and fire regime (Gill 1975). In the scrub areas the normal postfire succession has been altered by the removal of the *Eucalyptus* overstorey component in the last 100 years by a regime of frequent, severe fires associated with European settlement (King 1963). === p15 **Table 4. Density of soil seed germination from scrub (Acacia-Kunzea-Melaleuca) in lower slope sites compared to frequency of species in the vegetation in 15 plots 10 by 1 m** \*~ermination in five bare soil plots (30 by 10 cm) January to September 1980. B~ermination from 10 trays (30 by 10 cm to depth 3 cm) February to July 1980. The early stages of post-fire succession are strongly influenced by the composition of the previous vegetation or by its legacy of soil-stored seed. In this sense the succession is of the 'initial floristic composition' type of Egler (1954). Of the species present in the study area, 13% recover vegetatively from trunk buds, root stock or root suckers and 70% regenerate from seed, most of which is present in the soil seed bank. The relative density of seedlings and root suckers is shown in Table **3.** The invasion of the senescent === p16 *A. verticillata* stage by other shrubs suggests that in the local extremes of the habitat range, the succession conforms to the 'tolerance' model of Connell and Slatyer (1977). Thus, during the maturation of the dominant A. *verticillata* generation the upper slopes were invaded by the drought-resistant shrub K. *ambigua,* possibly by wind dispersal from fire-protected rocky outcrops. On the lowermost slopes M. *ericifolia* had regenerated by means of both root suckers and seedlings and had developed a distinct under- Table 5. storey. Therefore, with the onset of senescence and death of A. *verticillata,* the vegetation of the drier sites was rapidly dominated by K. *ambigua* and that of the wetter sites by tall M. *ericifolia.* In terms of dynamics, the mid and lower slopes represent a relatively stable stage since *A. verticillata* is regenerating; however, much will depend on the growth, toler === p17 ance and longevity of other dominants such as B. *marginata,* C. *quadrifida, K. ambigua* and *M. ericifolia.* The successfully regenerating species are either unpalatable or spiny at shoot maturity. The importance of the soil seed bank and the ability of species to avoid the sensitive seedling stage by vegetative spread is clearly seen in the potentially dense field and ground strata of this vegetation. In this area the scattered individuals of *A. verticillata* flowered after 5 years, thus restoring to some extent the soil seed bank of this species. The mid-slope areas show the greatest diversity both structurally and floristically. import sys, zlib, struct
src, dst = sys.argv[1], sys.argv[2]
x0, y0, x1, y1 = map(int, sys.argv[3:7])

crop = [row[x0:x1] for row in rows[y0:y1]]
cw, ch = x1 - x0, y1 - y0
# rotate clockwise: new width = ch, new height = cw; new[r][c] = old[ch-1-c][r]
rot = [bytes(crop[ch - 1 - c][r] for c in range(ch)) for r in range(cw)]
raw = b"".join(b"\x00" + row for row in rot)
def chunk(t, data): return struct.pack(">I", len(data)) + t + data + struct.pack(">I", zlib.crc32(t + data) & 0xffffffff)
png = b"\x89PNG\r\n\x1a\n" + chunk(b"IHDR", struct.pack(">IIBBBBB", ch, cw, 8, 0, 0, 0, 0)) + chunk(b"IDAT", zlib.compress(raw, 6)) + chunk(b"IEND", b"")

../bt9890001/b2.md:11:The observed germination of soil-stored seed in the field and in seed trays is given in Table 4. 26	## Summary
27	
28	 1 Banksia hookeriana is a serotinous nonsprouting shrub restricted to the fire-prone northern sandplain scrub-heaths of Western Australia. Evidence of the natural fire frequency to which the species is best adapted was sought through analysis of its seed demography using a computer model of canopy seed bank dynamics based on field data.
29	
30	 2 Plants began flowering at 3-4 years of age but storage of viable seeds in the canopy was rare for plants < 5 years. Infructescences (cones) contained a mean of 12 follicles, holding two seeds of which 62% were estimated to be viable.
31	
32	 3 Cone (and seed) production increased with plant age to 15 years, but then fluctuated widely around a mean of 17 cones per year. By this time the average plant had an estimated canopy seed bank of 700 viable seeds comprising seeds 1-10 years old.
33	
34	 4 Seeds were lost from the canopy seed bank through spontaneous follicle rupture (i.e. in the absence of fire), granivory by insect larvae, and decay. Most follicles remained closed for at least 5 years and up to 50% of follicles were still closed after 10 years. Insect granivores destroyed 18% of seeds in 1-year-old cones, and continued to destroy seeds in older cones at a rate of 2-3% per year.
35	
36	 5 The seed bank model predicted continued seed accumulation in the canopy to at least age 25 years (1400 seeds), but by this time more viable seeds (1 2200) had been lost to spontaneous opening, granivory and decay than were then stored on the plant. 6 Shannon-Weiner diversity (H') of seed ages in the canopy seed bank increased with plant age, while evenness (V') decreased at first (to plant age 17 years) and then increased.
37	
38	 7 On a time-scale of many generations, the likelihood of successful recruitment of individuals in the next generation (on average), occurs for a fire frequency of 15-18 years. At this frequency resource wastage in this low-nutrient environment would be minimized.
39	
40	 8 Recent fires have recurred within 7-11 years and indicate a human impact on the natural fire regime which may ultimately threaten the species.
